creator: reshamas
title: Add alt text to scikit-learn documentation
text:
## Describe the issue linked to the documentation
Adding alt text to images permits visually impaired users to have greater access.

## Suggest a potential alternative/fix

## About [Alt Text](https://moz.com/learn/seo/alt-text)

Alt text (alternative text), also known as "alt attributes," “alt descriptions," or technically incorrectly as "alt tags,” are used within an HTML code to describe the appearance and function of an image on a page.

Alt text uses:
1. Adding alternative text to photos is first and foremost a principle of web accessibility. Visually impaired users using screen readers will be read an alt attribute to better understand an on-page image.

2. Alt text will be displayed in place of an image if an image file cannot be loaded.

3. Alt text provide better image context/descriptions to search engine crawlers, helping them to index an image properly.


## Reference
- https://github.com/isabela-pf/scikit-learn/pull/1
- [Chartability](https://chartability.fizz.studio)
- [Meetup event](https://www.meetup.com/PyLadies-SWFL/events/280761048/) PyLadies SWFL & Miami, Python SWFL
  - Event Video:  [Make open source accessible: Isabela Presedo-Floyd and Mars Lee](https://youtu.be/dDpimPYOKuc) 

## Questions
1.  For scikit-learn, what is the maximum line length for writing alt text descriptions for images?
2. Is there a way to do a `grep` of the library and see how many images exist in the documentation?
3. Can you confirm that the images are static?  They are produced from code, within the documentation.  Are images always the same that are produced?

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment:
Images are not always the same. They change when an underlying model or method used to generate the data on the image changes. But they mostly stay the same.

Maximum line length would be the same as other places in the code, i.e. 88

I think this would be a nice improvement.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
> Images are not always the same. They change when an underlying model or method used to generate the data on the image changes. But they mostly stay the same.

During code review, we need to keep in mind that the alt text needs to be updated if the image changes. I agree most of the time the images are the same.

Another concern is if alt text increases the barrier of entry. If a contributor is at a point of adding a new image, then it should not be too difficult to describe it. I think the hard part would be "What makes a good alt text", but that can be improved over time.

Overall, I think having alt text is a net improvement.

events.author: reshamas
events.comment:
We were discussing this challenge last night, with @isabela-pf, @MarsBarLee, @InessaPawson, and others.
- How descriptive should we be?
- How much domain knowledge should be relevant?
- Is it better to describe the shapes, or the interpretation of the graph?
- Who is the audience? Is it a subject matter expert on that topic, or someone who is objectively looking at a visualization for first time, without specific context? 

### Example 1
This is my description of a heat map; it assumes the user knows what a heat map is. 
>The graph is a square heat map, 5x5, with axes from 0 to 250. The darkest 5 squares of heat map run diagonally from top left to bottom right.

### Example 2
Here is another commit describing clustering.
>Three distinct clusters created using affinity propagation.

We are curious to see how the core-devs review these alt text descriptions and if it's in agreement with your primary interpretation of the visualizations.

events.author: reshamas
events.comment: Also, this is for the next phase.  Are the colors currently used in creating visualizations color-blind friendly?

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
> Also, this is for the next phase. Are the colors currently used in creating visualizations color-blind friendly?

There has been work to updated our visualizations to be color-blind friendly: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/5435 (The issue links to PRs that update visualizations)

events.author: reshamas
events.comment:
> > Also, this is for the next phase. Are the colors currently used in creating visualizations color-blind friendly?
> 
> There has been work to updated our visualizations to be color-blind friendly: #5435

I think in addition to color specs for, say line plots, line types (dash, dotted) can also be considered.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
In recent versions of sphinx-gallery the example thumbnails should now come with the title of the figure as alt-text:

https://github.com/sphinx-gallery/sphinx-gallery/pull/668

This is better than nothing but not necessarily the best text description of the content of the image. In the context of the examples given in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/21214#issuecomment-932432430 this should match approximately example 2, that is, give a high level interpretation of the content of the figure but not necessarily describe enough the actual content of the plot.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: BTW sorry @lucyleeow for not giving you feedback on that PR, I missed the notification...

events.author: lucyleeow
events.comment: No worries, I'm sure you get many notifications!

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
For instance for:

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/cluster/plot_kmeans_plusplus.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-cluster-plot-kmeans-plusplus-py

The alt text is "K-Means++ Initialization" but it does not describe the actual content enough to draw the intented conclusions from the figure for the visually impaired. A more extensive description could be "Scatter plot with 4 well separated groups of data points in a 2D space. In each group of points, a candidate point has been selected as initial centroid by k-means++. While not lying at the center of the groups, the candidates found by k-means++ span all groups yielding a reasonably robust initialization for k-means on this data.". But then if we go deeper in this kind of analysis, maybe this should be in the text of the example to be visible by anybody, not just people reading the alt-text contents.

In particular I am not sure about how long should the alt-text be in general. I would suspect that one sentence would be good in many cases but maybe it can be helpful to write a small paragraph to highlight the interesting aspects of the figure that are not already stated in the surrounding text.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
Note: that some (many?) examples have plots without title which means that there is no meaningful alt text for the gallery thumbnails of those examples. Adding missing titles to would help both people who read the alt-text and people who "read" the image itself.

Also: when an image generated by an example is manually reused to illustrate a paragraph the user guide, the title of the plot (if present) is not automatically reused in the user guide figure in that case (instead the filename is used which is not very helpful). See for instance the first image on this page:

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/_sources/modules/clustering.rst.txt

events.author: reshamas
events.comment:
It seems like there is a lot of work that can be done here:  
1.  Add titles to visualizations where they are missing.
2. Add (more verbose) descriptions / interpretations to visualizations which will be accessible to all users.
3. Add (brief) visualization descriptions/interpretations to alt text.

events.author: lucyleeow
events.comment: I think 2 & 3 may require added functionality to Sphinx Gallery? Let me know if you have something in mind, I am happy to add the functionality or have a think about how to allow this.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
As I understand it, 2 is about improving the content of the examples themselves to make sure that the conclusions drawn from the plots in the main text of the example are made explicit enough to be understandable in the context of either watching the graphical plot itself or only the alt-text alone.  So no change required in sphinx-gallery.

3 is primarily about adding alt-text (not necessarily based on the title of the figure), to the alt attribute of the `figure` sphinx directives in the restructured text in sections of the user guide (outside of the gallery). This could be done manually.

For the figures directly displayed in the rendering of the sphinx gallery itself, it could be interesting to add the possibility to write longer alt-text independently from the title of the figure.

```python
...

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 100)
plt.plot(x, x ** 2)
plt.title("Quadratic function")
# alt-text: A symmetric parabolic curve with a minimum at zero that represents
# a 1d quadratic function

...
```

Maybe sphinx-gallery could also provide a new sphinx directive to make it easy to insert a figure in the main text of the documentation from an image generated by the gallery that would automatically reuse the accompanying alt-text (either from the matplotlib figure title or from a structured Python comment).

It would also probably be useful to add an option in sphinx-gallery to report the list of examples with figures that lack a title, maybe via warnings that could be enabled or disabled in the sphinx configuration file for instance.

events.author: isabela-pf
events.comment:
I'm here to respond to some of the thoughts listed above. I'm always happy to see an active discussion around these topics as we have a lot less resources to draw from when it comes to writing alt text for scientific diagrams specifically.

>Images are not always the same. They change when an underlying model or method used to generate the data on the image changes. But they mostly stay the same.

Responding to @adrinjalali, this is good to know! We had a few contributors to the [alt text mini sprint](https://www.meetup.com/PyLadies-SWFL/events/280761048/) mention the same thing when we were talking. 

A key part of writing helpful alt text is understanding the role and information an image provides in its surrounding context. This means that the same image used in different places might benefit from different alt text depending what it's meant to illustrate in that instance. Or, in the case that you are talking about, plots with differing content may be perfectly fine with the same alt text if they still serve the same role in the documentation. 

I'm not personally a user of scikit-learn (or anything similar), but when I was reading the docs my understanding is that many of the images are examples of a process described in the preceding paragraph. The images aren't usually adding new information (like a step-by-step guide on how to use the process) or relying on the reader to understand each point on the plot. So unless the type of plot or its axes are changing, I think this might be a less critical problem for this project.

(I had a similar discussion with people about [variable content in the numpy-tutorials repo](https://github.com/numpy/numpy-tutorials/pull/100#discussion_r688370952) when we worked on alt text there.)

>Another concern is if alt text increases the barrier of entry. If a contributor is at a point of adding a new image, then it should not be too difficult to describe it. I think the hard part would be "What makes a good alt text", but that can be improved over time.

Responding to @thomasjpfan, I agree on the making it easy for contributors. Some description is better than none (none usually just reads the name of the image), so if I were to one reviewing PRs I'd be looking for a non-empty alt attribute as the baseline.

As for "what makes good alt text," I have some resources that might help. The main resource I've found for plots (with the help of @marsbarlee) is [the Diagram center's checklist](http://diagramcenter.org/specific-guidelines-g.html#71) which asks for type of graph, axes, and points. Personally, I've found that we are usually dealing with far too many points to reasonably list out in the alt attribute, so I take this as a chance to describe the trend of the plot or any other defining features relevant to the text that surrounds it.

I also put together [a guide collecting resources and guidelines for different types of images](https://github.com/Quansight-Labs/jupyter-accessibility-workshops/blob/fd1d7f96ca40943eda050a339ba64bcf16dd638a/docs/alt-text-guide.md) that we've used to help people new to alt text  ignoring the few Jupyter-specific bits). 

And this is the checklist we used during the alt text mini-sprint:
```
The alt text has
- [ ] Correct spelling and no typos
- [ ] Periods and commas where relevant
- [ ] No more than three short, complete sentences
- [ ] A logical way of fitting in the rest of the documentation
- [ ] Consistent text and/or descriptions for the same elements in different images
- [ ] A description of any text in the image
```

I hope that helps! Let me know if you have any other questions or there's other ways I can help.

creator: bwegge
title: Support `dualtree=True` (or other kwargs) in `NearestNeighbors.kneighbors()`
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

`BallTree` and `KDTree` support `dualtree=True` (and other keyword arguments, such as `breadth_first`) in their `.query()` method which can provide significant speedups in some use cases. However, they do not provide out-of-the-box parallel processing support. On the other hand, the generic `NearestNeighbors` class supports parallel processing with `n_jobs>1`, but its `.kneighbors()` method seems to never call the underlying (KD- or ball-) tree with dualtree enabled.

So currently, we can either
- use  `NearestNeighbors` which supports parallel processing but not dualtree, or we can
- use `BallTree` or `KDTree` directly for dualtree support but without parallel processing,

but not enjoy both performance improvements at the same time.


### Describe your proposed solution

A quick solution would be to add the `dualtree` (and `breadth_first`) parameter (or more generically, a `**kwargs` argument) to `NearestNeighbors.kneighbors()` and pass that through to the underlying `tree.query()` function.
In fact, according to https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/neighbors/_base.py, it may be sufficient to pass it through to `_tree_query_parallel_helper()`, which already supports keyword arguments and passes them on to the `.query()` method of the tree.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

title: CountVectorizer(lowercase=True,strip_accents='unicode') may produce vocab that contains uppercase chars
text:
### Describe the bug

Some characters are transformed to uppercase chars (eg ™ -> TM), despite lowercase=True.
This then gives warning messages "UserWarning: Upper case characters found in vocabulary while 'lowercase' is True"
(OK, there are worse things happening in the world ;-). Thanks for scikit-learn)

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
x = ['This is Problematic™.','THIS IS NOT']

cv = CountVectorizer(
    lowercase=True,
    strip_accents='unicode',
    ngram_range=(1,1)
    )

x_v = cv.fit_transform(x)

from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
y = [1,0]

clf = LinearSVC(random_state=42).fit(x_v, y)
```

events.comment:
This comes down to the order we preprocess text in `CountVectorizer`:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/23afd5d95c18915c55070cecaecf9f3030ae9bbb/sklearn/feature_extraction/text.py#L70-L74

The accent function is applied after the `lower`. I see a two ways forward:

creator: lorentzenchr
title: FEA Add variable importance to linear models
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd like to have a feature importance method native to linear models (without L1 penalty) that is calculated on the training set:
```python
clf = LogisticRegression(with_importance=True)
clf.fit(X, y)
clf.feature_importances_  # or some nice plot thereof
```

### Describe your proposed solution
#### New proposal
Evaluate if the LMG (Lindeman,  Merenda  and  Gold, see [1, 2]) is applicable and feasible for L2 penalized regression and for GLMs. Else, consider other measures of [1, 2].

In short, LMG is Shapley value decomposition of R2 by the features.

**References:**
- [1] R package [relaimpo](https://cran.r-project.org/package=relaimpo) with JSS paper [U. Grömping (2006). Relative Importance for Linear Regression in R: The Package relaimpo](http://www.jstatsoft.org/v17/i01)
- [2] [U. Grömping (2016). Variable importance in regression models](https://prof.bht-berlin.de/fileadmin/prof/groemp/downloads/Gr%c3%b6mping2015_WiresCS_AcceptedVersion.pdf)

#### Original proposal
Compute the t-statistic of the coefficients
```
t[j] = coef[j] / std(coef[j])
```
and use the absolute, i.e. `|t|`, as measure of (in-sample)  importance. For GLMs like the logistic regression, see section 5.3 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.09169.pdf for a formula of `Var[coef]`.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Any general importance measure (permutation importance, SHAP values, ...) also works.

### Additional context

Given the great and legitimate need for interpretability, I would favor to have a native importance measure for linear models. Random Forests have their own native `feature_importances_` with the warning
> impurity-based feature importances can be misleading for high cardinality features (many unique values).

We could add a similar warning for collinear features like
> feature importances can be misleading for collinear or high-dimensional features.

I guess, in the end, this is true for all feature importance measures, even for SHAP (see also our [multicollinear example](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/inspection/plot_permutation_importance_multicollinear.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-inspection-plot-permutation-importance-multicollinear-py)).

Prior discussions like #16802, #6773,  #13048, focued on p-values which seem out-of-scope for scikit-learn for different reasons. I hope we can circumvent these reasons by focusing on feature importance only and not considering p-values.

I think that this is a very slippery slope: t-statistics are not well controlled outside of maximum-likelihood estimates.

Either people know what they are doing, and it's trivial to compute the above, or they don't, and they will misinterpret it (that's true of much of the model interpretation literature, that's been going around in circles for years because it is trying to give simple answers to problems that do not have a good solution in statistics).

I'm -1 on this line

events.author: lorentzenchr
glemaitre
events.comment:
By reusing the analysis that we did with the tree-based models, it seems that we had an understanding that there is no single good feature importance but rather feature importance methods that have some pros and cons. I assume that the same thing can be said about linear models, e.g. permutation importance vs. weights importance.

Adding a default `feature_importance_` to the linear models means that, by default, we legitimate a single method. I am not sure that this is the right thing to do since this is somehow what we would like to run away from in tree-based models.

So there is probably a choice of API to think about: use native importance vs. use helper functions to compute the importance. If we want to avoid legitimate a particular feature importance, each model should provide a parameter/a method to compute a specific type of importance. However, we would still have some default feature importance. In the case, that we use helper functions, the choice of the importance will be user-specified. The issue, in this case, will be the integration with estimators that relied on `coef_` and `feature_importances_` attributes, e.g. feature selector estimators. I think that we can make some machinery such that the methods can take a model and a feature importance functions.

For instance we could provide a utility function to compute "feature effects" for linear models to decompose the decision function for individual predictions as follows:

creator: jonaslandsgesell
title: Feature request: confusion matrix could report confidence intervals
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Motivation: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.11105.pdf

The values reported for the TP, FN, FP, TN rates are only estimates having an uncertainty.
It would be great if sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix could also return the estimates for the uncertainty (this is especially important for small numbers of classifications).

I guess as a start it would be enough to provide a confidence interval using the normal approximation or the F distribution, see "Exact Binomial Confidence Interval
for Proportions" Jeffrey T. Morisette and Siamak Khorram  https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Jeffrey-Morisette-2/publication/255630317_Exact_Binomial_Confidence_Interval_for_Proportions/links/5601ba7708aecb0ce881aea9/Exact-Binomial-Confidence-Interval-for-Proportions.pdf 

The confidence intervals would help to assess the quality of a classifier.

### Describe your proposed solution

sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix could optionally return a matrix with the (half width?) of the (potentially) asymmetric confidence intervals. Potentially, the 95% confidence level would be a good default.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

The user could bootstrap confidence intervals on his own via bootstrapping the standard error.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import bernoulli
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

#generate random examples for computing the confusion matrix
p=0.5
y_true = bernoulli.rvs(p, size=100)
y_pred = bernoulli.rvs(p, size=100)
cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, normalize = "true")
print("non-bootsrapped confidence matrix", cm)

data = np.vstack((y_true,y_pred)).T
def bootstrap(data, statistic, boostrap_size, num_boostrap_samples=1000):
    indices=range(len(data))
    confusion_matrices=[]
    for i in range(num_boostrap_samples):
        choice= np.random.choice(indices, size = boostrap_size, replace = True)
        y_true = data[choice,0]
        y_pred = data[choice,1]
        cm = statistic(y_true, y_pred, normalize = "true")
        confusion_matrices.append(cm)
    return np.average(confusion_matrices, axis = 0), np.std(confusion_matrices, axis = 0)
cm, standard_error_of_confidence_matrix= bootstrap(data, confusion_matrix, boostrap_size= len(data))
    
print("bootsrapped confidence matrix", cm)
print("bootsrapped standard error of confidence matrix", standard_error_of_confidence_matrix)
```

which outputs for 
```
non-bootsrapped confidence matrix 
[[0.53488372 0.46511628]
 [0.43859649 0.56140351]]
bootsrapped confidence matrix
 [[0.53863312 0.46136688]
 [0.44174818 0.55825182]]
bootsrapped standard error of confidence matrix 
[[0.07670171 0.07670171]
 [0.0663557  0.0663557 ]]
```
### Additional context

_No response_

title: Possibly biased KNeighborsClassifier for ties
text:
### Describe the bug

Hello team scikit-learn,

On investigating `KNeighborsClassifier` it seems that for an even number of neighbors, in case of a tie, the classifier incorrectly assigns a label to the outcome with a lower numerical value.

i.e. for a binary classification problem, if the labels are `0,1`, in case of tie, the `sklearn` implementation always returns `0`.
Since choice of labels is arbitrary, this indicates a bias in prediction. 
We ran a simple test by flipping the labels, and saw that the model's predicted accuracy changes quite a bit for the even neighbors case. (code below).

We believe that this *bias* is because of the use of `stats.mode` to find the prediction (which returns the first label sorted low to high).

We also suggest an alternative approach (credits to Pavlos Protopapas, Hayden Joy) in which a label is randomly selected in case of a tie.

```python3
    def _vote(self,labels):
        mean_vote = np.mean(labels)
        
        # if there is a tie, flip a coin
        if mean_vote == 0.5:
            mean_vote += np.random.randn(1)
        return 1*( mean_vote  > 0.5)   
```

Here's a sample plot comparing the two implementations.

![](https://i.ibb.co/ZBD8J9H/results.png)

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Link to [colab notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1JCGNVPlrxyKlRHTQsJdAOHragen2JOeV?usp=sharing)

### Expected Results

Similar predictions if labels are reversed.

### Actual Results

Different results when labels are reversed.

Plot comparison.

![](https://i.ibb.co/ZBD8J9H/results.png)

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.7.11 (default, Jul  3 2021, 18:01:19)  [GCC 7.5.0]
executable: /usr/bin/python3
   machine: Linux-5.4.104+-x86_64-with-Ubuntu-18.04-bionic

Python dependencies:
       pip: 21.1.3
setuptools: 57.4.0
   sklearn: 0.22.2.post1
     numpy: 1.19.5
     scipy: 1.4.1
    Cython: 0.29.24
    pandas: 1.1.5
matplotlib: 3.2.2
    joblib: 1.0.1

Built with OpenMP: True
```

events.author: AlekLefebvre
events.comment:
Hi @4722794 ,

This behavior is documented:

> Warning Regarding the Nearest Neighbors algorithms, if it is found that two neighbors, neighbor k+1 and k, have identical distances but different labels, the results will depend on the ordering of the training data.

This is because it uses scipy.stats.mode which says in its documentation: 

> Returns an array of the modal (most common) value in the passed array. If there is more than one such value, only the first is returned.

Since this is known and documented I don't think we should try to fix it.

events.author: stephantul
events.comment:
Hi @4722794 

The empirically most valid strategy would actually be to pick the label that is most frequent in your training data in case of a tie, instead of a random one. If the class distribution is the same for train and test, this should lead to better performance than just picking at random.

This conforms to the situation you'd get in a linear model, where two classes that have exactly the same feature weights can still have different probabilities because of a different intercept. If you think of the intercept as a prior, the prior will be higher for the more frequent class.

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
So I don't consider this a bug. So here we have to see if we want to break backwards compatibility or not.
Tagging this issue such that we can make a decision with core dev.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
Historically, we have added parameters such SVC's `break_ties` to help break ties and remain backward compatible. In this case, we can introduce a `break_ties` parameter to KNeighhbors with options:

1. "most_frequent": Chooses the more frequent class in the training set
2. "first": The current behavior

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
Maybe a "random" tie-breaking could be useful as well.

I assume that we would need a similar parameter in `RadiusNeighborsClassifier`.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment: From triaging meeting:  There are performance concerns with adding a tie breaking mechanism. For now, I am marking the issue as low priority and we may revisit in the future.

events.author: project-delphi
events.comment:
This behavior affects all points that are equidistant and fall within the nearest k. Relying on the ordering of training data undermines established resampling methods, which are designed to enhance model robustness and generalization.

I’d like to advocate for a random tie-breaking option in `KNeighbors*`.  Here’s why:

	1.	Bias Elimination: The current behavior introduces a bias towards the order in which data were presented, which might skew results if the labels were ordered, especially when dealing with balanced datasets or evenly distributed classes. Random tie-breaking ensures fairness, as no class is favored arbitrarily.
	2.	Lightweight Implementation: Random selection from a set of tied indices is computationally inexpensive and has minimal memory overhead. Ties would only require generating at worst case k random numbers without replacement, an `O(n)` operation.
	3.	Ties Are Rare: In practice, ties happen infrequently, so random selection would be used sparingly. The performance impact is negligible compared to the benefits of unbiased predictions.
	4.	Flexibility: Offering a “random” tie-breaking option alongside “most_frequent” or “first” gives users more control, allowing them to choose the most suitable method for their application.
       5.  Permutation Invariant Algorithm: `KNeighbors*` is permutation invariant,  the results of tie-breaking should correspond.

Randomness of the trained `KNeighbors*` can be controlled by fixing the random seed.

I believe this would be a valuable enhancement to the classifier’s functionality without significant downsides.

It should be said, this applies equally to `KNeighborsRegressor` and `KNeighborsClassifier`

events.author: project-delphi
events.comment:
As an alternative, note the reference implementation in `R`. The `knn` function of the `class` `R` package resolves ties without relying on the ordering of training examples.

>
>k-nearest neighbour classification for test set from training set. For each row of the test set, the k
>nearest (in Euclidean distance) training set vectors are found, and the classification is decided by
>majority vote, with ties broken at random. If there are ties for the kth nearest vector, all candidates
>are included in the vote.

See the [class package documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/class/class.pdf) for details. 

Using all candidates should minimize computational overhead, making it a more efficient option than randomization.

creator: markusloecher
title: Is _generate_sample_indices working correctly ?
text:
### Describe the bug

I fit two random forests (with just one tree each) with identical parameters, but for the second one I disable the row subsampling by setting `bootstrap=False` and instead pass the inbag data generated with _generate_sample_indices.

I believe that the only stochastic elements of a random forest are the row and column subsampling. I disable the former by setting `bootstrap=False` and the latter as well by choosing `max_features = p`.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble._forest import _generate_sample_indices
from sklearn.datasets import load_boston
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

boston = load_boston()
xtrain, ytrain = boston.data, boston.target
n_samples, p = xtrain.shape

rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=1, 
    min_samples_leaf =10,max_features = p)
rf.fit(xtrain, ytrain)

tree=rf.estimators_[0]
sampled_indices = _generate_sample_indices(tree.random_state, n_samples, n_samples)

rf0 = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=1, 
    min_samples_leaf =10,max_features = p, bootstrap=False)
rf0.fit(xtrain[sampled_indices,:], ytrain[sampled_indices])

p  =  rf.predict(xtrain)
p0 = rf0.predict(xtrain)

plt.scatter(p,p0)
```

### Expected Results

I would expect the two forests (consisting of a single tree) to be identical ?


### Actual Results

The predictions are quite different as you can see in the output

The fact that `fit` does not get the same training data (i.e., `xtrain` and then `xtrain[sample_indices]`) will have an impact on the randomness. Then, you are passing `tree.random_state` to `_generate_sample_indices`. I think that one needs to be extra careful here. The forest will regenerate seeds for each of the trees based on the forest `random_state`.

events.comment:
Yes, but would you agree that there should be NO randomness at all in the second forest fit, since bootstrap is disabled and all features are considered at each split. 
And the training data **should be identical**, since the first forest samples with replacement from `xtrain` which then ought to be the exact same data set as  `xtrain[sample_indices]` in the second forest/tree since there is no subsampling happening there.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
The random forest bootstraps by using sample weights and passing that along to the decision tree:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/517b38ad30f36c6fe9eaca2c4a496ac1c63b3f50/sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py#L171-L184

This only works if passing in the weights is the same as slicing. I do not think this is true for `DecisionTreeRegressor`:

```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
import numpy as np

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=1000, n_features=10, random_state=0)
n_samples, n_features = X.shape
n_samples_bootstrap = n_samples

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
indices = rng.randint(0, n_samples, n_samples_bootstrap)

# Fit with slicing
tree_slicing = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0)
tree_slicing.fit(X[indices], y[indices])

# Fit using sample_weight the same as random forest
sample_weight = np.ones((n_samples,), dtype=np.float64)
sample_counts = np.bincount(indices, minlength=n_samples)
sample_weight *= sample_counts

tree_weights = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0)
tree_weights.fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight)

p_slicing = tree_slicing.predict(X)
p_weights = tree_weights.predict(X)

# Errors
np.testing.assert_allclose(p_slicing, p_weights)
```

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
> Yes, but would you agree that there should be NO randomness at all in the second forest fit, since bootstrap is disabled and all features are considered at each split.

An easy way to find out whether there's some added randomness would be something like


```py
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


prev_pred = None
X, y = make_regression(n_samples=1000)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y)

for random_state in range(100):
    print(random_state)
    
    rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=20, max_features=X_train.shape[1], bootstrap=False,
                               random_state=random_state)
    
    rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
    pred = rf.predict(X_test)
    
    if prev_pred is not None:
        np.testing.assert_array_almost_equal(pred, prev_pred)

    prev_pred = pred
```

which fails at the second iteration.


Now, according to our docs:

> The features are always randomly permuted at each split. Therefore, the best found split may vary, even with the same training data, max_features=n_features and bootstrap=False, if the improvement of the criterion is identical for several splits enumerated during the search of the best split. To obtain a deterministic behaviour during fitting, random_state has to be fixed.

So it's possible that there are splits with an equal gain in the dataset you're using, which would explain the discrepancies between the 2 fitted trees.

How very interesting, thank you for pointing this out ! I do not understand yet why the result would differ since the data sets are identical, whether sliced or weighted ? 
Would this be considered a feature or a bug ?

@NicolasHug 

Many thanks for pointing out this additional source of randomness which I had not thought of.

My motivation was only to make sure that `_generate_sample_indices` `_generate_unsampled_indices` are working properly since many of my simulations depend on those functions.
Can I conclude that my examples do not provide evidence for a bug in those functions?

Interestingly, this hypothesis is difficult to settle for good since there is only one `random_state` parameter to fix, which probably controls both the random row and column sub samplings/permutations.

As @glemaitre pointed out, forests set estimators as such:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/28567a5073f7c51e14aef7abc5b3452e3f92a8b1/sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py#L430-L433

And for each estimator, the `random_state` parameter is generated as such:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/28567a5073f7c51e14aef7abc5b3452e3f92a8b1/sklearn/ensemble/_base.py#L46-L81

So @markusloecher, I must say it's a given that you will get different trees because trees are not using the same `random_state` as the forest. Each tree is getting a new `random_state` generated from the forest one. Otherwise, if all trees in the forest have the same `random_state`, they will just be identical! It has nothing to do with `bootstrap`, as trees just need to be different for the forest to work.

But, with that knowledge in mind... I wrote the following code:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble._forest import _generate_sample_indices
from sklearn.datasets import load_boston
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

boston = load_boston()
xtrain, ytrain = boston.data, boston.target
n_samples, p = xtrain.shape

curr_sample_weight = np.ones((n_samples,), dtype=np.float64)
sampled_indices = _generate_sample_indices(1791095845, n_samples, n_samples)
sample_counts = np.bincount(sampled_indices, minlength=n_samples)
curr_sample_weight *= sample_counts

rf = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=1, min_samples_leaf=10, max_features=p, random_state=1
)
rf.fit(xtrain, ytrain)

rf0 = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=1, min_samples_leaf=10, max_features=p, random_state=1, bootstrap=False
)
rf0.fit(xtrain, ytrain, sample_weight=curr_sample_weight)

p = rf.predict(xtrain)
p0 = rf0.predict(xtrain)

plt.scatter(p, p0)
print("Tree's random_state for forest with bootstrap:", rf.estimators_[0].random_state)
print("Tree's random_state for forest without bootstrap:", rf0.estimators_[0].random_state)
```

The output:
```
Tree's random_state for forest with bootstrap: 1791095845
Tree's random_state for forest without bootstrap: 1791095845
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20309845/136697527-6ea7badb-5ffc-4e97-b1d2-e687e42bbfbc.png)

I took advantage of already knowing what the tree `random_state` would be, using `random_state=1` for the forests. Then I followed the steps in the code: 

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/28567a5073f7c51e14aef7abc5b3452e3f92a8b1/sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py#L171-L184

Instead of directly applying the indices, the forest code uses `sample_weight` as the index control. Hope this proves that `_generate_sample_indices` is working properly~ After all, it's only a private function that represents part of the processing.

creator: Scoodood
title: Additional metrics in `sklearn.metrics.classification_report`
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Metrics are **Extremely Important** for benchmarking models' performance. But in **scikit-learn**, it is not easy to extract these metrics from a **multiclass classification** model. In the past, I had to combine different pieces of functions within the `sklearn.metrics` module in order to derive my own. But it is counterproductive, so I end up staying away from **scikit-learn**, and using other libraries such as [pycm](https://www.pycm.ir), [mlxtend](http://rasbt.github.io/mlxtend/), [yellowbrick](https://www.scikit-yb.org/en/latest/), ... etc to get the job done. It is not perfect and still requires some customization, but they are more complete, and much easier to use than **scikit-learn**. So it would be great if **scikit-learn** can improve a little more in this area, so that we can focus more on modeling than customizing the code.



### Describe your proposed solution

`metrics.classification_report` is a good start. The current `metrics.classification_report` return
- Precision (Positive Predictive Value)
- Recall (True Positive Rate)
- F1
- Support

It is great, but far from complete. The following 2 are very important as well
- Negative Predictive Value (NPV)
- Specificity (True Negative Rate, or TNR)

Once we can cover these 4 metrics for the multiclass classification
- Precision (Positive Predictive Value) --> requires (TP, FP)
- Recall (True Positive Rate) --> requires (TP, FN)
- Negative Predictive Value (NPV) --> requires (TN, FN)
- Specificity (True Negative Rate) --> requires (TN, FP)

we can pretty much derive the rest of the metrics, such as
- FNR (False Negative Rate = 1 - TPR)
- FPR (False Positive Rate = 1 - TNR)
- FDR (False Discovery Rate = 1 - PPV)
- FOR (False Omission Rate = 1 - NPV)
- ACC (Accuracy)
- MCC (Mathews Correlation Coefficient)
- Prevalence Threshold
- ...etc

These 2 are quite important as well, but it can be tricky to get for multiclass classification
- AUROC (Area under ROC)
- AUPR (Area under Precision-Recall curve)

The [pycm](https://www.pycm.ir) library is quite comprehensive. Perhaps you may consider integrating some of their goodies into **scikit-learn**.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

title: Warn subclassed UserWarning when unpickling model using different verison of sklearn
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I want to terminate execution if I'm unpickling a model using a different version of sklearn.

### Describe your proposed solution

Currently it warns with a `UserWarning`:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4abd9f2d9e12451fa3e32bd77a97b5c4d8be8b19/sklearn/base.py#L320-L334

If, instead, it used a subclassed UserWarning you could wrap up loading a model in a [catch_warnings](https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html#warnings.catch_warnings) context manager and filter that warning to raise instead, and then exit if it is raised.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

You could potentially do this by catching `UserWarning` and checking matching such as `user_warning.message.startswith("Trying to unpickle estimator")` but this is not very robust.

### Additional context

_No response_

I've seen the specializing issues/expcetions issue pop up from time to time, so there is a demand for them. I think it's common for a Python library to have specialized warnings and exceptions.

The only documentation we have for exceptions are in the [API docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/classes.html#module-sklearn.exceptions). The last specialized warning we added was `PositiveSpectrumWarning` which has limited scope.

As for this issue, I think a unpickling warning also has limited scope, which makes it easier to ensure consistency. (Limited scope == less places can use it == less need to think about consistency). To move forward, I think we can move ahead with a PR and see what everyone thinks.

creator: markusloecher
title: Add random forest row-subsampling without replacement
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I do appreciate the current option of disabling bootstrapping via the Boolean argument `bootstrap`.
However, currently there is only one alternative: If False, the whole (identical) dataset is used to build each tree.
There is well known research though (starting with the paper by [Strobl et al.](https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2105-8-25) from 2007) that in certain situations subsamples drawn without replacement leads to better performance.
Many well known random forest implementations (such as [ranger](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ranger/index.html) ) offer this sub sampling as an alternative to the bootstrap.

I would greatly appreciate it if sklearn would offer the same.


### Describe your proposed solution

**For both `RandomForestRegressor`  and  `RandomForestClassifier` allow the user to draw subsamples without replacement for each tree instead of the bootstrap.**
The user can choose the fraction of sub samples drawn for each tree (default: 0.632 )
Ideally the functions `_generate_unsampled_indices` and `_generate_sampled_indices` would still work.


### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

### API considerations
Currently, random forests have the option `bootstap=True` or `False`. If this new feature of tree-wise row-subsampling without replacement is added, there are several options:
1. Add a new option `with_replacement=True` (default), or `False`, that only takes effect if `bootstrap=True`.
   Disadvantage: The term bootstrap explicitly means sampling with replacement.
2. Add a new option `row_subsampling=True` (default) or `False`, which samples with replacement if `bootstrap=True` and without replacement if `bootstrap=False`.
   Disadvantage: It would change current behaviour for `bootstrap=False`, which currently means no sampling at all.
3. Add new option `sampling="bootstrap"` (default), and allow callable / splitter to be passed. Deprecate option `bootstrap` (proposed in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/20953#issuecomment-923957749).

In terms of API, I like the proposal of @adrinjalali 

In terms of including this new feature, I would be reticent. I would only consider this option if a clean benchmark shows that we can get clear/significant improvements sometimes. My reasoning is that our tree-based algorithms come with a large number of parameters and options already. Increasing the number of options and parameters make it difficult to document the important things regarding the algorithm.

So my reasoning here is if the option does not make a clear cutoff in generalization performance for at least a certain percentage of datasets (maybe a minimum of ~20%), then we might be able to leave without it. In this regard, I like the proposal of @adrinjalali because it opens the possibility for people to implement their strategy and avoid us to complexity our documentation with the available options implemented in scikit-learn.

creator: mfeurer
title: TransformedTargetClassifier
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I would like to be able to use a LabelEncoder as a wrapper for a classifier, similarly to what can be achieved with preprocessors on the y value for regressors via the [TransformedTargetRegressor](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.compose.TransformedTargetRegressor.html).

### Describe your proposed solution

Add a class TransformedTargetClassifier that accepts both a transformer on y and a classifier.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

An alternative would be to use the voting classifier with a single estimator, but that appears to be misusing that class.

### Additional context

I'm proposing this feature because in Auto-sklearn we use the LabelEncoder on a call to fit to have all classifiers we try use a simple, encoded representation. When using the Auto-sklearn classes we can undo the transformations ourselves. However, if the user would like to access an individual model, there's no way we can wrap the LabelEncoder around this models.

CC @eddiebergman

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
A bit of a workaround: we are not limiting the regressor to be a regressor. The following should indeed work:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

tt = TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=LogisticRegression(),
				transformer=LabelEncoder())
X, y = make_classification()
tt.fit(X, y)
print(tt.score(X, y))
```

> LabelEncoder on a call to fit to have all classifiers we try use a simple, encoded representation.

I think that most of the scikit-learn estimators already do that internally and call `inverse_transform` at `predict`. This is also linked with the `classes_` fitted attribute.

events.author: mfeurer
events.comment:
Thanks @glemaitre for that suggestion. Indeed, it gets us 90% of where we would like to be, but I see two small issues:

1) it is still called Regressor and is also a `RegressorMixin`
2) it doesn't support `predict_proba`

As I can see it right now it would be rather simple to extract all relevant code into a parent class and provide both a regressor and classifier. Please let me know if you'd be interested in that.

Regarding what the estimators do by themselves, we're aware of that, but to keep Auto-sklearn as simple as possible we aim to only handle integer classes internally. So one could say that the Auto-sklearn estimator aims to do that internally and we just need to find a way how to provide the user with the internal models in case they want to see them.

For our use case we want to be able to show predictions as either the original text labels or the probability of a given label.  PyCaret has a `TransformedTargetClassifier` implementation that can return the original text labels, but it doesn't implement `predict_proba`, so it only gives us half of what we need.  It would be great if scikit-learn had a full implementation of `TransformedTargetClassifier`.  Here's an example using PyCaret's implementation:
```
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.naive_bayes import CategoricalNB
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder
from pycaret.internal.preprocess.target.TransformedTargetClassifier import TransformedTargetClassifier


csv_url = 'https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/iris/iris.data'
col_names = ['sepal length (cm)', 'sepal width (cm)', 'petal length (cm)', 'petal width (cm)', 'species']
df = pd.read_csv(csv_url, names=col_names)
y = df.pop('species')
X = df

pipeline = make_pipeline(TransformedTargetClassifier(classifier=CategoricalNB(), transformer=LabelEncoder()))
pipeline.fit(X, y)
predictions = pipeline.predict(X)[[10, 25, 50]]
print(predictions)
# ['Iris-setosa' 'Iris-setosa' 'Iris-versicolor']
```

creator: thomasjpfan
title: TfidfTransformer does not support large sparse matrices on 32bit platforms
text:
`TfidTransformer` does not support large sparse matrices (indices as int64) because `_document_frequency` uses `np.bincount`. `np.bincount` works on arrays with dtype `NPY_INTP` which is int32 on 32bit platforms.

REF: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/20919

creator: swight-prc
title: get_params method in cross-validation splitters
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I would like to be able to recreate the cross-validataion splitters from parameters.

Presently, the cross-validation splitters do not have `get_params` or `set_params` options. I want to make different steps in my process stateless, and to do that I need to be able to retrieve the parameters used to create an object (and pass them out), then recreate the object (obviously in an unfitted state, but that doesn't matter for cv splitters) when the parameters are passed back in.


### Describe your proposed solution

`get_params` and `set_params` are already implemented in `BaseEstimator`. There are two possible options:

1. Copy the implementation into `BaseCrossValidator`
   This is faster to implement, but it isn't very DRY, and it isn't very maintainable. This could be done as a quick patch, but doing so might make problems for someone else later.
2. Pull the common API stuff backward to some kind of BaseSKObject class
  This is more maintainable, cleaner, and overall a better solution, but it will take thought, architectural consideration, and intentionality. This is not a quick patch.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

I can (and probably will) store the values I used to create the object in the first place, and pass them out when I build my parameter string. I don't think this will be completed right away (if it's even desired by the community at large), and the show must go on.

But having `get_params` and `set_params` common across all sklearn objects feels like a necessary step toward a more unified codebase. And it would make my life a lot easier!

### Additional context

_No response_

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment: Could you exemplify what you are trying to do. I am not understanding the exact use-case probably because I am not familiar with your terminology. A bit of Python code could solve this.

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
In the hope that this would perhaps help framing the discussion (which is a bit confusing to me still), here are a few notes regarding statefulness:

- The estimators are stateful across calls to `fit()` if at least one of these is True:
  - the `random_state` isn't an int
  -  `warm_start` is True
- The splitters are stateful across calls to `split()` iff `random_state` isn't an int

Meaning that if you set `random_state=some_int` you will **always** get the same splits when calling `cv.split(X, y)` multiple times.

events.author: swight-prc
events.comment:
> Could you exemplify what you are trying to do. I am not understanding the exact use-case probably because I am not familiar with your terminology. A bit of Python code could solve this.

Sure; I mean, a bit of python code could eliminate the need for `get_params` for all objects. But it makes life easier in a lot of cases, and it exists in _most_ of the API. I'm just looking for that to be extended.

Let's imagine you're building a ML system to reside on a cloud system. You build a front end that accepts parameters etc., then passes them to the backend. Maybe you have multiple steps going on (selecting your transforms, your scalers, etc.), and you want feedback after each step. You also want to be able to spin up multiple copies of the container it's in, so each transaction needs to be stateless. (This is the stateless I'm talking about, @NicolasHug, not within the objects themselves.) 

You have, as best I can tell, two options:

1) store each object in some session database and pass a session token back and forth
This adds a new piece - some kind of volume or database - and you have to manage it, deal with timeout, and manage history
2) send information back to the front-end about the objects you're creating, then recreate each object with each API request you get - especially if you're working pre-fit and building out a pipeline.
This allows the front end to store as much history of your job as you want. So if you want to allow the user to move back a step, you have the config from just before that step, so you can just send that in with whatever your user's new choices are, and bob's your uncle. It also minimizes the need to retrieve and store session objects between transactions. Creating these objects is O(1) I believe, and likely significantly faster than retrieving them and storing them.

Take, for example, the `OneHotEncoder` object. It has the following parameters (and defaults)
```python
enc1h_defaults = {
    "categories": 'auto',
    "drop": None,
    "sparse": True,
    "dtype": numpy.float32,
    "handle_unknown": "error"
}
```

If I create a OneHotEncoder object like this:
```python
>>> enc1h = OneHotEncoder(sparse=False)
```
then later I can
```python
>>> enc_params = enc1h.get_params()
>>> enc_params
 {"categories": 'auto', "drop": None, "sparse": False, "dtype": numpy.float32, "handle_unknown": "error"}
```
and I can store, send to the front end, or whatever else that set of parameters. (Gotta handle the numpy.float32 somehow if you wanna go JSON, but that's straightforward enough.)

so later, if I want to make an object in the same way, I can:
```python
>>> new_enc = OneHotEncoder(**enc_params)
```
I'd have to handle getting an object from the "numpy.float32" string, but again, straightforward enough.

I could do that having had no information concerning any previous session or state. If I received those parameters as a json string, converted it to a dictionary, and handled dtype, I could recreate that object. Since I'm working pre-fit, the result is that I have exactly (or at least functionally) the same object back.

With a little python code and some recursive magic, I can even build a json-safe nested dictionary for sklearn objects that contain other sklearn objects, like pipelines. However, when I get to an object that contains a splitter (like the RFECV object, for example), I can't.

Now, I don't know what the initial impetus was for creating the `get_params` method in the first place, but I do know that I find it quite useful. I assumed (wrongly) that it existed throughout the sklearn API, and now I'm looking at subclassing these objects and adding the functionality. But I also feel like it would make sense to pull that functionality out into the entire sklearn API, instead of having it only exist for BaseEstimator objects.

events.author: swight-prc
events.comment: (maybe O(n), where n is the number of objects. When I said O(1) I was thinking of each individual object)

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment: It is a bit out of my knowledge. It seems that you are interested to have a way to build estimators in a declarative manner but whenever scikit-learn will have some nested objects (CV splitters or even estimator) you will get into trouble. Am I getting it right?

events.author: swight-prc
events.comment:
> It is a bit out of my knowledge. It seems that you are interested to have a way to build estimators in a declarative manner but whenever scikit-learn will have some nested objects (CV splitters or even estimator) you will get into trouble. Am I getting it right?

Close. Estimators are fine, because anything that inherits from `BaseEstimator` has the `get_params` method.

events.author: swight-prc
events.comment:
Thing is, almost the whole dang library inherits from `BaseEstimator`. Transformers (like `OneHotEncoder` and `MinMaxScaler`) that do no estimation whatsoever inherit from `BaseEstimator`. So it's *almost* a universal base class.

I haven't done an exhaustive search, but cv splitters are the only subset of sklearn objects I've seen so far that do not inherit from `BaseEstimator`. Cool, no problem, but we lose the `get_params` method for it.

(There may be other reasons that inheriting `BaseEstimator` would be a bad idea for splitters. I'm not super familiar with the codebase, and I'm not railing against its inclusion. I just noticed a consequence thereof.)

events.author: swight-prc
events.comment:
Ha! This is all I have to do to fix it. Perhaps the best fix is just to include BaseEstimator as a base class for BaseCrossValidator

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold as SKF, KFold as KF
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator

class StratifiedKFold(SKF, BaseEstimator):
    ...

class KFold(KF, BaseEstimator):
    ...
```

(etc...repeat for any other splitter classes you're using)

events.comment:
OK got it. We also have the scorers that are in the same situation (while this is true that you can pass some strings).

It would be nice to have thoughts of others @scikit-learn/core-devs

creator: glemaitre
title: Allow `Pipeline` to whether pass or not `y` to some transformer
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Some transformers could be used in both a supervised and unsupervised setting. Currently, `y` is always passed at `fit` and it imposes that such transformers can only be used in a supervised way.

Such transformers could be:

- `PLSRegression`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/20783
- `UMAP`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/20815

### Describe your proposed solution

We might be able to change the `Pipeline` implementation.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

We could also delegate this option to the constructor the transformer that should specify if it should work in supervised or unsupervised mode. Something similar to `novelty=True/False` for switching from novelty detection vs. outlier detection for some estimator.

### Additional context

To give a succinct example:

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
import umap

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)

pipe = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler()), ('umap', umap.UMAP()), ('lr', LogisticRegression()
])
pipe.fit(X, y)
```

creator: freddyaboulton
title: Allow users to pass their own grid to partial dependence
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

The partial dependence function does it's own grid calculation that assumes all the data is numeric via the `np.unique` method call. This is problematic for pipelines where the input data is transformed into numeric values along the way. 

For example, this is an example trying to compute partial dependence on a categorical column with missing values. It errors out because `np.unique` does not work with categorical columns with missing values. 

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
import pytest

pl = Pipeline([("Imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
               ("OHE", OneHotEncoder()),
               ("RFC", RandomForestClassifier())])

X = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": ["a", "b", "a", "b"]})
y = pd.Series([0, 1, 0, 1])
pl.fit(X, y)

X_holdout = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": ["a", "b", "a", None]})

with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="'<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'str'"):
    partial_dependence(pl, X_holdout, features=1, grid_resolution=3)
```

I think this goes beyond just `np.unique`. I could have a pipeline that transforms a datetime into a numeric value. There are multiple ways of computing a grid for datetimes, like transforming into unix epoch time and computing quantiles or picking times every x timesteps apart. 

### Describe your proposed solution

Letting users pass in their own grid and values parameters.

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
import pytest

pl = Pipeline([("Imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
               ("OHE", OneHotEncoder()),
               ("RFC", RandomForestClassifier())])

X = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": ["a", "b", "a", "b"]})
y = pd.Series([0, 1, 0, 1])
pl.fit(X, y)

X_holdout = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": ["a", "b", "a", None]})
partial_dependence(pl, X_holdout, features=1, grid_resolution=3, grid=np.array([['a'], ['b']]), values=[['a', 'b']])
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

We could make the existing implementation more robust to categorical values by using a different function than `np.unique`.

### Additional context

If this is a welcome change but low-priority, I'd be happy to help!

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
Thank you for opening this issue! I see two separate items here that are related:

### 1. Categorical support with missing values
Currently, visualizations in partial dependence plot expects continuous  data. There is ongoing work at https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/18298 to expand the visualization for categorical data. At a glance, the implementation should also handle categorical data with missing values by treating missing as another category. I think that should resolve the issue with categorical data with missing values without needing a custom grid.

### 2. Custom grids for other datatypes such as timestamps
Allowing for custom grids for cases where partial dependence can not automatically figure out the grid seems useful. Let's say you have 20 features and you want to give a custom grid for the feature indexed at 16 and let `partial_dependence` automatically decide on the rest. As an API, I proposal passing in `custom_grid={16: custom_array}`.

@glemaitre What do you think about allowing for custom grids?

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
> @glemaitre What do you think about allowing for custom grids?

It might be handy. I would think that on our side it would make it easy if the `custom_grid` has the same structure as the one created internally. In this case, we only have to make minimal validation for it.

events.comment: @thomasjpfan @glemaitre Thank you for the feedback! I have a PR to address this here: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/21033

title: Rank about GridSearchCV
text:
### Describe the bug

row 934-936 in `_search.py`:
```python
            if rank:
                results["rank_%s" % key_name] = np.asarray(
                    rankdata(-array_means, method='min'), dtype=np.int32)
```
maybe it is more correct to rank with both of `array_means` and `array_stds`, bigger mean and smaller std means better performence, if the mean is equal, may we need to continue to rank by std

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

row 934-936 in `_search.py`:
```python
            if rank:
                results["rank_%s" % key_name] = np.asarray(
                    rankdata(-array_means, method='min'), dtype=np.int32)
```

### Expected Results

rank with both of `array_means` and `array_stds`

creator: adam2392
title: Adding Oblique Trees (Forest-RC) to the Cythonized Tree Module
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I am part of the @neurodata team. We are proposing to add a cythonized module that allows for building oblique trees.

Oblique trees, otherwise known as `Forest-RC`, originally proposed by, Breiman 2001 [1], would enable a more flexible class of decision trees. Breiman called a version of these Forest-RC, as compared to what most people call random forest, which he called Forest-RI. He noted:

"Forest-RC does exceptionally well on the synthetic data sets. Overall, it compares more favorably to Adaboost than Forest-RI."

In other words, in Breiman's paper introduction random forest over 20 years ago, with over 75,000 citations, he presented 2 algorithms, and argued that the one which does sparse linear combinations of features worked better than the naive one which most people have used since. More recently, several authors have corroborated these original results [2-6]. Oblique trees in general open up a wide class of flexibility for trees to take advantage of structure in data. 

[1]: Breiman, L. Random Forests. Machine Learning 45, 5–32 (2001). https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1010933404324
[2]: T. M. Tomita, J. Browne, C. Shen, J. Chung, J. L. Patsolic, B. Falk, J. Yim, C. E. Priebe, R. Burns, M. Maggioni, and J. T. Vogelstein. [Sparse Projection Oblique Randomer Forests](https://jmlr.org/papers/v21/18-664.html). Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2020.
[3]: Tyler M Tomita, Mauro Maggioni, and Joshua T Vogelstein. Roflmao: Robust oblique forests with linear matrix operations. In Proceedings of the 2017 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining, pages 498–506. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, 2017.
[4]: Rainforth, Tom & Wood, Frank. (2015). Canonical Correlation Forests. 
[5]: Perry, R., Li, A., Huynh, C., Tomita, T.M., Mehta, R., Arroyo, J., Patsolic, J., Falk, B., & Vogelstein, J. (2019). Manifold Oblique Random Forests: Towards Closing the Gap on Convolutional Deep Networks.
[6]: Menze, Bjoern & Kelm, Bernd & Splitthoff, Daniel & Köthe, Ullrich & Hamprecht, Fred. (2011). On Oblique Random Forests. 453-469. 10.1007/978-3-642-23783-6_29. 

### Describe your proposed solution

The implementation of Forest-RC (oblique forests) was ported into a scikit-learn fork (https://github.com/neurodata/scikit-learn/pull/11/). The Forest-RC Cython implementation currently builds cleanly on top of the existing cython code for the regular Decision Trees and thus does not affect the runtime, or performance on Random Forests at all. Moreover, it improves upon RF in certain cc_18 benchmarks (see figure below). 

The `.pxd` files can also be included in each scikit-learn release, so that other sklearn-compatible forest modules can build upon our implementation of the Oblique tree.

### Relevant Benchmarks

To ease scikit-learn developer concerns on incorporating such a large piece of code change, we can provide the following benchmarks and tests on Cythonized Forest-RC vs Cythonized Forest-RI. These benchmarks were ran on the OpenML CC-18 dataset. Max features were set to n_features, so runtime was very high for both RF and oblique forests in e.g. Fashion-MNIST.

1. **benchmark tests on cc_18 vs Random Forests** (see two figures below) Forest-RC is significantly better then RF on this benchmark suite. A paired one-sided Wilcoxon signed test was ran. Forest-RC was significantly better then RF with a PValue ~ 1e-20.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3460267/132111028-689a64cc-15c3-4177-a92e-a0503d873d33.png)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3460267/130329139-b27484f3-365b-4e03-a977-2b0e35f66c7e.png)

2. **overall runtime (training times on cc_18) vs Random Forests**

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3460267/132111128-c2ed2ec6-74f9-4766-b147-26df53069e59.png)

3. **Runtime benchmarking dependency on number of features and number of samples:** In addition, we performed a benchmarking the runtime performance of oblique trees/forests using the code provided in `benchmarks/bench_tree.py`. The notebook is shown in this gist: https://gist.github.com/adam2392/a652aa1c88ba94f0d6aab96ccd3ade24

4. **visualizing the intuitive differences between Oblique and Axis-aligned trees:** Per a discussion with @thomasjpfan , he wanted to see how we can educate an incoming user when/how oblique trees are different. We can extend the [existing example in sklearn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/tree/plot_iris_dtc.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-tree-plot-iris-dtc-py). The following notebook shows the decision surface of an oblique tree vs axis-aligned tree: https://gist.github.com/adam2392/78519091104cecfeb8ff796eac7e8115
 

### Additional context

cc: @jovo 

Some action items are:

1. Unit testing (I will probably need some direction as to where tests can be added as say parametrization, and what sort of tests the maintainers would like to see)
2. Make the official PR so developers/maintainers can track progress

creator: krey
title: Support for 2d sample weights for MultiOutputEstimators
text:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable
Consider a multioutput estimation problem where there are missing values in the outputs.

Imagine that `y` is
```python
array([[ 1., -1., nan],
       [-1., nan,  1.],
       [-1.,  1.,  1.]])
```
Then the sample weights would be
```
array([[1., 1., 0.],
       [1., 0., 1.],
       [1., 1., 1.]])
```

### Describe your proposed solution

Change the end of `sklearn.multioutput._MultiOutputEstimator.fit` from
```python
        self.estimators_ = Parallel(n_jobs=self.n_jobs)(
            delayed(_fit_estimator)(
                self.estimator, X, y[:, i], sample_weight,
                **fit_params_validated)
            for i in range(y.shape[1]))
        return self
```
to something like
```python
        slice_sample_weight = sample_weight is not None and len(sample_weight.shape) == 2
        
        self.estimators_ = Parallel(n_jobs=self.n_jobs)(
            delayed(_fit_estimator)(
                self.estimator, X, y[:, i], sample_weight[:, i] if slice_sample_weight else sample_weight,
                **fit_params_validated)
            for i in range(y.shape[1]))
        return self
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

creator: lorentzenchr
title: FEA SplineTransformer difference penalty
text:
#### Describe the workflow you want to enable
When using `SplineTransformer` as part of a larger feature preprocessing pipeline that ends in a linear model, e.g. `Ridge`, I'd like the splines to get a penalty on the (first) differences of the coefficients instead of the usual L2 penalty:
```python
alpha * sum(squared_norm(np.diff(coef))) 
```
instead of
```python
alpha * sum(squared_norm(coef))
```

The reason is that such a penalty penalizes the curvature (integral over square of second derivatives of splines) and therefore has better interpolation and smoothness properties.
The B-splines would then be called P-splines, see Eilers & Marx "Flexible smoothing with B-splines and penalties" https://doi.org/10.1214/ss/1038425655
Properties (see Chapter 5):
- P-splines show no boundary effects, as many types of kernel smoothers do.
- P-splines can fit polynomial data exactly (with polynomial degree=k, a P-spline with k+1 difference penalty or higher)
- P-splines can conserve moments of the data. For a GLM with canonical link with P-splines of degree k+1 and a penalty of order k+1, or higher, it holds that `sum_i x_i^k y_true_i = sum_i x_i^k y_predict_i`.
  => 1st order P-splines conserve zero, first and 2nd momentum on training data.

#### Describe your proposed solution
I see 2 solutions:

1. Somehow (SLEP006 ?) pass the information that those columns are B-splines and should get a different penalty to the final linear regressor.
2. Add an additional option to `SplineTransformer`, like `diff=True`, that triggers to return `np.diff(X)` instead of `X`. The usual L2 penalty of, e.g. `Ridge`, is then equivalent to L2 of the difference of coefficients of the original `X`.
3. Further ideas?

events.comment:

> alpha * sum(np.diff(coef))
> ```

you mean instead of:

```python

```

Out of curiosity, I would be interested in seeing a case where a ridge penalty on diff spline features yields a significantly different outcomes to using the original features. That would help me get a clearer picture of the inductive bias of such a reparametrization of spline linear models.

creator: dobos
title: Support reusing of joblib thread pools in parallel routines
text:
#### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'm using `pairwise_distances` for fairly large matrices and, at the same time, long vectors. It's worth starting up the parallel threads for the matrices but not for the vectors. It would be great, however, if the thread pool could be reused to benefit for parallelism for the smaller computations as well.

#### Describe your proposed solution

`pairwise_distances` calls  `_parallel_pairwise` internally which creates a new thread pool (by instantiating `Parallel`) every time. Being able to pass the joblib parallel context as an argument would enable reusing the thread pool.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/3ae7c7615343bbd36acece57825d8b0d70fd9da4/sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py#L1416

```
        self._check_feature_names(X, reset=True)

        self._validate_transformers()
        self._validate_column_callables(X)

```

title: BallTree and KDTree query radius out of memory (optimisation or bug)
text:
#### Describe the bug

The BallTree and KDTree have a method query_radius that returns all the points near a certain radius. 
I have noticed that when you query via iteration point by point there is no issue with memory allocation but when you perform on the entire array it saturates the memory. I am not sure whether this is a memory leak or requires some form of optimization.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Example:
```python
import gc

import sklearn
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
import numpy as np
from memory_profiler import memory_usage
import psutil

def get_memory_usage():
    return memory_usage(timeout=0.2)[0]

vmem = psutil.virtual_memory()
print('sklearn:', sklearn.__version__)
print('Initial memory usage: %.2f MB' % get_memory_usage())
print('RAM available: %.2f GB' % (vmem.available/1e9))

N = 60000
X = np.random.rand(N, 2)  # Random data

print('Allocated X: %.2f MB' % get_memory_usage())
print('X.nbytes == %.2f MB' % (X.nbytes / 1e6))
print('X min %.2f' % X.min())
print('X max %.2f' % X.max())
```

Now let's try to find all neighbours:

```
# query via all elements crashes memory
ind = tree.query_radius(X, r=0.5) 
```

That will exhaust all your memory, increase or decrease N for testing.

#### Expected Results

If I query via iteration it all works well:

```
# query by iteration all elements
all = []
for i in range(X.shape[0]):
  ind = tree.query_radius(X[i:i+1], r=0.5) 
  found = ind[0].shape[0]
  all.append(found)
  assert found>0
print('Allocated with tree: %.2f MB' % get_memory_usage())
```
About 21 seconds on Colab and around 10 MB additional memory.

#### Actual Results

Out of memory on a 13 GB RM colab setup. Please change N parameter in case you have a larger setup.
