events.comment: Both lloyd and elkan were improved recently. Lloyd got a bigger boost than elkan (due to the use of gemm indeed) so elkan is not always faster than lloyd as it kind of was before. However, I observed that which is faster depends on the dataset. When the clusters are well separated elkan tends to still be faster than lloyd because the number of distances to compute quickly drops. So I'm not sure the default should be changed. Maybe running a benchmark on a set of standard datasets would give us a hint.

events.author: jim0421
events.comment: When it comes to improving the ```kmeans elkan```, I compared the code of kmeans between 0.22 and 0.23-dev0 and I found that the ```double-layer for loop with scipy dot function when updating sample-cluster distance``` was replaced by ```scipy dgemm function``` in ```kmeans lloyd```. However, ```kmeans elkan``` can not directly use this way for acceleration since the it eliminates many meaningless euclidean distance calculation. So I wonder whether we have chance to use ```dgemm-like``` api in ```kmeans elkan``` by rearranging the data or some change to the algorithm. Besides, do you have any suggestion for further optimization for ```kmeans elkan```?

events.author: jeremiedbb
events.comment:
> So I wonder whether we have chance to use dgemm-like api in kmeans elkan by rearranging the data or some change to the algorithm

When working on it I haven't found a way to do that. Seems unlikely though since for elkan all the distances we need to compute can't be expressed as a pairwise distances between 2 sets of points.

> Besides, do you have any suggestion for further optimization for kmeans elkan?

If I had, I would have implemented them when reworking kmeans :) so unfortunately no :/

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: We should probably update the documentation of the ELKAN option to emphasize that it can be slower than the default Lloyd solver and that this heavily depends on the natural "blob-iness" of the data.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: Maybe we could even add or update an example that compare the performance of the 2 solvers on different synthetic datasets where the difference is expected to be most extreme (e.g. `numpy.random.uniform` and `sklearn.datasets.make_blobs`).

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: I put the Moderate label for this issue as interested contributors should first be really familiar with the inner workings of both algorithms (Elkan vs LLoy) before considering submitting a PR to address my above comments. If not, please read the scikit-learn documentation, the source code of the 2 implementations and the references linked in the chapter of the user guide on K-means.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
Because of this observation, the Lloyd solver was enabled by default in #21735.

But the poor performance of the Elkan implementation can be caused by a bad interaction between the iterated calls to 2 distinct threadpools (one from OpenBLAS and one from OpenMP) as diagnosed in #20642.

To confirm this, it might we worth measure the performance of both methods in a conda-forge environment where both the OpenBLAS from scipy and the scikit-learn compiled extensions are linked to a unique OpenMP runtime to make sure that the Operating System scheduler only deals with a single active threadpool when fitting the model as explained here: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/20642#issuecomment-994776032

creator: Yukimura66
title: add stratified split for "shuffle=False" in train_test_split
text:
<!--
If you want to propose a new algorithm, please refer first to the scikit-learn
inclusion criterion:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/faq.html#what-are-the-inclusion-criteria-for-new-algorithms
-->

#### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When splitting time series data, data is often split without shuffling. But now `train_test_split` only supports stratified split with `shuffle=True`.
It would be helpful to add stratify option for `shuffle=False` also.

#### Describe your proposed solution

Add option `shuffle` in `StratifiedShuffleSplit`, and only permutate indices when `shuffle` option is `True`.
Then, use `StratifiedShuffleSplit` with shuffle option in `train_test_split`.   
For example:
```
def train_test_split(*arrays, **options):
    ...
    if shuffle is False:
        if stratify is not None:
            cv = StratifiedShuffleSplit(test_size=n_test, train_size=n_train,
                         random_state=random_state, shuffle=False)
            train, test = next(cv.split(X=arrays[0], y=stratify))
        else:
            train = np.arange(n_train)
            test = np.arange(n_train, n_train + n_test)
    ...

class StratifiedShuffleSplit(BaseShuffleSplit):
    def __init__(self, n_splits=10, test_size=None, train_size=None,
                 random_state=None, shuffle=True):
        super().__init__(
            n_splits=n_splits,
            test_size=test_size,
            train_size=train_size,
            random_state=random_state)
        self._default_test_size = 0.1
        self.shuffle=shuffle

    def _iter_indices(self, X, y, groups=None):
        n_samples = _num_samples(X)
        y = check_array(y, ensure_2d=False, dtype=None)
        
        ...

        rng = check_random_state(self.random_state)

        for _ in range(self.n_splits):
            # if there are ties in the class-counts, we want
            # to make sure to break them anew in each iteration
            n_i = _approximate_mode(class_counts, n_train, rng)
            class_counts_remaining = class_counts - n_i
            t_i = _approximate_mode(class_counts_remaining, n_test, rng)

            train = []
            test = []

            for i in range(n_classes):
                if self.shuffle:
                    permutation = rng.permutation(class_counts[i])
                    perm_indices_class_i = class_indices[i].take(permutation,
                                                                 mode='clip')
                else:
                    perm_indices_class_i = class_indices[i]

                train.extend(perm_indices_class_i[:n_i[i]])
                test.extend(perm_indices_class_i[n_i[i]:n_i[i] + t_i[i]])

            if self.shuffle:
                train = rng.permutation(train)
                test = rng.permutation(test)

            yield train, test
```

#### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Alternative idea is adding split process directly in train_test_split (like case `Shuffle=False` and stratify is None), or add new method. But that new code is very similar to StratifiedShuffleSplit, so modifying StratifiedShuffleSplit would be better.

events.comment:
No I haven't. But before I post this issue, I confirmed the code works. 
I can create pull request.

I require this exact functionality at the moment for splitting interaction data for a recommendation system.  Can you create PR for this?

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
I think adding `shuffle=False` to `StratifiedShuffleSplit` where the class name contains **Shuffle** can be a bit confusing.

As the documentation states, `train_test_split` was originally designed for shuffling:

> Quick utility that wraps input validation and `next(ShuffleSplit().split(X, y))`

The `shuffle=False` was added in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/8845 and seems strange considering the `train_test_split` docstring.

The current `shuffle=False` & `stratify=False` option feels like a `next(KFold().split(X, y))`. Note that the indices will be different because the first split from `KFold.split` uses the first fold as the test set.

In principle, we can call `next(StratifiedKFold().split(X, y))` for the `stratify=True` case if we can configure `*KFold` with the parameters of `train_test_split`. For example, if you want `train_test_split` with `test_size=0.25`:

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification()

# Use n_split = 4 to mean test_size=0.25
train_idx, test_idx = next(StratifiedKFold(n_splits=4).split(X, y))
X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test = X[train_idx], y[train_idx], X[test_idx], y[test_idx]
```

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
> This is needed especially for time-series test_train_split when you want to sort your data based on a timestamp and then 

For time series, I recommend looking into `TimeSeriesSplit`. Currently `train_test_split` with `shuffle=False` always has the training set first then the test set, but it is undocumented behavior. In principle, `train_test_split` can use indices `[1, 2, 3, 4]` for the training set and `[0]` for the test set and the data was not shuffled.

> get a test/train split stratified on something, e.g. user_id.

In this context, stratifying usually refers to the target. Assuming that `user_id` is not a target, but a [group](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-groups) there is a PR for adding `GroupTimeSeriesSplit`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/16236

title: score() and score_samples()
text:
#### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

<!--
Tell us about the confusion introduced in the documentation.
-->
 Hi all, 

target:I am trying to predict the bandwidth of the KernelDensity() on sklearn by using randomized search and bayesian optimization (fmin() from hyperopt). 

Issue: score_samples() and score() are not really clear to me. In the source code, the probability density is mentioned, then the total log density and likelihood. The are already challenging concepts by themselves and I find them hard to interpret when implementing my code. For instance I get a negative score which for  a log density would imply the log of a very small probability number if I am not wrong, which I find it odd. I have browsed the internet many times  and there are no real examples. 
For instance, understanding a PDF when it comes to determining the chance of rain between a specific interval is relatively easy, but when the model is about other things, like interest rate, bandwidth (using KernelDensity()) the interpretation is not so straightforward. The same goes for the likelihood, one thing is interpreting it when it is about a coin toss, and another thing is when it is about more variables combine together. 

Furthermore, the surrogate function which is defined with a cross_val_score gives a negative score, so also that one is not of immediate interpretation, and cross_val_score takes the default function, i.e. score() of the KernelDensity() when the scoring is not applied. Of course, the choice of the optimal bandwidth should be "somewhat" explained by the best score result.

title: make_regression should include categorical variables with weights

Currently `make_regression` does not do anything with categorical variables. You can only simulate continuous variables that can then be converted to categorical variables (e.g., `1 if x>0 else 0`). However in many cases it is necessary to have categorical variables (e.g., a city ID).

In many cases these categorical variables are not equally distributed. There may be many rows in a data set for some category values while few rows for other data. Thus the fraction of categories present should be available as an option like they are for outcome variables in make_classification.

creator: Dylan-Cunningham
title: Choose first feature to use in Tree and/or choose the order of features to use in the Tree
text:
The idea: Allow a user to pre-select which feature to first split off of and/or allow a user to pre-select which order of the features to split off of.

First example: I might want to first split on a seasonal feature. So, the model would be forced to split on that feature first, and optimize entropy/gini from there. (I am not telling the tree which value to split off of, just which feature to use.)

Second example: I might want to force the model to use 5 features in a specific order. The model would be forced to optimize entropy/gini in the order I specify.

Third example: I might want to force the model to use 3 features in a specific order, but I might pass 10 features to the model. The model would be forced to use the first 3, in the order I specify, then the model could use which other features necessary as specified by the other params.

The story: In finance/trading, sometimes we wish to force which features to make decisions off of (and the order!): all we need is an algo that tells us which levels to trade off of. 

We also find it useful to first force a seasonal difference (e.g., winter vs summer), then build a tree from there (one for winter and one for summer). Yes, we could build two trees after first splitting a dataset on our criteria; however, having one model that would do this makes things more succinct. Furthermore, when splitting the dataset like this, the number of rows gets reduced (bad). Mind you, in finance, sometimes it's difficult to get a lot of data.

One might argue that this defeats the purpose of using a model, like a decision tree, which optimizes the levels to trade and chooses which features are more important, but it doesn't. Sometimes optimizing is too prone to overfitting. Plus, the combination of human knowledge (subject matter experts) and data driven models can be better than one, or the other.

If this isn't the best algo or place to suggest this at, I would love some feedback. I would also love to see someone else enhance this idea.

events.author: onshek
events.comment: This sounds good to combine machine learning tools and expert knowledge on the finance market, and this also enable you more explanation about the whole model. While I'm also afraid this idea may be departure from sklearn itself.

events.author: Dylan-Cunningham
events.comment:
Hi Honfung Wong. Thank you for your quick response. You've mentioned two things, and I'll address both.

I appreciate your opinion about the idea I've presented. I do believe the mix of expert knowledge with ML tools combine to very valuable outcomes.

I have to respectfully disagree with your final statement that sklearn would not be a place for this idea. My idea (which I should/will clarify now) is to implement such logic in the Decision Tree scikit-learn algorithm (and maybe more, if it makes sense).

A decision tree decides which features to split, and splits based on a level in such a way as to optimize entropy/gini recursively, one-by-one. Currently (unless I am mistaken), the DecisionTreeClassifier and DecisionTreeRegressor classifiers do not allow a user to enforce which features must be used, nor the order they must be used, by the algorithm in order to optimize entropy/gini. On the contrary, these classifiers make all the "decisions" for the user.

It is advantageous, in some domains (like finance/trading), to give a user more control, if you will.

Do you know matplotlib.finance, which is used for the visualization of financial data (candlestick)? It was then split out of matplotlib to [mpl-finance](https://github.com/matplotlib/mpl-finance), and now it has been transferred to [mplfinance](https://github.com/matplotlib/mplfinance).

What I wanna say is that, the new features you mentioned above dose make sense (especially for quant) but, I also worry this can cause unnecessary trouble for other users.

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
Thanks both for the disucssion. Sounds like LightGBM supports this through `forcedsplits_filename`.

I think this is something that we might ultimately consider but there are a few technical challenges. 

The main obstacle is that we typically don't support feature properties with estimators for now, but this is something we are actively working on. i) we are discussing new kinds of input data, where passing feature information like this one would be more natural than with pure numpy arrays. And ii) we're also developing new estimators (i.e. the histogram-based gradient boosting trees) that now accept a feature-aligned argument for monotonic constraints, and that will hopefully soon also accept categorical feature masks. The forced-splits parameter would be of a similar nature. But these estimators are experimental, and the API is subject to change in the future: typically, these parameters would be better suited for the `fit` method rather than for the `__init__` method, but we don't have support for that kind of workflow yet.

events.author: mayer79
events.comment:
@lorentzenchr In LightGBM, there is the option of using [forced splits](https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Parameters.html#forcedsplits_filename):

>path to a .json file that specifies splits to force at the top of every decision tree before best-first learning commences

I think there are indeed a couple of interesting use cases, e.g., in insurance pricing:

1. Dataset with private cars and commercial cars. Important features like driver age are available only for private cars. In this case, it would be nice to specify: "Please first split on the "private/commercial" dummy feature, not on "driver age" (missing yes/no)", especially when thinking about model interpretability (variable importance, SHAP).
2. Dataset with (small) vans and (large) trucks. Here, splitting first on van (yes/no) dummy instead on "weight" might bring the necessary logic into the model.

I think in both cases, such an option avoids having to build and maintain two separate models.

creator: anntzer
title: Document order of patches in extract_patches_2d
text:
#### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

AFAICT, when `max_patches` is None and the input array is C-ordered `feature_extraction.image.extract_patches_2d` returns all patches "in the same order as would naive nested loops iterating in C order" -- IOW, the order expected by `reconstruct_from_patches_2d`.  However this is not documented; in fact the behavior for `max_patches=None` (the default) isn't documented either.

#### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

- Document that `max_patches=None` returns all patches (I can write a PR for that).
- Document order in which the patches are returned, and whether the input array needs to be C-contiguous to achieve that (that I don't know, and I don't know whether you want to guarantee the return order as well).

Description

 

In multifold.MDS  stress value doesn’t correspond to returned coordinates.

 

How to reproduce:

 

Apply MDS to four points in 2d-plane:

 

X   Y

1   4

If distances are Euclidean, then disparities matrix will be:

 

disparities =

 [ 4.                      3.                     0.                                    2.82842712  ]

 [ 2.82842712      2.23606798     2.82842712                    0.                  ]

 

Perform multidimensional scaling:

 

mds = manifold.MDS(n_components=2, dissimilarity="precomputed", random_state=42, metric = True)

results = mds.fit(disparities)

coords = results.embedding_

 

cords =

 [ -0.32503572      1.78399044 ]

 [  0.09843686      0.87890749 ]

 [  1.47842546     -1.76761757 ]

 [ -1.2518266      -0.89528037 ]

 

stress = results.stress_

0.0045113518633979315

 

Now calculate stress by hand.

 

First calculate Euclidian distances which correspond coordinates returned:

 

dis = euclidean_distances(coords)

 [ 0.                   0.9992518       3.98326395      2.83503675  ]

 [ 0.9992518     0.                     2.98470492      2.22956362  ]

And now we can calculate stress value:

0.0020293041020245147

 

So, the real stress calculated using returned coordinates doesn’t correspond to the stress value

results.stress_ = 0.0045113518633979315

 

After some debugging it is clear that MDS returns coordinates for the current iteration and stress for the previous iteration.

 

 

Here is the script to reproduce:

from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import euclidean_distances

import pandas as pd

creator: YashaPushak
title: Unexpected KNN kd_tree training times
text:
I've been analyzing the empirical performance scaling of the training times for a few different classifiers on the MNIST digits data set. I was surprised to find that KNN training times appear to grow faster than expected from theory (_i.e._, _n*log(n)_ -- the time that should be required to build the kd-tree).

To be precise, I collected some data on the training times of
`model = sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier(weights='distance', algorithm='kd_tree', leaf_size=1, metric='minkowski', p=10)`
 for 2501 random subsets of the MNIST training dataset. The number of training instances in each training subset was varied from [2 500, 2 519, ..., 50 000]. 

I used the running time measurements from the smaller 30% of the training instance sets to fit a few running time scaling models to the data as a function of the number of training instances in each instance set. For example: `a*n*log(n) + b`, where `a` and `b` are the parameters of the running time model that I fit, and `n` is the number of training instances in each subset. The model that I fit was `2.50e-05*n*log(n) - 0.0247`. 

I then used this model to make predictions for the running times on the larger training instance sets (let's call these larger training instance sets "challenge data" for the models).  Surprisingly, the larger challenge running time data was quite a bit larger than model's predictions. I also performed some bootstrap analysis of the procedure to produce 95% confidence intervals for the running times of the challenge data and the model predictions, which quite clearly do not overlap with each other. 

I also performed this analysis with a polynomial model `a*n**b` and an exponential model `a*b**n` as references. The polynomial model fits `b=1.12`, and provides a better estimate for the challenge running times, but it also clearly under-estimates them. The exponential model, not surprisingly, clearly over-estimates the running times for the challenge data. You can see a plot of the resulting analysis for yourself below:

[fitted-models-knn-v0.22.2.pdf](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/files/4429763/fitted-models-knn-v0.22.2.pdf)

Note: There are confidence intervals for both the observed median running times as well as for each of the fitted models. Their shown as shaded regions using the same colours as the models. However, they don't show up well in the plot because they are very small -- there isn't a lot of variability in these running times that cannot be explained by the size of the training set.

I've tried tinkering with the experimental setup that I used to do this analysis to see if I could find a means of accounting for this performance. For example, I tried dropping some of the running times for the smaller training set sizes to see if perhaps there are some lower order terms that are affecting the models when fit to the smallest support sizes (e.g., perhaps some data structure initialization can initially dominate the running time costs). However, I've had no luck with any such attempts. They all produce similar results or leave me without enough data to learn anything that is statistically significant. I would think it could possibly also be attributed to the apparent jump discontinuities around each power of two; however, I would then expect it to be possible for the models to over-estimate the challenge data in some of these runs, but it never did that either.

Does anyone have any guesses as to what could cause the training time scaling to be greater than log-linear? From my understanding of the theoretical bounds of the algorithm, it shouldn't be able to scale worse than log-linear, so I wonder if this could be some kind of a performance bug -- or perhaps the theory isn't correctly accounting for a relevant cost that is reflected in the running times?

creator: brunofmf
title: MultiOutputClassifier missleading score
text:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/95d4f0841d57e8b5f6b2a570312e9d832e69debc/sklearn/multioutput.py#L421

Well, just to let you know that when using a MultiOutputClassifier I was finding the score results to be surprisingly low. After digging a bit, I found that the score of a MultiOutputClassifier was being calculated as the mean of y being equal to y_pred for all targets: 
`np.mean(np.all(y == y_pred, axis=1))` 

For me, that was not, at all, the expected behaviour when you state that score "_Returns the mean accuracy on the given test data and labels_"! Indeed, I was expecting the returned accuracy to consider all hits. Something like: 
`np.mean(np.mean(y == y_pred, axis=0))`

A simple example:
```
y = [['low', 'medium', 'medium'], ['medium', 'medium', 'medium'], ['medium', 'high', 'high']]
y_pred = [['medium', 'medium', 'medium'], ['medium', 'high', 'medium'], ['low', 'high', 'high']]
```
Would return an accuracy of 0 instead of 0.667!
Why not give the user the chance to choose?

Anyway, if you find the current behaviour to be the expected one, feel free to close this issue.

creator: bhishanpdl
title: Feature Request: Include p-values attribute for logistic regression
text:
`Scikitlearn` is the de facto home for all kinds of modeling algorithms. It has a plethora of
algorithms but still one thing that seems to be missing is the implementation of `LogisticRegression` where we can have p-values.


It would be great if we have something like `model.p_values_` attribute for the Logistic Regression Models.

I know that there is another statistical library `statsmodels` which provides p_values, but a lot of programmers use `sklearn` and they build models based on this library. It is somewhat
inconvenient to use `statsmodels` just to get p-values and run other models such as `Random Forest` in `sklearn`.

Afterall, the API of `statsmodels` and `sklearn` are quite different. `sklean` is trend setter and 
most people feel comfortable with `sklearn` API, however, `statsmodels` follows R-programming API and they are quite different.

In conclusion, It would be great if `sklearn` provides `p-values` for linear models.

Considering how this request gets repeated pretty frequently, could someone chime in with some clearer justification that could be added to the documentation? Or this feature could find a home in scikit-learn contrib and then could be linked to? I'm unclear on the reasoning for not including p-values.

Reasoning in [#6773](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/6773):
> I am afraid that this is out of scope for scikit-learn for two reasons:
> 
> First the scope of scikit-learn is really predictive models, whereas the
> confidence intervals, p-values and related are in the scope of
> statsmodels.

First, scikit-learn exposes statistical tests via the [feature_selection](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/classes.html#module-sklearn.feature_selection) module, and they're very useful. It's not like scikit-learn does no stats.

Second, I would argue that p-values are part of model interpretation, and scikit-learn has an [inspection](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/classes.html#module-sklearn.inspection) module that has model interpretation capabilities. Scikit-learn supports model intepretation for tree-based models with [feature_importances_](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/search.html?q=feature_importances_). Granted, linear models expose the coefficients_. But why not add more interpretation capabilities if that's what people want?

> 
> Second, as far as I know, the research on the topic of confidence
> intervals and p-values in high dimension is still very much open.

This comment implies that p-values should not be added because there's uncertainty on how when p-values are reliable. The same comment could be made about other parts of the library, such as trusting the feature importances of tree-based models in a multicollinear dataset. From [#16860](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/16860):

> I think we need to help people avoid big mistakes, but advice can be hard
> because the literature is frequently revised and needs to be considered in
> the context of the user's task.

I think this philosphy applies to p-values. They are generally accepted as a useful statistical technique when used in the proper way. It's up to the user to use them appropriately. But people definitely want this feature (myself included :) ).

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
Interesting discussion so far. In my (incomplete and not unbiased) point of view there are several different layers to consider:
1. Inference, inspection, prediction: What is your use case?
   1. p-values and confidence intervals (CI): If my goal is to test a typical hypothesis, "feature x has no effect on the target y", then I'm better of with statsmodels as it is build, among other things, for statistical tests.
   2. Inspection/interpretability: How important is feature x in my fitted model? This can, for example, be answered with the help of permutation importance.
   3. Prediction interval: What is the uncertainty of my model's prediction? This is, for example, available in `GaussianProcessRegressor.predict(X, std=True)`.
2. Technical
   Although there are formulae for p-values and CI for linear models, even with penalties, there are at least two advantages to only predict expectations or quantiles (what scikit-learn regressors and classifiers do more or less exclusively):
   1. They need less assumptions than p-values and CI.
   2. They do not need the estimation of variance parameters (scale, dispersion, ...). This simplifies things a lot.
3. Responsibility: Does the benefit outweigh risks and costs?
   Apart from maintenance costs, there is a also a risk of misguided usage of CI, especially in sensible domains such as health and the medicine sector. On the other side, it's the user's responsibility to correctly use provided functionality.

 
My personal opinion about a few of those points:
   - 1.i. hypothesis testing: I would not duplicate functionality that is already reliably available in python.
   - 1.ii. inspection/interpretability: Having t-statistics for linear models would make sense to me, see [Molnar 4.1.1](https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/limo.html#interpretation). The tricky part is OHE categorical variables and penalties...
   - 1.iii. I'd love to have prediction intervals, but this is another story and has several other open issues.

Assumptions differ whether they are about control on the coefficients or on the prediction. The control on the prediction is much more lax then the control on the coefficients.

> Should sklearn not be able to do what statsmodels (sm) can do?

No. No need to duplicate functionality across packages.

creator: fdrobnic
title: Allow different scoring when "Some inputs do not have OOB scores." warning
text:
#### Background
Random Forests: When the "Some inputs do not have OOB scores." warning is emitted during training, it appears that the scoring method calculates the score using the inputs with the OOB scores only. E.g. if calculating accuracy, it is calculated as the ratio of number of correctly classified inputs vs. the number of inputs with the OOB scores (non-nan values).
#### Proposed solution
It would be interesting to be able to get the accuracy calculated as the ratio of number of correctly classified inputs vs. the number of all inputs considered, probably by introducing a new parameter. This would automatically eliminate cases in GridSearchCV where the num_estimators is too low. This is currently more challenging to achieve. It would be also helpful to mention this behavior in the docs.

creator: adrinjalali
title: `check_estimator` for estimators which require a mandatory extra fit param.
text:
Right now the `check_estimators` will fail if the given estimator requires a parameter to `fit` other than `X, y`. https://github.com/fairlearn/fairlearn/pull/342 is an example of where it fails.

In some use-cases, it makes sense to require an extra parameter. For instance, in the case of fairness, you may require the `sensitive_features` to be passed as well as the data itself. How should we handle these cases?

An alternative would be to have feature names during fit and set the _sensitive feature names_ in `__init__`.

@thomasjpfan would you have an idea?

events.author: rth
events.comment:
Maybe we can introduce `_required_fit_parameters` by analogy with `_required_parameters` for `__init__`?

Though generally it would likely mean that we would just skip all tests for estimators that require fit parameters, since it's hard to know what should be passed there in common tests.

events.author: amueller
events.comment: So in effect it would be the same as "_skip" right? Unless we provide a mechanism to create a valid column for arbitrary data ;)

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment: In our monthly call we talked about this, and it seems we're okay with having a mechanism in the estimator checks, for the test suite to provide a data generator. This would have the benefit of keeping the estimators clean from test specific code, and yet allow third party developers to further tune the estimator checks. Afterall, one primary goal of estimator checks is to make sure they can be used in a pipeline and/or a grid search, and we know right now estimators can fail in the tests and yet be _compatible_ with our pipeline/GS/etc.

creator: rth
title: Document/standardize how to skip network tests
text:
Following discussion in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/16743 I think it would be good to document and standardize how we skip tests that require network or download (this could also apply to tests that are skipped for other reason). Currently there are these mechanisms,
 1. `SKLEARN_SKIP_NETWORK_TESTS` for some tests
 2. `network` pytest marker for other tests, meaning that such tests can be deselected with `-m "not network"` pytest option
 3.  also the `--skip-network` pytest option, that skips tests with the `network` marker. The issue with this is that it requires a `conftests.py`, which is currently not available e.g. when scikit-learn is installed and tests are run with `pytest --pyargs sklearn`. 


I would propose to remove 1, and standardize/document the use of either 2 or 3. If we go with 3 we might need to move `conftests.py` under the `sklearn` folder, although it's also not ideal.

creator: lorentzenchr
title: Doc/Discussion: Discrimination in examples and user guide
text:
#### Goal
A space to discuss thougtfully and amicably, if the topic of discrimination and bias should be addressed in the documentation (examples and user guide):
- bias in model
- bias in data

#### Non Goal
Endless and pointless discussions. So please, use every word wisely and sparingly.

#### Possible Solutions
Mention in example X that the data may contain bias and reference a link to a good source for further insights.
Discover model bias in example Y for a certain feature subspace and investigate a little.

#### References
The examples [Poisson regression and non-normal loss](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_poisson_regression_non_normal_loss.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-linear-model-plot-poisson-regression-non-normal-loss-py) and [Tweedie regression on insurance claims](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_tweedie_regression_insurance_claims.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-linear-model-plot-tweedie-regression-insurance-claims-py) use an insurance dataset, example [Common pitfalls in interpretation of coefficients of linear models](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/auto_examples/inspection/plot_linear_model_coefficient_interpretation.html) uses a wages dataset.
Some concern where pointed out in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/16648#discussion_r388974502.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> Some concern where pointed out in #16648 (comment).

To copy this discussion here, for future reference

@adrinjalali :
> The issue is that the data is biased and we can't even measure that bias because we don't even have the features we need (like race and gender). Not using those features doesn't mean we're not going to have biased model discriminating against a certain group, and I'm very very worried about putting an example out there which people would then use as a reference to [unintentionally] discriminate against people. @romanlutz, do you happen to have a good example for this one?

@rth :
> I'm all for better examples for controlling for bias, but I also don't think this PR is the right place for this discussion. It merely refactors an existing example, we should have this discussion in a separate issue.
>
> As a side note, I imagine there could indeed be some sample selection bias in the the data (i.e. company chooses customers), however the target variable (frequency or cost of accidents) shouldn't be too biased, I think? At least significantly less biased than in other examples such as scikit-learn.org/dev/auto_examples/inspection/plot_linear_model_coefficient_interpretation.html for predicting wage. Also pricing policy of an insurance company doesn't directly impact how often one has accidents, so at least there is no immediate feedback loop with the training data. I'm not an expert on this, and there are likely other effects, but I'm just saying that we should discuss it in a separate issue.

@romanlutz:

> I don't disagree with the suggestions to discuss this elsewhere. For more information on what @adrinjalali is referring to I recommend "Big Data's Disparate Impact" by Barocas and Selbst. file:///C:/Users/rolutz/AppData/Local/Temp/SSRN-id2477899.pdf section I.D. The entire piece is actually relevant for such a scenario, but that's the section that discusses excluding sensitive features such as race & gender. Other than that there's still potential bias in how the data got collected (I.A, I.B, I.C).
> I think there's value in acknowledging such potential shortcomings so that people don't assume that it's the best (or only) way to approach the task. We wouldn't want users to end up on [my list of questionable or unethical use cases](https://github.com/romanlutz/ResponsibleAI). With the acknowledgment it should be clear that it's just a demonstration of scikit-learn. At least that's my point of view :-) Thanks for asking!

events.comment:
Thanks @lorentzenchr we don't actually have that much discussion on this topic in scikit-learn so far.

I would propose to add,
 - (possibly) a small section to the user guide under "3. Model selection and evaluation" regarding bias in data in models, with a few classical examples of applications and references to further reading. Don't we have an issue about it already somewhere @adrinjalali ?
 - an example, that controls for bias with a few protected variables (for instance on the wage dataset). If possible to correct the model for it without using external dependencies, or otherwise point to relevant external resources.

I'm not sure how useful it is to say in examples using real-word datasets that the data is biased. Since most data, particularly related to human interaction, is biased in some way.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
To go back to the car accidents dataset,
> > The issue is that the data is biased and we can't even measure that bias 
because we don't even have the features we need (like race and gender)
>
> Not using those features doesn't mean we're not going to have biased model discriminating against a certain group, and I'm very very worried about putting an example out there which people would then use as a reference to [unintentionally] discriminate against people.

Absolutely I agree about not using sensitive features not being a solution in general.  I'm just not fully sure how this applies to the car accidents dataset.

 Sure, there could be some data collection bias. Still putting aside regulatory constraints & practices in insurance industry (of which I don't know much), say we are trying to model car accidents frequency. Generally there are variations for variables that could be considered protected, e.g.,
 - young drivers have more accidents
 - possibly, women are safer drivers and have fewer accidents [[1](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/15389580309857)]

and that the model reflects that.
Would you then say that the data is biased (with an age/gender discrimination) and that the model needs be corrected for it? I can understand doing that from a social fairness point of view, but I still wouldn't call it problematic bias in the training data in this case.

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
I my point of view, one has make a distinction between
- Discrimination: This raises ethical questions about fairness and solidarity that a society has to answer, e.g. via laws and institutions like regulators. I would not expect scikit-learn to comment on that.
- Bias:
    - Model bias should (almost) always be a concern, e.g. Ridge regression (and most others) makes a trade-off between bias and variance. There are good statistical means to measure this.
    - Data bias: Here, it depends on the use case and assumed statistical population of which the dataset is a - possibly biased - sample.
Let's stick to the car insurance claim dataset of the examples linked above. If the goal is to measure portfolio quality, the dataset should give good answers. If the goal is to price new business (new customers), the difference between the portfolio of the dataset and the porfolio on the market might be a huge concern.

I'd also like to mention [Discrimination-Free Insurance Pricing](https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3520676), which shows that one might need all possibly discriminatory features in order to compute discrimination-free prices.

events.author: romanlutz
events.comment:
I'm not an anthropologist or domain expert, so I certainly don't want to make the claim that I can tell you whether this is fine or not. I have come across many applications that seemed benign at first and turned into something much less benign when deployed in practice. For that purpose I've put together a list of questionable or outright unethical use cases https://github.com/romanlutz/ResponsibleAI .

I do understand that the purpose here is simply to show how scikit-learn is used for a certain task. The point of the notebook is not necessarily to say "this is how you approach this problem and this is the one and only solution". That can also be acknowledged to be 100% transparent about this and  to make sure people don't get the wrong idea.

About the actual criticism of the use case:
- Car insurance is definitely a domain where certain candidates for sensitive features such as age might correlate very well with the risk, e.g. young drivers have more accidents as @rth mentions above. Therefore young drivers without prior experience end up paying more than slightly older drivers. This seems to be generally accepted by society (or at least it's in place), although I can't speak about legal background. It is true that a group of people as defined by one or more features may or may not need to be "protected" (by law) depending on the application scenario. What "protected" means can also vary. If you survey the fairness literature you'll easily find 20+ definitions and you'll need to consult domain experts & anthropologists to figure out which ones are sensible (with no guarantee that they'll agree).
- Let's take a different commonly used sensitive feature: gender. @rth you write above that "possibly, women are safer drivers and have fewer accidents". I did a quick search and there are various articles that seem to suggest that women indeed pay less for car insurance. Is that because of a better track record (traffic offenses, etc.), or because of gender? Do men, women, and non-binary people pay the same with the same track record? Suddenly this becomes a much harder question to answer than whether women should on average pay less without quantifying how much less, and answering questions like the ones I posed. ML interpretability can help a little bit with that, but essentially it leads you back to what @adrinjalali said: "we can't even measure that bias because we don't even have the features we need (like race and gender)". 
- Let's take yet another sensitive feature: race. Again, we can't measure that in this case because we don't have the feature. Let's just assume that there's some difference in the data between race A and race B. Can we really justify that A should be paying more than B? If we focus in on the US to examine this, then things like socio-economic status will play a role. If people of your race have basically been forced to live in a worse area then you potentially have a higher risk for damage to your car. I could come up with a few more consequences of how the historical discrimination would affect the current scenario, but I'll leave it at that. [Note: Every country has a different history that would have to be examined. I'm just using the US since that's one context that I'm somewhat familiar with.] Now as a modeler you get into the tricky spot of making calls such as "Should our model treat all races fairly/the same?" (bonus: "what is fair?"), "Should our model compensate for historical discrimination?", and from a company perspective certainly also "Will this model get us on the front page of the <insert your favorite newspaper> because we're treating certain (sub)groups of people much worse than others?".

I'm sure actual domain experts would be able to point out dozens more questions one could ask. I barely scratched the surface here, without even looking at any data. The point was merely to show that a supposedly simple scenario isn't always as simple since this data represents the real world which is much more complicated than just features and labels/scores.

@lorentzenchr captures this: "This raises ethical questions about fairness and solidarity that a society has to answer, e.g. via laws and institutions like regulators. I would not expect scikit-learn to comment on that." The point is that scikit-learn is so popular that perhaps you need to make this absolutely clear. I'll reiterate my sentence from the start: That can also be acknowledged to be 100% transparent about this and to make sure people don't get the wrong idea.

I'm not a contributor to this project and just shared my 2cts because @adrinjalali asked. I certainly appreciate the situation you find yourselves in, but I think a little disclaimer/acknowledgment of the problem would go a long way (and without you having to replace the entire scenario). It's your call, of course.

creator: jnboehm
title: Pipeline requires both fit and transform method to be available instead of only fit_transform
text:
#### Describe the bug
Calling a pipeline with a nonparametric function causes an error since the function `transform()` is missing.  The pipeline itself calls the function `fit_transform()` if it's present.  For nonparametric functions (the most prominent being t-SNE) a regular `transform()` method does not exist since there is no projection or mapping that is learned.  It could still be used for dimensionality reduction.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Example:
```python
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

make_pipeline(TSNE(), PCA())
```


#### Expected Results
A pipeline is created.

#### Actual Results
Output:
```
TypeError: All intermediate steps should be transformers and implement fit and transform or be the string 'passthrough' 'TSNE(angle=0.5,...
```
#### Possible Solution
Editing this https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/95d4f0841/sklearn/pipeline.py#L179
to the following in order to reflect the change:
```python
if (not hasattr(t, "fit_transform")) or not (hasattr(t, "fit") and hasattr(t, "transform")):
```

#### Versions
```
import sklearn; sklearn.show_versions()
System:
    python: 3.8.2 (default, Feb 26 2020, 22:21:03)  [GCC 9.2.1 20200130]
executable: /usr/bin/python3
   machine: Linux-5.5.9-arch1-2-x86_64-with-glibc2.2.5

Python dependencies:
       pip: 20.0.2
setuptools: 46.0.0
   sklearn: 0.22.2.post1
     numpy: 1.18.1
     scipy: 1.4.1
    Cython: 0.29.15
    pandas: 1.0.1
matplotlib: 3.2.0
    joblib: 0.14.1

Built with OpenMP: True
```

events.comment: Yes, tsne, at least in our conception and implementation of it, does not induce a model that can be applied to a test set..

events.author: jnothman

events.author: jnboehm
events.comment: That's a fair point, I was trying to use it for a single pass pipeline, essentially.  I see how the lack of an internal model could become an issue once test data is introduced.  Anyways, thanks for the explanation.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: Oh, I didn't note that you made no attempt to run any methods on the pipeline. I agree that it should be possible to construct the pipeline and run fit_transform on it, even if it is a somewhat degenerate pipeline. Thanks for reporting!

events.author: jnboehm
events.comment: In that case, what should the behavior be?  Should it check the `transform` property of the transformer and raise a `TypeError` before trying to call the function [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/d205638475ca542dc46862652e3bb0be663a8eac/sklearn/pipeline.py#L713)?  Or should it warn at construction time that only fit_transform is available (or that this pipeline can only be called once)?

events.author: johannfaouzi
events.comment:
I would go for the latter. It's a degenerate pipeline but users would expect it to work.

It would require to change https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/95d4f0841/sklearn/pipeline.py#L179-L180 so that, if an intermediate step has only `fit_transform`, the available methods for the pipeline are:
* `fit` (as always),
* `fit_transform` if the last step is a transformer (i.e. has a `transform` method),
* `fit_predict` if the last step has a `fit_predict` method.

An error should probably be raised if the last step is not compatible (i.e. is a predictor without a `fit_predict` method).

Edit: TSNE could be the last estimator of the pipeline, so the check should be run for all the steps. It might a good idea to perform a check on all the estimators first, to see if there is an estimator with limitations (only `fit_transform` for any transformer), then perform a `if else` loop for both cases (we could keep the current code for one case, we raise a warning for the other case).

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
It should be fine to fit, but raise an error when transform or predict etc
are called. It might make it a bit of a nuisance for people who try putting
tsne in a pipeline and only get an error after fitting... So I wonder if
it's worth warning in the case that an intermediate step does not support
transform.

>

events.author: jnboehm
events.comment:
I personally would just opt to warn in case an intermediate step only supports `fit_transform`.

Is my assumption correct that the `@if_delegate_has_method` would take care of raising errors already?  Then simply warning during construction and letting it crash if the user specifies an unsupported operation would in my opinion be sufficient.  Or should more cases be handled after the warning?

Since `fit_transform` will be preferred over `transform` I'm not sure whether the code needs to be changed for that at all.

Also, in what way do `validate_steps` and `validate_transformers` differ?  This is a bit unclear to me.  For now I'll change both functions.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
if_delegate_has_method does not check the intermediate estimators, only the
final one.

FeatureUnion._validate_transformers handles all the transformers
identically. Pipeline._validate_steps has to handle the last step
differently.

creator: bryant1410
title: Support typing
text:
#### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Support Python typing, which is available in Python 3.5+, compatible with scikit-learn. This can enable tools to automatically get the estimator arg types (e.g., linters), for example. And it's a Python standard now.

#### Describe your proposed solution

For example, `SVC` could be like this:

```python
def __init__(
    self,
     C: float = 1.0,
     kernel: Union[Callable[[np.ndarray, np.ndarray], np.ndarray],
                   Literal["linear", "poly", "rbf", "sigmoid", "precomputed"]] = "rbf",
     degree: int = 3,
     gamma: Union[float, Literal["scale", "auto"]] = "scale",
     coef0: float = 0.0,
     shrinking: bool = True,
     probability: bool = False,
     tol: float = 1e-3,
     cache_size: int = 200,
     class_weight: Optional[Union[Mapping[int, float], Literal["balanced"]]] = None,
     verbose: bool = False,
     max_iter: int = -1,
     decision_function_shape: Literal["ovo", "ovr"] = "ovr",
     break_ties: bool = False,
     random_state: Optional[Union[int, RandomState]] = None,
 ) -> None:
```

#### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

An alternative is to keep the types just in the docstrings. However, is hard for tools to parse the arg types.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
I think this is nice to have as long as we restrict it to the `__init__` arguments. Most of our parameters are not long union types, so this is a net benefit.

The fun one is to figure out what "array-like" is. For example, what would be the type of `OneHotEncoder`'s `categories`? Maybe as a starting point we can have the `array-like` be `Any`.

events.author: bryant1410
events.comment: What about `Sequence[Any]` for array-like?

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: We can just not annotate array-likes yet...

events.author: bryant1410
events.comment: What problem do you folks see with `Sequence[Any]`? AFAIK, anything with `__getitem__` and `__len__` complies with it.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
```
>>> isinstance(np.arange(5), Sequence)
False
```

events.author: bryant1410
events.comment: I see. Don't linters process these annotations (such as `Sequence`) in general as duck types and not as strict subclasses?

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> I see. Don't linters process these annotations (such as Sequence) in general as duck types and not as strict subclasses?

The issue is that ndarray is more general (and can besides be a pd.DataFrame or scipy.sparse.csr_matrix for input). So even if it worked it would result in static analysers errors when methods not available in Sequence are used (related https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/12953). The long term solution might be https://github.com/numpy/numpy-stubs but for now I would just not type anything that is an array and leave it as `Any` by default.

Also see related discussion in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/11170

We could also define frequently used types somewhere (e.g. `sklearn.typing`) BTW, `Litteral` is Python 3.8+, and would need backporting cf https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/14063 

You could propose a PR for one class `__init__` to start to see how it goes. However, it's likely that we would need mypy or another static analyzer running in CI as otherwise I don't see how we can enforce that annotations are correct (and stay correct as code evolve). So https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/12953 might need fixing first.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> We could also define frequently used types somewhere (e.g. sklearn.typing) 

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/master/pandas/_typing.py Is an example of what this could look like.

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment: In addition to linter, I really would like that typing to help us to automatically manage some part of the dosctring of the estimators.

events.author: rth
events.comment:

Yes, I'm hoping that as well. See https://github.com/numpy/numpydoc/issues/196 Some work would be needed in numpydoc, but it should be doable I think.

events.author: bryant1410
events.comment:
> We could also define frequently used types somewhere (e.g. `sklearn.typing`) BTW, `Litteral` is Python 3.8+, and would need backporting cf #14063

For `Literal`, `typing_extensions` can be used.

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
I feel like we might need to write a SLEP  before we start using type annotations.

IMHO, from a contributor standpoint, annotations are difficult to deal with because they basically require learning a whole new language - much like learning our docstring conventions. This will raise the **barrier to contribute even higher**, and it will also add work to us as maintainer: think of all the time we already spend reviewing docstring formatting.

Another thing that I've personally experienced using annotations, is that annotation + `mypy` prevents from using some really basic workflow. For example:

```py
x = [1, 2, 3]
# <do something that requires x to still be a list>
x = set(x)
```

`mypy` will complain with an Incompatible types error (you need to declare `x` as e.g. `Union[list, set]`). That too will make contributors lives harder, and will potentially make our code more convoluted.

Automatic docstring generation is a strong incentive to start using annotations, but there are also some issues that I think we should not sweep under the rug. We should also clearly define *where* we want annotations. It seems like we're aiming for estimators `__init__` only, which would likely limit the number of issues / surprises.

It'd be nice to have all this clearly laid out in a SLEP so we can all make an informed decision.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
I agree that it would be good to have this discussion, and the above concerns are valid, but I'm not sure a SLEP is the right format for it. Can't we have this discussion in this issue, then summarize it in the documentation? My issue with the SLEP is that it adds months if not years delay for talking a decision, which is fine for large architectural changes, but less so for something like this. People will not read SLEPs when contributing either.

> This will raise the barrier to contribute even higher, and it will also add work to us as maintainer: think of all the time we already spend reviewing docstring formatting.

Well the idea is that some of that work can now be done by mypy, as opposed to asking maintainers to review docstring formatting. [Numpy](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/9e85b3701f80a5e48ca5e7fc5281af2aba591870/doc/release/upcoming_changes/16515.new_feature.rst#numpy-is-now-typed), [scipy](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/ac49c61d92fc11719b4a6a1ad09145ee607dd76f/doc/release/1.5.0-notes.rst#other-changes) and pandas are currently incrementally adding type annotations. I doubt they would have done so if it was a significant barrier to contribution or a large maintenance burden. I would be more interested in getting some feedback of how it's working for them, and prototyping in scikit-learn on an optional basis rather than SLEP like formal spec of how they should be used.

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
> Can't we have this discussion in this issue

I guess we can, but issues are harder to read and parse due to their conversational structure. It's much easier to miss something important when reading an issue than when reading a SLEP (assuming the issue is read at all, which I would say is an optimistic assumption ;) ).

Writing a SLEP doesn't have to be that long IMO. The reason SLEPs take forever is because of the async between the writer and the reviewers. If 2+ core devs commit to writing/reviewing the SLEP in a timely manner, it should go fast. I have a minor bias against annotations for now so I wouldn't be the best champion, but I'm happy to provide timely reviews if a SLEP is made.

> prototyping in scikit-learn on an optional basis

what do you mean by that? I feel like we either want to go all in with annotations, or not at all?

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
> Numpy, scipy and pandas are currently incrementally adding type annotations. I doubt they would have done so if it was a significant barrier to contribution or a large maintenance burden. I would be more interested in getting some feedback of how it's working for them

@rgommers @jorisvandenbossche would you mind sharing your thoughts on the tradeoffs you've identified regarding the adoption of type annotations? Thanks!!

events.author: rth
events.comment:
>  annotation + mypy prevents from using some really basic workflow. For example:

About that, yes, I also run into it in the past: see https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/common_issues.html#redefinitions-with-incompatible-types and it's likely that using the [`--allow-redefinition`](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/command_line.html#cmdoption-mypy-allow-redefinition) in the config would address some of it.

events.author: rgommers
events.comment:
> Another thing that I've personally experienced using annotations, is that annotation + mypy prevents from using some really basic workflow. 

Agreed, this is one of the more common annoyances. Something like
```
out = func(x)
out = [y for y in out]
```
It is usually easy to work around, but may introduce some churn.

I think type annotations have just become relevant this year, after we all dropped Python 2.7. There is a significant amount of interest in having them. I agree it's extra work, but it also may attract new contributors - that has certainly been the case for NumPy, we have two new maintainers that are focusing on type annotations.

It has been hard going for things like `ndarray`/`array_like` and `dtype`s. The reasons for why those are hard do point at things that are now considered mistakes in early design decisions (things like dtypes not having a good type hierarchy, and `array_like` being too flexible). That does tell me that there's a real benefit in supporting type annotations for maintainers - it prevents you from introducing new constructs that may turn out to be mistakes.

On the whole I'd say it's more work than I had thought beforehand, there's as much of a chance of hitting limitations/bugs in `mypy` than finding real bugs in your own code base (`mypy` is fairly immature still), but it's probably worth it in the long term.

events.author: jorisvandenbossche
events.comment:
I share the concerns of @NicolasHug about this being yet another barrier for contributors, and the experience of regularly running into mypy issues that isn't necessarily an issue in your code. Even for me, being a long time pandas dev but not someone who really dived into the annotation topic, this is regularly a hurdle. So if doing this, this requires very good docs and guidelines for specific cases in the contributing guidelines about this (I still find the pandas ones somewhat lacking in this regard).

Regarding the trade-offs in pandas, I might not be the best person to ask this, because I am mainly encountering hurdles and not yet experiencing benefits (but I am also not that that much day-to-day *coding* development on pandas) (cc @simonjayhawkins)  
And also: I think the *real* benefit will only be seen later on. In the beginning, when gradually adding typing, the typing itself isn't that valuable yet (because many things are not yet typed), while it already adds an extra hurdle in contributing. I assume that over time, the benefit increases and the hurdles decrease (better docs, more examples already in the code to look at, people getting more familiar with it). But to say: the trade-off might initially not be favourable, but we do it with the idea it will become so later on.

Some other aspects of my experience with it:

- In pandas, the main problem is that we have a very loose typing in the user-facing methods, making the typing rather inconvenient (very long and complicated or otherwise general type definitions) and therefore also less useful typing-wise. On the one hand, you can say that this points to a design issue in pandas (and that's certainly correct), but on the other hand: this has historically grown like this, and it is how it is now, and we have to deal with it if we want to add type annotations now (changing the public API can of course be done, but is a longer process, and sometimes the flexibility in what it accepts is also convenient). I think the situation in scikit-learn is a quite a bit better in this regard, though, so this might be less of an issue (there is of course stil the case of "array-like").

- Given the above, the main benefit as a pandas developer I have experienced is in *internal functions* where the typing is often much stricter (or can be made stricter with some refactoring, which often cleans up the code). So from a scikit-learn/pandas developer point of view, I would personally start there. But of course, this is at odds with the demand of (power) users to have type annotations in the *public interface* (and a reason this might attract new contributors).

- I am personally strongly opposed to the idea of "type annotations can replace the types in the docstring" (but this is a very personal opinion to be clear ;)), and thus I don't think this should be a motivation to do this. To me, they serve a different purpose, although there is overlapping information. The type annotations are more oriented towards developers (or tools), while the docstring explanation is meant to be readable by regular (and thus including newbie) users. 
  For example, in a docstring, I prefer that a user doesn't need to parse a type explanation like `Optional[Union[Sequence, np.ndarray, pd.DataFrame]]`, but can rather read something `array-like or DataFrame, optional`. As discussed in https://github.com/numpy/numpydoc/issues/196 somewhat, there might be ways to convert from the one to other format (for simple cases), of course, or to have validation of consistency between the two formats.
  (sidenote: the reason that I feel this way is maybe also largely because of the loose typing in pandas, which I mentioned in the first bullet point. Because this gives annotations like *"Union[List[Callable], Tuple[Callable, ...], Mapping[Union[str, int], Callable], NoneType]"* (from https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/33025#issuecomment-604689444))

creator: hrbzkm98
title: Loss Function (All-Threshold Loss) for ordinal response variables HistGradientBoosting
text:
<!--
If you want to propose a new algorithm, please refer first to the scikit-learn
inclusion criterion:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/faq.html#what-are-the-inclusion-criteria-for-new-algorithms
-->

#### Describe the workflow you want to enable
If the target is discrete multiclass, but ordinal (ordered) in nature (e.g. Likert scale, user ratings, preference levels), as opposed to nominal, would be great to have support for loss function that recognize the ordinal nature of the target variable.

(Note the difference between "learning-to-rank" and "ordinal classification". "learning-to-rank", implemented by popular boosting libraries XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, produces relative ordering between items, and the output predictions are not class labels, while "ordinal classification" does produce class labels. Here is a blog post to introduce the reader to [loss functions for ordinal classification](http://fa.bianp.net/blog/2013/loss-functions-for-ordinal-regression/).)
#### Describe your proposed solution
All-Threshold loss is the proposed solution. [Rennie, et al](https://ttic.uchicago.edu/~nati/Publications/RennieSrebroIJCAI05.pdf) described the All-Threshold loss function. Here is an easy-to-understand blog post introducing readers to [loss functions for ordinal classification](http://fa.bianp.net/blog/2013/loss-functions-for-ordinal-regression/).
Fabian, et al implemented the [mord](https://github.com/fabianp/mord) package using logistic regression with All Threshold Loss

#### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
Historically, in Logistic Regression, popular approach proposed by McCullagh ([paper](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2984952)) uses Cumulative Logit link function. Here is the main disadvantage of this approach:
> Probabilistic models for discrete ordinal response have also
been studied in the statistics literature [McCullagh, 1980;
Fu and Simpson, 2002]. However, the models suggested are
much more complex, and even just evaluating the likelihood
of a predictor is not straight-forward.
From Page 2 Rennie, Jason D. M. and Srebro, Nathan . [Loss functions for preference levels: Regression with discrete ordered labels](https://ttic.uchicago.edu/~nati/Publications/RennieSrebroIJCAI05.pdf).

Note that Cumulative Logit is the probabilistic approach, proposed by McCullagh in 1980.
All threshold loss is much easier to scale to large datasets, which is very much the purpose of HistGradientBoosting.
#### References
Papers
[1] Rennie, Jason D. M. and Srebro, Nathan, Loss functions for preference levels: Regression with discrete ordered labels.
[2] Dembczynski, Krzysztof and Kotlowski, Wojciech and Slowinski, Roman. Ordinal Classification with Decision Rules.
[3] Pedregosa, Fabian and Bach, Francis R. and Gramfort, Alexandre. On the Consistency of Ordinal Regression Methods.
[4] Li, Ling and Lin, Hsuan-Tien. Ordinal Regression by Extended Binary Classification.

events.author: hrbzkm98
events.comment:
Hi all,
I am writing my thesis on this - I have an “almost working” version implemented based on HistGradientBoosting and I currently forked the project to refactor my code. If you are curious, I can post my draft thesis here. The main challenge is that the threshold parameter, “theta”, would have to be jointly optimized with leaf weights, w. It requires the aggregation of a third gradient statistics, which is the vector of second order gradients with respect to w and theta. Computing the reduction in loss after split is also different, since due to the need to optimize theta jointly with w, when a split is proposed, the optimal weight on other leaves are changed due to this. But I have worked out the math and come up with an efficient way to evaluate all this. Lastly, the hessian matrix in terms of leaf weights and theta is singular. The solution is to use majorization minimization, making the hessian matrix positive definite and thus invertible.

creator: allentran
title: MultiOutputRegressor doesn't support sparse y matrix
text:
This snippet works fine because the sparse `y` is converted to a numpy array. 
```
from sklearn import linear_model, multioutput
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix

x = csr_matrix((13, 5))
y = csr_matrix((13, 2))

m_reg = multioutput.MultiOutputRegressor(linear_model.SGDRegressor())
m_reg.fit(x, y.toarray())
```
Same snippet without converting the sparse `y` matrix:
```
from sklearn import linear_model, multioutput
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix

x = csr_matrix((13, 5))
y = csr_matrix((13, 2))

m_reg = multioutput.MultiOutputRegressor(linear_model.SGDRegressor())
m_reg.fit(x, y)
```

This is the traceback:
```
/apps/python3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/sklearn/utils/validation.py in check_X_y(X, y, accept_sparse, accept_large_sparse, dtype, order, copy, force_all_finite, ensure_2d, allow_nd, multi_output, ensure_min_samples, ensure_min_features, y_numeric, warn_on_dtype, estimator)
    758                         dtype=None)
    759     else:
--> 760         y = column_or_1d(y, warn=True)
    761         _assert_all_finite(y)
    762     if y_numeric and y.dtype.kind == 'O':

/apps/python3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/sklearn/utils/validation.py in column_or_1d(y, warn)
    795         return np.ravel(y)
    796 
--> 797     raise ValueError("bad input shape {0}".format(shape))
    798 
    799 

ValueError: bad input shape ()
```

My reading of the source is that the line [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/95d4f0841d57e8b5f6b2a570312e9d832e69debc/sklearn/utils/validation.py#L785 ) does not convert a sparse matrix into a numpy array. That is
```
np.asarray(csr_matrix((13, 2)))
```
does not return a numpy array of shape `(13, 2)`, instead it is a shape `()` array containing the sparse matrix as its only element.

Converting each `y` as necessary would be fine as long as you don't convert the entire `y` at once (which obviously the user could just do on their own).

creator: lorentzenchr
title: Tweedie deviance loss for tree based models
text:
#### Describe the workflow you want to enable
If the target `y` is (approximately) Poisson, Gamma or else Tweedie distributed, it would be beneficial for tree based regressors to support [Tweedie deviance loss functions](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html#mean-poisson-gamma-and-tweedie-deviances) as splitting criterion. This partially addresses #5975.

#### Describe your proposed solution
Ideally, one first implements
- [ ] differentiable loss functions #15123

and then adds the different loss criteria to the tree based models:
- [x]  `DecisionTreeRegressor` (poisson only) https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/17386
- [x] `RandomForestRegressor` (poisson only) https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/19836
- [ ] `GradientBoostingRegressor`
- [x] `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` (poisson and gamma but no other tweedie cases) https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/16692

#### Open for Discussion
For Poisson and Tweedie deviance with `1<=power<2`, ther target `y` may be zero while the prediction `y_pred` must be strictly larger than zero. A tree might find a split where one node has  `y=0` for all samples in that node, resulting naively in `y_pred = mean(y) = 0` for that node. I see 3 different solutions to that:
1. Use a log-link function, i.e. predict `y_pred = np.exp(tree)`
    See #16692 for HistGradientBoostingRegressor. This may be no option for DecisionTreeRegressor.
2. Use a splitting rule that forbids splits where one node has `sum(y)=0`.
    One might also introduce some option like `min_y_weight`, such that splits with  `sum(sample_weight*y) < min_y_weight` are forbidden.
3. Use some form of parent child average `y_pred = a * mean(y) + (1-a) * y_pred_parent` and forbid further splits, see [1].
(Bayes/credibility theory motivates to set `a = sum(sample_weight*y)/(gamma+sum(sample_weight*y))` for some hyperparameter `gamma`.)

There is also a dirty solution that allows `y_pred=0` but sets the value `min(eps, y_pred)` in the loss function for some tiny value of `eps`.

#### References
[1] [R rpart library](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rpart/vignettes/longintro.pdf), chapter 8 Poisson regression

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
I would start with `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` which is order of magnitude more scalable and therefore useful that the other models.

The Gradient Boosting models already have the notion of link functions tied to their loss. Tthis is necessary to Bernoulli / logit expected values for binary classifications, and Categorical / softmax expected values for multiclass classification for instance. At the moment the link function is hard-coded for each loss and I think this is fine as a first step.

+1 for using the log link for Tweedie / Poisson / Gamma by default.

events.author: ogrisel

Or having a fast implementation RF with Poisson/Gamma/Tweedie response variables by adding such ?

Nowadays, whenever I tried HistGradientBoostingClassifier/Regressor vs RandomForestClassifier/Regressor both with default hyperparams, the former was always the fastest with better predictive performance. Hyper-parameter tuning often imrpoves a bit but is often not critical. So to me HistGradientBoostingClassifier/Regressor is the new no-brainer baseline.
