creator: csbrown
title: MeanShift predict method is incorrect
text:
#### Describe the workflow you want to enable

The `predict` method on the `MeanShift` class takes in a point and returns the nearest "cluster center" from the final iterations of the training data.  However, `MeanShift` is a lazy learner.  The normal process for `fit`ting is to simply store the training data.  The `predict` method should then perform all of the logic that is currently in the `fit` method.

Note that the current implementation is actually a weighted KMeans.  It is not MeanShift.

#### Describe your proposed solution

Fix MeanShift.  I'm happy to do it if there is agreement that this is broken.

events.author: jeremiedbb
events.comment:
>  However, MeanShift is a lazy learner

What makes you say that ?

`MeanShift` is not knn. It's an iterative algorithm which updates the means at each iteration to find the best partition of the data. The predict method concerns unseen data for which we just want to find the closest center based on the best means found by the algo on the training data. The means are not (and should not be) updated in this case.

events.author: csbrown
events.comment: "The means are not (and should not be) updated in this case." Agreed.  But the way that one classifies an unseen point with MeanShift is by applying MeanShift to that point.  Since this is the case, the part in `.fit` where the implementation finds the cluster of the training data is (mostly) irrelevant and unnecessary.  MeanShift is a hill-climbing algorithm on the Kernel Density Estimate.  Which cluster a point is in depends on which hill it happens to be lying on.  In order to tell which hill a point is on, you have to climb the hill.

events.author: csbrown
events.comment: One reason why one might wish to cluster the training data first is to enumerate the modes of the kernel density function, so that we know how many clusters there are.  There is no guarantee that this scheme will find them all, but I would expect it to do a pretty good job in most cases.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: I'd be interested in seeing the proposed implementation

events.author: csbrown
events.comment:
NOREPLY: Just keeping track of this tidbit somewheres.

The docs currently make claims to use an RBF kernel, but then later says it uses a "flat" (uniform) kernel, which is what it is actually using.

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
Yep, I saw that in the documentation, I did not check the code.

@csbrown We could still use `fit` to compute a density estimate. Where I see your point is at predict, where we are using nearest centroids instead, we could use the density estimate to make a hill-climbing prediction, isn't it?

events.author: csbrown
events.comment: @glemaitre that is the basic idea.  Currently, `.fit` doesn't really "compute a density estimate", but it does make an attempt to find the location of the modes of the density estimate.  The way that it does it efficiently by choosing "seeds" is quite clever.  That could be a useful thing, but isn't necessary in order to make predictions.

creator: zachmayer
title: TfidfVectorizer handles multiple text columns
text:
It's really nice that transformers such as `sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder` and `sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` can operate on multiple data columns simultaneously.

`sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer` on the other hand, can only process one column at a time, so you need to make a new transformer for each text column in your dataset.  This can get a little tedious and in particular makes pipelines more verbose.

It'd be nice if `TfidfVectorizer` could also operate on multiple text columns, using the same settings for each column, perhaps with an option to make one vocabulary per column, or use a shared vocabulary across all the columns.

It might be easiest to implement this as a new class that wraps `TfidfVectorizer` [sagemaker-scikit-learn-extension](https://github.com/aws/sagemaker-scikit-learn-extension/blob/master/src/sagemaker_sklearn_extension/feature_extraction/text.py#L22) takes this approach.

If this seems like a good idea, I'd be happy to make a PR.

events.author: zachmayer
events.comment: If this seems like a good idea, I'd be happy to make a PR

events.author: rth
events.comment:
I agree that it could be a useful feature, that would also facilitate integration with `ColumnTransformer` somewhat. 

However, implementation wise `TfidfVectorizer` already does too many things and we need to find a way to simplify it cf https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/14951 so I don't think that adding this new functionality there would be a good idea. Besides, there is an expectation of somewhat comparable API for `CountVectorizer` and `HashingVectorizer`, and we don't want to add this feature there either. 

As far as I understand there are 3 following use cases (with approximate code),

**Separate vocabularies**
```py
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer


vect = TfidfVectorizer()

pipe = make_column_transformer([
   (clone(vect), 'col_1'),
   (clone(vect), 'col_2')
]).fit(df, y)
```

**Shared vocabulary, weighting and normalization**
(assuming bag of words without n-grams)
```py
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

def concat_cols(df):
    assert len(df.columns) >= 2
    res = df.iloc[:, 0].astype('str')
    for key in df.columns[1:]:
       res = res + ' ' + df[key]
    return res

vect = TfidfVectorizer()

pipe = make_column_transformer([
   (make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(concat_cols), vect), ['col_1', 'col_2'])
]).fit(df, y)
```


**Shared vocabulary, independent weighting and normalization**

```py

vocabulary = (TfidfVectorizer()
                .fit(concat_cols(df[['col_1', 'col_2']])
                .vocabulary_)

vect = TfidfVectorizer(vocabulary=vocabulary_)

pipe = make_column_transformer([
   (clone(vect), 'col_1'),
   (clone(vect), 'col_2')
]).fit(df, y)
```

(with possibly other variations). I'm not sure if there is any way to make these easier, short of writing another meta-estimator (if we don't want to modify TfidfVectorizer).

events.author: zachmayer
events.comment:
Those 3 cases seem to pretty much cover it to me.  I'd be happy to try my hand at writing a meta estimator.  I agree that `TfidfVectorizer` is already very complicated.

I've mostly been writing code from case 1 on your list above, and I've found that it can result in code that's verbose to the point of being unwieldy:

```python
pipe = make_column_transformer([
   (clone(vect), 'col_1'),
   (clone(vect), 'col_2'),
   ...
   (clone(vect), 'col_100')
]).fit(df, y)
```

I've found myself writing various forms of a meta-estimator that loops over the columns, fits a vectorizer to each, and then keeps track of which vectorizers should be used to transform which column.  The result is a lot easier to read:
```python
pipe = make_column_transformer([
   (MetaTfidfVectorizer(vectorizer=vect), ['col_1', 'col_2', ..., 'col_100'])
]).fit(df, y)
```

And then the `MetaTfidfVectorizer` does the cloning and orchestration of the vectorizers.

I think this class could also be made to cover case 1 and 3 on your list.

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
Of the cases that @rth listed we have 1 covered with column transformer (slightly awkward but not too bad), 2 is string concatenation but 3 is not trivial right now, right? I'm not sure if 3 is that common, I would probably hold off on doing something special for it.

I'm not entirely sure if having a wrapper for 1 is useful, but I think adding something to the user guide at the CountVectorizer would be great.


It's a bit of a shame that we can't really write this down as a more flexible column transformer. Usually a column transformer can take a callable to map to an arbitrary number of columns, but if you have multiple text columns, you can't create the column transformer before you know the number of columns. That's a bit of a bummer. With the list comprehension, you can not write down the example in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/10603#issuecomment-578301631 nicely because you can't replace ``MultiColumnTfidfVectorizer`` with a ColumnTransformer.

We *could* add a meta-estimator that says "apply this transformer to each column" (I think that's the helper that @zachmayer wants), or we could add a feature to the ColumnTransformer that says "make every column be it's own transformer for this set of columns".
Both of these are kinda ugly, and if we do the first one I *know* people will abuse it when it's not necessary.

Either way, having a part of the docs that shows concatenation vs ColumnTransformer for CountVectorizer would be good, I think.

events.author: zachmayer
events.comment:
@jnothman @amueller Here's an example pipeline I was debugging today.  It follows a common failure pattern I've seen a few times now:

1. Categorical preprocessing handles multiple columns
2. Numeric preprocessing handles multiple columns
3. Text preprocessing ~~handles multiple columns~~ *oops*

```python
# Categorical pipeline
categorical_preprocessing = Pipeline(
[
    ('Imputation', SimpleImputer(strategy='constant', fill_value='?')),
    ('One Hot Encoding', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore')),
]
)
# Numeric pipeline
numeric_preprocessing = Pipeline(
[
     ('Imputation', SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')),
     ('Scaling', StandardScaler())
]
)
text_preprocessing = Pipeline(
[
     ('Text',TfidfVectorizer())       
]
)
# Creating preprocessing pipeline
preprocessing = make_column_transformer(
     (numeric_preprocessing, numeric_features),
     (categorical_preprocessing, categorical_features),
     (text_preprocessing, text_features),
)
# Final pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline(
[('Preprocessing', preprocessing)]
)
test = pipeline.fit_transform(x_train)
```

I fixed this bug by replacing `TfidfVectorizer` with `sagemaker_sklearn_extension.feature_extraction.text import MultiColumnTfidfVectorizer`.

The fact that AWS added this to their sagemaker_sklearn_extension extensions indicate their users frequently run into this problem too.

creator: tomMoral
title: PERF predict_proba is slow when n_jobs > 1 for random forests
text:
The use of `n_jobs > 1` for small batch can slow down the prediction for forest models. This is probably due to the overhead incurred by using `joblib` (create thread, check system info, ...) which is dominate the runtime compared to the computations. This was reported originally in joblib/joblib#982.

A couple of ideas to solve this:
- Set `n_jobs=1` when the size of the batch is small.
- Introduce a `n_jobs_predict` parameters that would default to `1/n_jobs` for forests but that can be set separately.

title: API: do we allow a list of generic objects as X?
text:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/15557 introduced a change in the GP module to allow a list of generic objects and kernels on those data, which is nice, but it violates our API AFAIK.

If we're going to allow that, there are many other places we can/should allow that as well (SVMs for instance).

But that doesn't really play well with the rest of the library (pipeline, GS, etc).

ping @scikit-learn/core-devs

creator: kno10
title: Hidden additional iteration in k-means, max_iter appears to be off by two
text:
The runtime of k-means (including "full") is not proportional to the maximum number of iterations.
But it clearly should be.

Benchmark code (use the MNIST data set):
```python
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
import time
seeds=data[np.random.RandomState(0).choice(data.shape[0], 10)]
runtimes = []
for i in range(1, 61):
  kml = KMeans(n_clusters=10, init=seeds, max_iter=i, n_init=1, random_state=0, tol=1e-15, algorithm="full")
  start = time.time()
  kml.fit(data)
  runtime = time.time() - start
  runtimes.append([kml.n_iter_,runtime])
  print("%d\t%d\t%f" % (i, kml.n_iter_, runtime))

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
runtimes = np.array(runtimes)
plt.plot(runtimes[:,0], runtimes[:,1]/(runtimes[:,0]), label="current")
plt.plot(runtimes[:,0], runtimes[:,1]/(runtimes[:,0]+1), label="+1")
plt.plot(runtimes[:,0], runtimes[:,1]/(runtimes[:,0]+2), label="+2")
plt.legend()
plt.show();
```
Resulting in the following plot.
![kmeans](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3997899/72097110-efe33580-331b-11ea-90f2-9f9df2393486.png)

It will converge at 63 iterations; when it converged the iteration count will be okay. This plot indicates that the current k-means algorithm performs TWO more iterations than advertised. And it is not just startup cost, unfortunately.

There is one hidden additional iteration performed (not completely, but most of an iteration) here:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/50d3fe963c3d2823b2ba2a534b8a50dba620fc5e/sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py#L452-L455
This is almost the entire cost of an iteration hidden here... (c.f. line 420-423). Hence, the "max_iter" count in these cases is at least "off by one". But it seems there is at least another hidden iteration somewhere else.

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
I look at the code and apart of the extra-step E-step to be sure that clusters are also samples in the data. I don't see any issue. I think that the time measure in your example is too small and affected by over validation steps that we perform around.

I time only the relevant iteration divided by the number of iteration done:

```
Average iteration time: 0.127 sec
1       1       1.458629
Average iteration time: 0.192 sec
2       2       1.415144
Average iteration time: 0.164 sec
3       3       1.980477
Average iteration time: 0.158 sec
4       4       2.802380
Average iteration time: 0.127 sec
5       5       2.230284
Average iteration time: 0.103 sec
6       6       2.050179
Average iteration time: 0.119 sec
7       7       2.242768
Average iteration time: 0.102 sec
8       8       2.583579
Average iteration time: 0.123 sec
9       9       2.359695
```

I would not be surprised that the average cost at 1 iteration is much smaller than at 10 since the E-step will have a bigger impact with a lower number of iteration and become insignificant then

events.author: kno10
events.comment:
There is an additional redundancy due to the way the loop is organized in Elkan's (I haven't checked Lloyd yet, and given the pending changes it does not make sense to check the old code).
For Elkan, this is fixed in #16083. If you set max_iter=1, it will perform 3x assignment, and 1x mean update. Updating the means is fairly cheap compared to assigning points, hence this does appear to cost 3 iterations. #16083 reduces this to two, while giving the exact same result. It would be trivially be possible to make this one (essentially by counting iterations beginning with 1, not 0); but it is largely a question of how the tool should behave.
Right now, `max_iter` refers to the number of times the mean is updated (cheap), not the maximum number of assignment steps (expensive); so (with my fix) in one sense it is consistent, in the other it is not, and you cannot have both.
But I'd argue that a user that chooses `max_iter=1` may want to simply assign each object to the current nearest mean once. This is currently not possible in the current implementation, although useful to quite some users (means are predefined by the application; you want to assign each point to the nearest mean, never update the means). Of course you could also provide this functionality by setting `max_iter=0` (except that this is currently prevented by an if statement); and in the end there is no benefit of (ab-)using k-means for this rather than simply using a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier.
For education, it would be nice to actually be able to execute k-means iterations one at a time without additional overhead. I.e. run one iteration of k-means, plot the result, run one iteration, plot, repeat.
With the current implementation, k-means with elkan always performs "assign+assign+updatemean+assign" (no typo; three assignments, one of which is redundant) if you set max_iter=1. With #16083, this reduces to "assign+updatemean+assign", but that nevertheless does to much work to use this to demonstrate k-means. But for a complete visuatization of k-means, one would need to be able to stop at both E and M steps anyway.

events.author: jeremiedbb
events.comment:
It's true that we always do an extra E-step when there is no convergence. This is necessary for us to have the predicted labels match the cluster centers. So the basic iterations scheme is EMEM...E. I don't think we want to change that.

I can't find the third E step you mention. Looking at the code of lloyd and elkan it seems the iterations scheme is as I described above. In elkan, there's a first step to initialize the lower and upper bounds. Maybe you refer to that ?

events.author: kno10
events.comment: Yes, that step makes the first E in the EM loop redundant. It _already_ assigned each point to the nearest center when initializing the bounds. Flipping the logic to iterate ME not EM elegantly solves this, and also removes the need to the final E (because there always was an E last). Implemented in #16083.

creator: chmendoza
title: Missing argument `ensure_2d=False` in call to check_array()
text:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4fe4d27eb1b88cc799199f2176ac734bbc16ca31/sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py#L268

According to the docstrings of euclidean_distances(), `X_norm_squared` is 1D.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
Internally, `euclidean_distances` function takes advantage of making `X_norm_squared` 2D because it uses broadcasting later to calculate the distance.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4fe4d27eb1b88cc799199f2176ac734bbc16ca31/sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py#L303-L305

As a side note, it looks like we test `X_norm_squared` with `(1, n_samples)` and not `(n_samples,)` as stated in the docstring:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4fe4d27eb1b88cc799199f2176ac734bbc16ca31/sklearn/metrics/tests/test_pairwise.py#L620-L637

And from the code, `X_norm_squared` could be anything as long as one of the dimensions match `X.shape[0]` and the other is 1.

events.author: chmendoza
events.comment:
There is an asymmetry in the way `XX` and `YY` are treated:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4fe4d27eb1b88cc799199f2176ac734bbc16ca31/sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py#L285

It seems that, for `XX`, `np.np.atleast_2d` should be called in place of `check_array`, or at least before it.

creator: Gitman-code
title: Add subsample and max_features parameters to HistGradientBoostingRegressor
text: The parameters **subsample** and **max_features** in GradientBoostingRegressor are useful. Is it possible to add equivalent parameters to HistGradientBoostingRegressor?

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
Do you use these because of computation time, or for a bias / variance tradeoff?

I suppose you could expect some speed ups. However,
Since the HistGradientBoosting estimator first bin the data, these parameters might not have the same effect regarding bias / variance

events.author: Gitman-code
events.comment: It was to prevent overfitting. I have read LightGBM has issues with overfitting so I thought this would be a good solution. If things are different in this method please explain.

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
Looks like LightGBM has `bagging_fraction` for subsampling, and `feature_fraction` for dealing with overfitting.

I think it's worth implementing, WDYT @ogrisel @adrinjalali?

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
I believe that if we implement both `bagging_fraction` and `feature_fraction` and set a low learning rate (and large number of boosting iterations) you can get boosted trees to behave more like random forests, hence can probably better deal with overfitting.

This is probably also interesting to get better calibration of the `predict_proba` output (in classification problems) which can be useful to report meaningful confidence levels when deploying the system.

Having the ability to resample each boosted tree independently could also be a very efficient way to deal with imbalanced classification problems: the majority class could be subsampled. This would warrant additional parameters though to deal with class-wise bagging fractions. Related to:  #13227.

events.author: amueller
events.comment: For the feature_fraction, is that on a tree-basis or a per-split basis? Our GradientBoosting does "max_features" which is on a per-split basis....

events.comment: Doing it on per-split basis is the preferred method

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: I agree. My intuition is that if `max_depth` / `max_leaf_nodes` are high enough, the tree still has a chance to recover from a bad feature subset draw at a given split nodes while if we do it a tree-based level, the whole tree is wasted.

Is anyone working on the sampling part of HistGradientBoostingClassifier/Regressor? Apart from acceleration, sampling strategy also provides regularization on the entire GBDT system and improves its performance.

Here are some commonly-used sampling strategies on a tree-basis in other GBDT libraries:
* **Stochastic Gradient Boosting** (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost)(https://astro.temple.edu/~msobel/courses_files/StochasticBoosting(gradient).pdf)
* **Gradient-based One-Side Sampling** (LightGBM)
(https://papers.nips.cc/paper/6907-lightgbm-a-highly-efficient-gradient-boosting-decision-tree.pdf)

events.comment:
@gbolmier is currently working on feature and sample subsampling.

However the GOSS strategy from LightGBM is out of scope (at least for now) as it departs quite significantly from traditional GBDTs.

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
> Doing it on per-split basis is the preferred method

@mayer79 Do you think the same for column/feature subsampling?

events.author: mayer79
events.comment: @lorentzenchr :  Ideally, we could have both options. But "per split" is also my favourite. Given that it is not interferring too much with interaction constraints!

events.author: lorentzenchr

[LightGBM]() has 2 `feature_fraction` alias `colsample_bytree` and `feature_fraction_bynode` alias `colsample_bynode`. The last one is for split-based subsampling.

creator: aggvarun01
title: Add multiclass support for brier_score_loss
text:
Feature Request: The original formulation for Brier score inherently supports multiclass classification [[source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brier_score#Original_definition_by_Brier)]. This is currently absent in scikit-learn, which restricts Brier score to binary classification. 

I have found it useful to have multiclass brier_score_loss when comparing calibration, and have a custom function for the same.  I would be happy to work on this and port the code to the scikit-learn API.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
Yes I agree. Would you be interested in contributing a PR? Note that for multiclass problems, the user should not have to pass a `pos_label` param, even we have string labels.

Related to #18183 and that might also impact what we are doing in #18114.

events.author: aggvarun01
events.comment: The version of Brier Score currently implemented in scikit-learn is: (where y_hat is the probability of the positive class) This can be replaced by the multi-class formula, which is valid for the binary case as well: Unless we use the new formula, we still need 'pos_label' for the binary case. However, if the new formula is used for the binary case, it won't be backwards compatible, since when the new formula is used for the binary case, it is **twice** the value obtained from the old formula. This also means that the range of Brier Score will no longer be between 0 and 1 for the multiclass case. The workaround I can think of is to keep the binary case as is, and then implement the new formula for the multi-class case which can ignore 'pos_label'. The only downside to this approach is that users can expect to see a sudden jump in brier score when going from 2 classes to 3. However, I don't expect users to compare Brier Scores across models with different number of classes, so I think this should be fine. The second workaround, similar to the 'measures' package in R, is to have a separate function called multiclass_brier. Will be very happy to implement this. **[EDITED]**

creator: sweichwald
title: [ENH] ICA based on AJD (SOBI, AMUSE, NSS)
text:
While developing an extension of ICA to grouped data (as opposed to simply pooling data), we (@NiklasPfister & myself) also implemented a variety of related linear ICA algorithms.
They are based on approximate joint matrix diagonalization and, as opposed to FastICA, do not rely on non-Gaussianity of the sources. In particular, the following ICA-algorithms are implemented for the right choice of parameters by our UwedgeICA sklearn transformer:
* NSS-JS, NSS-TD-JD (NSS = non-stationarity in time or space) as well as
* the popular SOBI (second-order) and its predecessor AMUSE

(references can be found in the paper below).
Additionally, the CoroICA transformer implements confounding-robust extensions of those aforementioned methods.

* [Code](https://github.com/sweichwald/coroICA-python/)
* [JMLR Paper](http://www.jmlr.org/papers/v20/18-399.html)
* [Website](https://sweichwald.de/coroICA/)
* [Documentation](https://sweichwald.de/coroICA-python/)
* We are attaching a MWE below.

We guess it should be quite doable to include those in sklearn as our current implementation is already sklearn flavoured and built upon the respective mixins, PEP8 compatible, and comes with examples and documentation. Also the sklearn examples available for FastICA could be easily adapted and extended to demo the different ICA variants.

We are raising the issue to get early feedback and gauge the interest — what do you think?

@GaelVaroquaux @agramfort

--

Get current implementation: `pip install coroica`.

```python
from coroica import UwedgeICA
from coroica.utils import md_index
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA


np.random.seed(0)


# generate 2 sources with changing variance
S = np.random.randn(1000, 2) \
    * np.c_[np.sin(np.arange(1000) / 1000),
            np.cos(np.arange(1000) / 1000)]
A = np.random.randn(2, 2)
X = (A.dot(S.T)).T

# transformers
fastica = FastICA(random_state=0)
uwedgeica = UwedgeICA(partitionsize=50)

# fit both ICAs
fastica.fit(X)
uwedgeica.fit(X)

print(f'MD(A,V_fastica) = {md_index(A, fastica.components_):.2f}')
print(f'MD(A,V_uwedge) = {md_index(A, uwedgeica.V_):.2f}')

# yields:
# MD(A,V_fastica) = 0.04
# MD(A,V_uwedge) = 0.02
```

events.comment:
At a first quick glance, I am not sure that it passes the criteria for

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/faq.html#what-are-the-inclusion-criteria-for-new-algorithms

events.author: NiklasPfister
events.comment:
Thanks for the quick replies!
Which criteria in particular are you referring to?

Regarding the well-established'ness: SOBI ICA is a very well established algorithm that has been developed/published in 1997 and has been cited 2993 times as per Google Scholar (https://scholar.google.de/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=0%2C5&q=A++Blind++Source++Separation++Technique+Using+Second-Order+Statistics&btnG=). Furthermore, it has been shown to  be "the best procedure" in comparison with FastICA and JADE, see https://www.iiis.org/CDs2017/CD2017Spring/papers/ZA832BA.pdf. Basically it
complements FastICA and works well for different source characteristics. Beyond SOBI, our implementation includes also the following ICA algorithms that are well established (as in published some years ago):
* AMUSE (Tong et al, 1990)
* NSS-JS and NSS-TD-JS (Choi et al. 2001; Choi and Cichocki 2001)

These algorithms come basically for free, just by setting the timelags and instantcov parameters accordingly. The robustified extensions may be less established.

The contribution could single out a SOBI transformer (well-established, complementary) and in the Docstring one could clarify for which particular parameter setting of the SOBI algorithm one essentially recovers one of the other mentioned ICA algorithms.

What do you think?

events.author: agramfort
events.comment: @NiklasPfister my feeling is that you would go faster by consolidating a python package for ICA-like techniques. You would be able to do fast updates / release cycles. We have FastICA for historical reasons. Infomax PR was never merged. I myself worked on https://github.com/pierreablin/picard with some fast solvers for joint diag https://github.com/pierreablin/qndiag during the phd of @pierreablin . Maybe @pierreablin would be happy to help a bit too. So +1 for a contrib package to start with.

events.author: GaelVaroquaux
events.comment:
I don't think that the classic ICA methods are out of scope. The question
is: which one should we add, and how do we make sure that people with the
corresponding expertise stick around.

events.author: pierreablin
events.comment:
I would indeed be happy to help.

Frist, I think having a contrib package with many ICA algorithms with a common API would be extremely valuable, and I would happily contribute. 

Second, I think that SOBI is among the most widely used ICA algorithms, and importantly it differs quite starkly from FastICA since it leverages spectral diversity rather than non-Gaussianity. The output of FastICA and SOBI can therefore be quite different. The implementation is also very robust using uwedge (compared for instance to Infomax for which finding good hyperparameters is a burden). 

I think AMUSE and NSS-JS/ NSS-TD-JD are not so widely used. I understand that they basically come for free once you have a good joint-diagonalization algorithm, but I do not think it is worth the pain.

So +1 for adding SOBI.

events.author: GaelVaroquaux
events.comment:
Pierre, thanks for your input, this is very useful.

I would say: +1 for SOBI in scikit-learn, based on this assessment, with
a good example demonstrating the difference with FastICA.

events.author: NiklasPfister
events.comment:
Thanks for your input. We agree that SOBI is the most widely used and hence relevant addition to scikit-learn. In our current implementation all of the 4 mentioned ICAs are realized by the exact same code base but only with different parameter settings (this is because all methods jointly diagonalize different (auto)-covariance matrices). We would therefore propose to do the following:
1) add SobiICA transformer to scikit-learn based on our current UwedgeICA implementation
2) allow users to adjust Sobi parameters that specify the considered timelags
3) additionally add to the documentation for which parameter settings Sobi reduces to AMUSE and NSS-variants.
4) add example that uses both FastICA and SobiICA and illustrates the differences
In our opinion keeping the code base close to our current implementation also eases future maintenance efforts.

If that sounds good to you we would start with a WIP-PR.

events.author: GaelVaroquaux
events.comment:
We need to reduce the combinatorials of methods in scikit-learn, both for
our users as more options makes it harder for them to solve problems
efficiently (think about the old windows printing menus) and for the
developers as every subclass, every conditional, every line of code,
every additional variable is a cognitive overhead.

We will not accept a contribution with code that is too complex. Hence I
am not sure that we will accept the contribution with complexity of
implementing the general case. Scikit-learn is not a package made for
research on ICA (nor on any variant of machine learning), it is a package
for general-purpose machine-learning practice.

I cannot tell without looking at the code or the example, but I can
foresee the difficulties, and I would prefer if we started with the right
objectives.

Thank you

events.author: pierreablin
events.comment:
For what it's worth, here is a ""minimal"" example where SOBI can unmix signals that FastICA cannot unmix: FastICA cannot recover sources which only have spectral diversity:

```python
import numpy as np
from coroica import UwedgeICA
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


rng = np.random.RandomState(0)

n, p = 300, 3
n_power_bands = 4
# Spectral power in each band
sigmas = rng.rand(p, n_power_bands)

# Generate white complex Gaussian noise
t_len = n // 2
S_t = rng.randn(p, t_len) + 1j * rng.randn(p, t_len)
window = t_len // n_power_bands
# Fix its norm in each frequency band
for i in range(n_power_bands):
    S_t[:, i * window:(i + 1) * window] *= sigmas[:, i][:, None]
S_t = np.concatenate((S_t, S_t[:, ::-1]), axis=1)
# Sources are the inverse Fourier transform of this
S = np.real(np.fft.ifft(S_t))

# Generate mixing
A = rng.randn(p, p)
X = np.dot(A, S)

# Try to unmix with FastICA
A_fastica = FastICA(random_state=rng).fit(X.T).mixing_
# Plot unmixing difference (should be diagonal)
plt.matshow(np.abs(np.linalg.pinv(A_fastica).dot(A)))
plt.title('FastICA')
plt.show()

# Try to unmix with SOBI (should have a .mixing_ attribute
# and a random_state)
V_sobi = UwedgeICA(timelags=np.arange(1, 10)).fit(X.T).V_
# Plot unmixing difference (should be diagonal)
plt.matshow(np.abs(V_sobi.dot(A)))
plt.title('SOBI')
plt.show()
``` 
 `UwedgeICA` does not have the same signature / attributes as FastICA so far.

@NiklasPfister and myself will get a WIP PR going for SOBIICA; to be expected sometime during the next two months ;-)

creator: johannfaouzi
title: [Feature Request] Add class_weight parameter for multiclass wrappers
text:
#### Description
Most (perhaps all?) binary classifiers in scikit-learn can be generalized to multiclass classification with a `multi_class` parameter. These classifiers also have a `class_weight` parameter to give different weights to different classes.

However, multiclass wrappers such as  [OneVsOneClassifier](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.multiclass.OneVsOneClassifier.html#sklearn.multiclass.OneVsOneClassifier) and [OneVsRestClassifier](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier.html#sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier) do not have a `class_weight` parameter, which means that only uniform weights (`None`) and balanced weights (`'balanced'`) provided to the binary classifier are available.

The main use case would be to generalize custom binary classifiers to multiclass classification with a `class_weight` parameter.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Since this works:

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(n_classes=4, n_clusters_per_class=1)
clf = LogisticRegression(multi_class='ovr', class_weight={0: 1, 1: 3, 2: 5, 3: 6})
clf.fit(X, y)
```

one could expect this to produce the same results:
```python
from sklearn.multiclass import OneVsRestClassifier

clf = OneVsRestClassifier(
    LogisticRegression(), class_weight={0: 1, 1: 3, 2: 5, 4: 6}
)
clf.fit(X, y)
```

#### Proposed changes

creator: glemaitre
title: Wrongly implemented test in RidgeCV
text:
The following test does not actually test anything:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/bdf1ae9e4a739abf06076e67dc453774ffc886a7/sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_ridge.py#L478-L502

`gcv_ridge` will compute the error by aggregating all predictions and compute the `explained_variance` on all predictions.

However, `loo_ridge` will make a `GridSearchCV` which will compute the score for each individual sample (because of a LOO CV) and then report the mean. However, the explained variance will always be 1.0 since we are computing the variance on a single sample.

So the test is passing by chance.

We need to implement a test which test what was intended at first.

title: TfidfVectorizer ngrams does not work when vocabulary provided
text:

<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description

The `TfidfVectorizer` does not honor the `ngram_range` argument when the `vocabulary` is provided.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Example 1, vocabulary is *not* provided, this works as expected:

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

X = ['abc',
     'bcd',
     'cde']

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words=None,
                        analyzer='char',
                        ngram_range=(2, 2))

sps = tfidf.fit_transform(X)
print(tfidf.get_feature_names())
# ['ab', 'bc', 'cd', 'de']
```

Example 2, when vocabulary is provided. This does *not* work as expected:

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

X = ['abc',
     'bcd',
     'cde']

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words=None,
                        analyzer='char',
                        vocabulary={'a': 0, 'b': 1, 'c': 2, 'd': 3, 'e': 4},
                        ngram_range=(2, 2))

sps = tfidf.fit_transform(X)
print(tfidf.get_feature_names())
# ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']
```

Note that it works if the vocabulary I provide are the ngrams themselves:

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

X = ['abc',
     'bcd',
     'cde']

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words=None,
                        analyzer='char',
                        vocabulary=['ab', 'bc', 'cd', 'de'],
                        ngram_range=(2, 2))

sps = tfidf.fit_transform(X)
print(tfidf.get_feature_names())
# ['ab', 'bc', 'cd', 'de']
```

But that seems kind of silly, since I can't possibly know all of the ngrams a priori for a large dataset.

#### Expected Results

Expected to still get ngrams when vocabulary is provided, but did not.

#### Actual Results

See steps to reproduce above.

creator: glemaitre
title: [RFC] return Series for target when using as_frame and return_X_y
text:
This a general question regarding the API of `as_frame` and `return_X_y` with our loader/fetcher. We have an inconsistent behaviour which could be solved straight away.

`fetch_opeml` introduced `as_frame` exposing `frame` attribute in the `Bunch` which is a Pandas DataFrame. In conjunction with `return_X_y=True`, we exposed `data` and `target`. `data` will always be a `DataFrame` while `target` is supposed to be a `DataFrame` or a `Series` depending on the number of columns in the `target`.

```python
X, y = fetch_openml('iris', as_frame=True, return_X_y=True)
y
```
```
0         Iris-setosa
1         Iris-setosa
2         Iris-setosa
3         Iris-setosa
4         Iris-setosa
            ...      
145    Iris-virginica
146    Iris-virginica
147    Iris-virginica
148    Iris-virginica
149    Iris-virginica
Name: class, Length: 150, dtype: category
Categories (3, object): [Iris-setosa, Iris-versicolor, Iris-virginica]
```

In https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/15950, we introduce `as_frame` to `fetch_california_housing`. The API is the same apart of the `target` output. The `target` is a `DataFrame` even with a single column.

```python
X, y = fetch_california_housing(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
y
```
```
       MedHouseVal
0            4.526
1            3.585
2            3.521
3            3.413
4            3.422
...            ...
20635        0.781
20636        0.771
20637        0.923
20638        0.847
20639        0.894

[20640 rows x 1 columns]
```

So my question is: what type of `target` do we want when the target is 1D?

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
IMO, would be to return a pandas Series when we are in a 1D setting.
First, `fetch_openml` is already released while `fetch_california_housing` is not released yet. The change would avoid warning about a change of behaviour.
Then, we usually give a 1D numpy array and I would think that a pandas Series is the equivalent.

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment: ping @amueller @jorisvandenbossche @ogrisel @rth @thomasjpfan @reshamas

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
A series was returned because of how estimators prefer 1D numpy arrays. For example this would raise a `DataConversionWarning`:

```py
X, y = fetch_california_housing(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
mlp = MLPRegressor().fit(X, y)
```

I would prefer `fetch_california_housing` to return a Series as well.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I like the idea of returning a Series but we do need to ensure this
integrates reasonably in estimators.

creator: ogrisel
title: Integration testing for downstream dependencies
text:
We need a new Continuous Integration configuration to launch the tests of some popular downstream projects.

Candidate projects:

- xgboost and or lightgbm as very popular third party libraries
- skorch
- imbalanced-learn not necessarily as popular as others but with high use of sklearn's API
- autosklearn?
- any other suggestion?

Those test would not be run in PRs unless we use a specific tag in the commit message for instance. This test setup would be run by maintainers in the release branches.

We do something similar in the cloudpickle project with the `[ci downstream]` commit tag:

https://github.com/cloudpipe/cloudpickle/blob/master/.travis.yml#L37-L70

For scikit-learn this would probably need a bit more scripting as the build is more complex than for a pure python project such as cloudpickle but the general idea would be the same.

events.comment: A cron job or something like then one you proposed would make the trick. But if a change is mandatory the maintainers need somehow to be notified early, no? But I suppose that is for internal use and to detect a potential impact of a change to the downstream libs.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Frankly the downstream packages should be doing this integration testing by
testing various use cases and checking with scikit-learn master. We should
be encouraging downstream packages to include such integration tests (e.g.
various usages of their estimators with grid search).

But it's reasonable that we at least run a suite of integration tests as
part of a release cycle. Putting this in Azure makes it easier for our
maintainers.

I don't mind if we also run a Cron job but then we will have to deal with
more false alarms (e.g. downstream test suites failing due to poor or
delayed management of their other dependencies).

creator: gstiefel
title: Crossvalidation on estimator fails when using option multioutput = 'raw_values' in make_scorer function
text:
<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description

I wanted to perform a cross validation of a PLS2 model. Therefore I used the mean_squared_error as scorer function.
As I'm interested in the individual error of individual futures in Y, I used option multioutput = 'raw_values' in the definition of the 'make_scorer' function.
Python throws the error: 
```
  File ""C:\Users\___\Anaconda3\envs\main\lib\site-packages\sklearn\model_selection\_validation.py", line 602, in _score
    raise ValueError(error_msg % (score, type(score), name))
ValueError: scoring must return a number, got [0.00317655 0.00193264 0.00349379 0.00108055] (<class 'numpy.ndarray'>) instead. (scorer=score)
```

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
# import moduls
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression 
from sklearn.metrics import make_scorer, mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from scipy.stats import norm

# create X and Y data sets: X is the sum of ks Gaussians with the Amplitude factor in Y
ns = 100 # number of samples
ms = 100   # number of x futures
ks = 4 # number of y futures
x = np.zeros([ns,ms]) # X data set
y = np.zeros([ns,ks]) # Y data set
x_scale = np.linspace(-3.,3.,ms)
x_gauss_center = np.random.uniform(-3.,3.,ks)
x_gauss_scale = 0.1 
for n in range(ns):
    x_gauss_amp = np.random.uniform(0,1.,ks)
    x[n,:] = np.sum([ norm.pdf((x_scale-xgc)/x_gauss_scale)*y_par for xgc,y_par in zip(x_gauss_center,x_gauss_amp)],0)
    y[n,:] = [y_par for y_par in x_gauss_amp]
    ''
# add some noise to the data sets
x_noise = 0.005
y_noise =0.005
x += np.random.normal(0.,x_noise,[ns,ms])
y += np.random.normal(0.,y_noise,[ns,ks])

# prepare the model
regression_model = PLSRegression(n_components = ks)
regression_model.fit(x,y)

# prepare scorers: mean_sqaured_error with option multioutput
mse_scorer_object_passes = make_scorer(
                                mean_squared_error, 
                                greater_is_better = True, 
                                multioutput = 'uniform_average'
                    )
mse_scorer_object_fails = make_scorer(
                                mean_squared_error, 
                                greater_is_better = True, 
                                multioutput = 'raw_values'
                    )

# passes: do crossvalidation with multioutput = 'uniform_average'
mse_per_block =  cross_val_score(regression_model, 
                                x, 
                                y, 
                                cv = 5, 
                                scoring = mse_scorer_object_passes)

# fails do crossvalidation with multioutput = 'raw_value'
mse_per_block =  cross_val_score(regression_model, 
                                x, 
                                y, 
                                cv = 5, 
                                scoring = mse_scorer_object_fails)
```

#### Expected Results
a numpy array with size (  cv = 5 -> <number_of_folds>, ks <y_futures>)

#### Actual Results
An error:
```
  File "C:\Users\___\Anaconda3\envs\main\lib\site-packages\sklearn\model_selection\_validation.py", line 602, in _score
    raise ValueError(error_msg % (score, type(score), name))
ValueError: scoring must return a number, got [0.00317655 0.00193264 0.00349379 0.00108055] (<class 'numpy.ndarray'>) instead. (scorer=score)
```

We are moving to support scorers that aren't just returning numbers

creator: qinhanmin2014
title: How to do LeaveOneOut cross validation
text:
Currrently, we have two ways to do LOO cv in scikit-learn
The first one is in GridSearchCV, where we calculate the score of each fold (i.e., each sample) and then take the average.
The second one is in RidgeCV, where we calculate the prediction of each fold (i.e., each sample), put them together and calculate the score.
I think this inconsistency is annoying.
Another issue is that whether we should consider sample_weight when averaging the scores in the first option and when calculating the scores in the second option. We do so in RidgeCV, but don't do so in GridSearchCV.
Related to RidgeCV issues ping @glemaitre

creator: lorentzenchr
title: Bias correction for TransformedTargetRegressor
text:
#### Description
If one is interested in predicting the  (conditional on `X`) expected value of a target `y`, aka mean, then `TransformedTargetRegressor` should use a bias corrected inverse transform.

It would be nice to have an option for bias correction in `TransformedTargetRegressor`. At least, I would mention this in the user guide.

#### References
https://robjhyndman.com/hyndsight/backtransforming/

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
Here is an example based on [plot_transformed_target.html](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/compose/plot_transformed_target.html) for the Boston house prices dataset. For simplicity, I used `LinearRegression` instead of `RidgeCV` and a `PowerTransformer(method='box-cox')` instead of ` QuantileTransformer`, so that one can use the bias corrected backtransformation of the Box-Cox given in the referenced link above:
```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import scipy

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import load_boston
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, median_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


def BC_inverse(y, lam, sig):
    """Back transform Box-Cox with Bias correction.
    See https://robjhyndman.com/hyndsight/backtransforming
    """
    if lam == 0:
        return np.exp(y) * (1 + 0.5 * sig**2)
    else:
        res = np.power(lam*y + 1., 1/lam)
        res *= (1 + 0.5 * sig**2 * (1 - lam) / (lam*y + 1.)**2)
        return res

dataset = load_boston()
X = dataset.data
y = dataset.target
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=123, test_size = 0.25)

model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
model_trans = TransformedTargetRegressor(
    regressor=LinearRegression(),
    transformer=PowerTransformer(method='box-cox', standardize=False)).fit(X_train, y_train)

lam = model_trans.transformer_.lambdas_[0]
# standard deviation of transformed target
z_train = model_trans.transformer_.transform(y_train[:, np.newaxis]).ravel()
z_predict = model_trans.regressor_.predict(X_train)
sig = np.sum((z_train - z_predict)**2)
sig = np.sqrt(sig / (len(y_train) - len(model_trans.regressor_.coef_) - 1))

# simple calibration factor, as a Linear Model with intercept should
# have sum(predicted) = sum(observed) on training set
corr_fac = y_train.sum() / model_trans.predict(X_train).sum()

d = {"untransformed": np.sum(y_train - model.predict(X_train)),
     "transformed": np.sum(y_train - model_trans.predict(X_train)),
     "bias corrected": np.sum(y_train - BC_inverse(model_trans.regressor_.predict(X_train), lam, sig)),
     "rescaled": np.sum(y_train - corr_fac * model_trans.predict(X_train))
}
print("Model calibration on training set (perfect is 0):")
print(d)

d = {"untransformed": r2_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)),
     "transformed": r2_score(y_test, model_trans.predict(X_test)),
     "bias corrected": r2_score(y_test, BC_inverse(model_trans.regressor_.predict(X_test), lam, sig)),
     "rescaled": r2_score(y_test, corr_fac * model_trans.predict(X_test))
    }
print("r2 score on test set (perfect is 1):")
print(d)
```
**Result**
Model calibration on training set (perfect is 0):
- 'untransformed': 9.414691248821327e-12
- 'transformed': 115.6547264252301
- 'bias corrected': 5.4043223163621334
- 'rescaled': 7.673861546209082e-13

R2 score on test set (perfect is 1):
- 'untransformed': 0.6862448857295753
- 'transformed': 0.7405742064643839
- 'bias corrected': 0.7423703905632908
- 'rescaled': 0.7424282009454282

**Summary**
The bias corrected results are better calibrated (on training set) and even have a higher R2 score (on test set).

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
What about adding an argument `bias_correction` to `TransformedTargetRegressor` with the options:

- `None`: No bias correction (as is).
- `rescale`: Acts like a post-fit-step. After fitting, calculates `c = sum(y)/sum(predict(X))` and then multiplies every prediction by `c`.
- `recenter`: Acts like a post-fit-step. After fitting, calculates `c = mean(y - predict(X))` and then adds `c` to every prediction.
- `transformer`: Uses the bias correction of the transformer if it has one implemented.

Edit:
This must be adapted, if the aim is not the expectation (mean) but ~the median for example~ some other property of the target distribution.
Note: Quantiles are invariant (don't change) under monotone (increasing) transformations and therefore don't need a bias correction.

@glemaitre @jnothman @amueller might be interested (as you did #9041)

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment: Is this something scikit-learn would consider implementing and is a PR worth the effort? A short comment from a core developer would be very welcome.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I don't feel very confident to speak to this without more research or
experimentation. When would you say this is likely to be useful / not?

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
If your goal is to predict the expectation E[Y|X] and for some reason transforming Y before fitting is favorable, then I'd say it is **always** useful and even **strongly** advised from a statistical point of view.

In the example above—which I should  maybe replace with the diamonds dataset— the bias corrected versions don't show any disadvantage that I'm aware of.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment: Is there a reference comparing the different options for bias correction?

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
Unfortunately, I'm not a domain expert here nor do I know a reference. Maybe, if we ask kindly enough, @robjhyndman or @mayer79 could have a look and help out?

My understanding is, that the bias corrected inverse Box-Cox transformation has at least a theoretical advantage over the simple global correction factor approach: It is a true second order correction, potentially different for every sample. Disadvantage is that you need analytic formulae for every transformation (2nd derivative, so not too difficult).

events.author: robjhyndman
events.comment: It can also be done numerically. This is how bias correction is handled in fabletools (for R) so that any transformation can be used: https://github.com/tidyverts/fabletools/blob/master/R/transform.R#L102

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment: @robjhyndman Thank you for pointing to the numerical solution. If I understand correctly, this is an additive correction, i.e. the biased corrected prediction is `predict_biased + bias_correction`.

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment: Is this something we want for scikit-learn? An implementation in line with fabletools seems like a small addition with great impact on the modelling side.

events.author: lorentzenchr
events.comment:
#### Summary
Let's say, we want to model $\mu_Y = E[Y|X]$, transform to $Y = f(Z)$ (inverse transform $f$), actually model $\mu_Z = E[Z|X]$ and finally want to transform back. Then there are 2 options:
1. Use (Taylor series) $\mu_Y \approx E[f(Z)|X] = f(\mu_Z) + \frac{\sigma_Z^2}{2}f^{\prime\prime}(\mu_Z)$ with $\sigma_Z^2 = Var[Z|X]$.
  - Advantage: The bias correction $\frac{\sigma_Z^2}{2}f^{\prime\prime}(\mu_Z)$ is $X$-dependent.
  - Disadvantage:
    - We usually do not know/model the conditional variance $\sigma_Z^2$. Guassian processes may be the exception. We could approximate it by the unconditional variance, which is easily computed on the training sample.
    - The second derivative $f^{\prime\prime}$ might require a numerical approach rather than an analytical.
2. Use an
    - additive $E[f(Y)|X] \approx c \hspace{2pt} f(\mu_Z)$
    - or multiplicative $E[f(Y)|X] \approx c + f(\mu_Z)$
   
   approach.
  - Advantage: $c$ can be easily calculated on the training sample.
  - Disadvantage: It does not capture the $X$-dependence.

#### Recommendation
Because in most cases the variance is not available, I favor the second approach with a multiplicative or additive constant where a user can specify whether additive or multiplicative.

class _NotAnArray:

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment: The following https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/15952#issuecomment-568606084 is particularly important to fix this bug and questioning the semantic of the `sample_weight` particularly in the context of the RANSAC estimator.

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
We add some more thinking regarding this current bug with @ogrisel and how best we can handle it. It seems that we have two directions to go forward.

One possibility is to not pass the `sample_weight` parameter to the underlying parameter and instead use it at the sampling stage of the RANSAC algorithm. In expectation, we should respect the semantic and property associated with the `sample_weight` in scikit-learn. We should be testing this behaviour and properties: zero-weights should be equivalent to not consider the sample while a weight of 2 should be equivalent to observe twice the same sample (duplicate it).

The proposal in #23371 is an alternative where we can impact the thresholding by computing the weighted median and dispersion to select the subset of data to fit a weighted model. But we are unsure if it will retain the properties above.

creator: thomasjpfan
title: RFC Support for Some Developer Utilities
text:
On the [Utilities for Developers](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/utilities.html) page, it states:

> **Warning:** These utilities are meant to be used internally within the scikit-learn package. They are not guaranteed to be stable between versions of scikit-learn. Backports, in particular, will be removed as the scikit-learn dependencies evolve.

If we want to provide utilities to support third-party estimators, we should treat some of these utilities as "first class" citizens.

For example `safe_indexing` would be extremely useful for third parties that want to support DataFrames as input. Currently, the options for third-party developers is to build their own "safe_indexing" or depend on our private version which may not be stable.

Another example is https://github.com/scikit-learn/enhancement_proposals/pull/22, which defines a `n_features_in_` contract where we will internally use private methods to cohere with the contract. Third-party estimators would need to build their own methods or functions to work with the SLEP.

**TLDR:** Now that much of the utilities are "private", we can make deliberate decisions about what utilities should be public and supported by us. This would mean deprecation cycles, etc. If we support some of the `utils` module, it will make it easier to build estimators, which will enrich the ecosystem of scikit-learn compatible estimators.

CC @scikit-learn/core-devs

events.author: GaelVaroquaux
events.comment: +1 on the general idea!

events.author: NicolasHug
events.comment:
> Warning: These utilities are meant to be used internally within the scikit-learn package. They are not guaranteed to be stable between versions of scikit-learn. Backports, in particular, will be removed as the scikit-learn dependencies evolve.

In practice, that's not true. We've been treating all these utilities as public, and we've always deprecated things smoothly with the 2 versions rules. Case in point: `safe_indexing`, which we just deprecated in 0.22.

It seems that the questions are:

- Do we want a developer API? If yes, what are the rules regarding deprecations?
- What utilities become part of the developer API (if any), which ones go private, and which ones stay public?

I'm happy to consider a proposal :)

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Yes, we should define a developer API more clearly. It should include
things that make passing check_estimator easier, and that make passing new
checks added to check_estimator easier (e.g. a validate_data helper helps
with n_features_in_ and with error messages for X.shape[1] discrepancies;
and when updated to include pandas column reordering stuff, this would be
seamless for 3rd party devs).

I also think that it's safe to bring back things deprecated in 0.22.0 into
0.22.1.

events.author: glemaitre
events.comment:
> a developer API more clearly

I'm +1 with that. Then, we should ensure some deprecation cycle if we have breaking changes but we could make it as with `experimental` to have fast adoption (and we can use `DeprecationWarning` to warn the end-user :)).

I think that we can come with a list of utilities. Another way would be to ask third-party which tools they are using?

events.author: qinhanmin2014
events.comment:
> In practice, that's not true. We've been treating all these utilities as public, and we've always deprecated things smoothly with the 2 versions rules. Case in point: safe_indexing, which we just deprecated in 0.22.

I guess not @NicolasHug , see #14545, we change the behaviour of check_is_fitted without a deprecation cycle (You can say that there's a deprecation cycle, but I'd argue that since we no longer support the old behaviour, the deprecation cycle there is meaningless).

Perhaps we should introduce a deprecation cycle if we want to change public functions in sklearn.utils.

creator: rth
title: META OHE / OrdinalEncoder: NaN support, unfrequent cat. and pd.Categorical
text:
There have been 3 significant improvements proposed for `OneHotEncoder` (and to a lesser extent `OrdinalEncoder`), often with an associated PR,
 - NaN handling (issue https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/11996, PR https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/13028)
 - support of `pd.Categorical` dtype (issue https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/14953, PR https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/15396)
 - handling of infrequent categories (issue https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/12153, PR https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/13833)

the goal of this issue to have a high level agreement on the desired solution, that it is consistent/compatible for different available encoders, or encoders that we may want to add in the near future (e.g. target encoder, https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/5853). Some of the possible solutions for the above 3 features are mutually exclusive. Also putting aside aside backward compatibility constraints for a start, what default options we would want ideally.

I have not followed in detail all past discussions about encoders (in particular about ordering concerns https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/15050). Following are some of the observations / open questions I have, please add more if I missed something/link with existing comments.

**NaN support**

 - Mainly if we want to implement support directly or suggest to use an imputer for the pre-processing step (as one can do now).

**pd.Categorical support**
 - Do we say that `categories='dtype'` would make OHE categories match categories in the dtype 
? Including the ordering? But then, this means only at fit since, for transform, the test set could have unknown categories. 
 - Actually, if one does a train test split, some categories from the dtype can be missing from the train set as well. Do we then create a column with 0s in `fit_transform`, or disregard this column breaking the assumption of conforming to dtype categories? Solution proposed by @thomasjpfan in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/15396#issuecomment-552065493
 - Finally, if we do not conform to the dtype categories, and only use `pd.Categorical` for computational efficiency internally, what is the point of defining a `categories='dtype'` in the first place (or warning that categories order doesn't match the order of categories in dtype https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/15050).
 
**Infrequent categories**

Overall the plan seems fairly clear in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/12153#issuecomment-561774199

**NaN & pd.Categorical**

 - Handing `NaN` as a separate category, means we are no longer using purely the categories from the dtype (even with `dtype='category'`) which can be fine as long as we agree on it.
 - Another possibility is to implement a say `CategoricalPreprocessor` to add `NaN` as a new dtype category in a separate preprocessing step,
   ```py
   df[column].cat.add_categories("NaN", inplace=True)
   df[column].fillna("NaN", inplace=True)
   ```
   which can make interpretation simpler. Say `df[column].value_counts()` would then show NaN properly and one might want to do it for exploratory analysis in any case. 
 
**NaN & infrequent categories**

- Do infrequent categories rules apply to NaN or is it always a separate category (even if passes the infrequent criteria)?

**pd.Categorical and infrequent categories**

- Similarly we could consider a preprocessor that would add `infrequent` as a category to dtype, instead of doing that internally in encoders. Say to evaluate how many infrequent elements one has, I find that doing (approximately),
  ```py
  ohe = OneHotEncoder(categories='dtype', min_frequency=5)
  X = ohe.fit_transform(df['col'])
  unfrequent_idx = ohe.get_feature_names().tolist().find("infrequent")
  print(X.sum(axis=0).A1[unfrequent_idx])
  ```
  very awkward as opposed to,
  ```py
  df['col'].value_counts()["infrequent"]
  ```
  where it was properly added to `df['col'].cat.categories` previously and we are using all the nice features of `pd.Categorical`. 

So there is some tension here between adding these features to scikit-learn and keeping exploratory analysis with pandas user friendly (and not asking users to implement the same thing twice).

Given the complexity of this interaction, maybe separating "Imputer + Unfrequent categories conversion with pd.Categorical support" and "OneHot, Ordinal, Target etc encoder" into 2 or 3 estimators might be easier to understand? Not sure about usability though. The alternative that would mean we also plan to add these features (and enforce consistency) for any future encoder.

cc @thomasjpfan @NicolasHug @glemaitre @jorisvandenbossche  @amueller @jnothman @ogrisel

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
> handling of infrequent categories (issue #12153, PR #13833)

I note that OrdinalEncoder does not currently have any handling of categories not seen at fit.

> Mainly if we want to implement support directly or suggest to use an imputer for the pre-processing step (as one can do now).

If we want to support estimators, here and elsewhere, that learn directly from data with missing values, we're best propagating the missingness rather than imputing.

> Do we say that categories='dtype' would make OHE categories match categories in the dtype
? Including the ordering?

I think so. I think ordering should be respected even when ordered=False, since ordered=False is the default, and since it would be easier to use s.codes than to remap them. But I could be persuaded to respect the order only when ordered=True.

> But then, this means only at fit since, for transform, the test set could have unknown categories.

I think if there is a categorical dtype at fit time, then unknown categories appearing at transform time should raise an error. This should be included in `_validate_data` across the board.

> some categories from the dtype can be missing from the train set as well. Do we then create a column with 0s in fit_transform, or disregard this column breaking the assumption of conforming to dtype categories?

I'm not certain, but maybe just make the column with 0s, for correspondence with when one explicitly sets the categories.

> Infrequent categories: Overall the plan seems fairly clear in #12153 (comment)

This does not pertain to OrdinalEncoder, where we don't even know how to handle unknowns. But infrequent category handling is more straightforward than unknowns when ordinal encoding, because at least in the case of infrequents, we "know" the order where the value should appear, and either conflate with the greater or lesser category.

> Handling NaN

I think in OrdinalEncoder, the only encoding of NaN should be as NaN.

I don't think that handling NaN as a separate category is a problem in OHE (and I don't see why we need to modify the dtype). When absent from training, I would just output a row of zeros.

> Do infrequent categories rules apply to NaN or is it always a separate category (even if passes the infrequent criteria)?

My instinct is to treat it as special, not an infrequent cat, but I am not wedded to this position.

> Similarly we could consider a preprocessor that would add infrequent as a category to dtype, instead of doing that internally in encoders. 

I don't get why we're modifying the dtype, except for efficiency. And if for efficiency, then we do whatever is pragmatic, as long as it's hidden from the user, i.e. creates no API stability issues.

> ohe.get_feature_names().tolist()

The convention is to return a list from `get_feature_names()`

> as opposed to, df['col'].value_counts()["infrequent"] where it was properly added to df['col'].cat.categories previously and we are using all the nice features of pd.Categorical.

It's fine to ask the user to handle infrequents themselves (with the caveat that they'll likely mess up the train-test split)... but if we want to handle it in our encoders, then I don't think we can do that by modifying the input... so I don't understand this suggestion, until I read the next paragraph where I see you are considering handling infrequent categories in a different transformer.

If we can design an InfrequentCategoryTransformer, I'm okay with that... I'm not yet convinced that it will work without duplicating a lot of the stuff (either the implementation, or the need to specify parameters redundantly) from OHE or OrdinalEncoder, nor am I convinced that we can decouple the handling of pd.Categorical from encoders entirely.

I'd be keen to see this framed around some test cases as @thomasjpfan has done for one small piece of the pie.

creator: GregoryMorse
title: StratifiedKFold yields slightly different class label distributions (prior to 0.22 different train and test sizes)
text:
#### Description
Unfortunately, probably due to the stratification balancing, the train and test size can vary between iteration.  This is pretty highly undesirable and it should always rebalance to same sizes.  Otherwise combining all the folds and using efficient vectorized operations to do computations in a matrix with an extra dimension is not easily possible.

This honestly feels like a poor stratification algorithm.  At worst this is a flat out bug.  At best, its a mode of operation, and a Boolean flag should be added such as something like `force_exact_division=True`.  Of course, in some cases it is impossible to balance the classes, but even in those cases, it could still prefer to guarantee equal distribution, rather than guarantee equal class sizes since we are talking about only fractional remainders here - and the class sizes are not going to be perfect percentage wise balanced anyway as it can be impossible for example if only 1 value belongs to a class.  This is surprisingly awkward functionality.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
kfold = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
X, y = np.arange(7590)[:,np.newaxis], np.random.RandomState(0).randint(0, 3, 7590)
for (train, test) in kfold.split(X, y):
    print(len(train), len(test))
kfold = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for (train, test) in kfold.split(X, y):
    assert(len(test) == 7590/5)
    assert(len(train) == 7590*4/5)
```

#### Expected Results
```
6072 1518
6072 1518
6072 1518
6072 1518
6072 1518
```

#### Actual Results
```
6071 1519
6071 1519
6072 1518
6072 1518
6074 1516
Traceback (most recent call last):

  File "<ipython-input-106-1c41a73d61b2>", line 8, in <module>
    assert(len(test) == 7590/5)

AssertionError
```

Seems to always be in order from `min(len(train))` to `max(len(train))`

#### Versions
Windows-10-10.0.18362-SP0
Python 3.7.4 (default, Aug  9 2019, 18:34:13) [MSC v.1915 64 bit (AMD64)]
NumPy 1.17.3
SciPy 1.3.1
Scikit-Learn 0.21.3

events.author: GregoryMorse
events.comment: Reference #10767 where @jnothman mentions the StratifiedKFold algorithm needs a complete redo and #11777 which although a different issue still involves the way it balances classes.

events.author: GregoryMorse
events.comment: It is not impossible to vectorize with different sizes, but it adds complications as the extra dimension will not work.  Instead the rows would be concatenated, the train and test sizes will need to be tracked so it can be split apart again.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: Fixed in #14704. Please confirm that this issue is fixed in 0.22, and help us identify other related issues that can be closed. Thanks

events.author: GregoryMorse
events.comment:
@jnothman, excellent sorry I did not search the PRs only the issues.  This is perfect if it preserves the train-test size and the class value distribution amongst folds.  Allows for some really clever vectorized operations to be done on all at once in certain contexts.

I realized 0.22 was just freshly released.  It is indeed working there but since I did not check class label distribution so let us do that now:
```py
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
kfold = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
X, y = np.arange(7590)[:,np.newaxis], np.random.RandomState(0).randint(0, 3, 7590)
counts = []
for (train, test) in kfold.split(X, y):
    _, ctrain = np.unique(y[train], return_counts=True)
    _, ctest = np.unique(y[test], return_counts=True)
    counts.append((len(train), len(test), *ctrain, *ctest))
print(counts)
assert(all([counts[0] == x for x in counts[1:]]))
```

```
[(6072, 1518, 2031, 2079, 1962, 508, 520, 490), (6072, 1518, 2031, 2079, 1962, 508, 520, 490), (6072, 1518, 2031, 2079, 1962, 508, 520, 490), (6072, 1518, 2031, 2080, 1961, 508, 519, 491), (6072, 1518, 2032, 2079, 1961, 507, 520, 491)]
Traceback (most recent call last):

  File "<ipython-input-1-b0c88890b497>", line 11, in <module>
    assert(all([counts[0] == x for x in counts[1:]]))

AssertionError
```

So it almost looks perfect.  The train-test is divided in equal sizes each time.  But the 5th run we see class value counts for train and test differing between `2031, 2079, 1962, 508, 520, 490` and `2032, 2079, 1961, 507, 520, 491`.  I think the test code above might be worthy of integration as a unit test.

@jnothman is this a failure for the algorithm, or is equal class label group sizes not guaranteed?

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
No we cannot guarantee equality.

Please see
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/5f3c3f0378f2f30f3c4340bd9bf1e211e96d5c3c/sklearn/model_selection/_split.py#L613
for
the set of invariances that should hold.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I'm pretty sure there is no issue here.

The docs could be updated to add the general kfold invariances: the test sets together constitute a partition of the full dataset into n_splits subsets, and each test and train set constitute a partition of the full dataset. 

With all of these constraints, I think this is as good as it gets.

events.author: GregoryMorse
events.comment:
Yes everything looks good here especially from a theoretical data science standpoint.  The invariance listed are holding.

However, for practical purposes having equal group sizes could be very beneficial in some tasks.  Here is the idea: a flag `force_equal_class_sizes=True`.  It would have some theoretical problems as rows would never be included and some would be included twice but these are outliers and not statistically relevant.  As long as this is acceptable and understood.  Take the remainders of `classes_counts % n_splits`.  All 0 remainder do not have a problem and are already in the current code fine.  The remainders are sorted in descending order.  The top half or largest of the remainders will be in the `+1` category while the bottom half of the remainders will be in the `-1` category.  A middle value would be in the `0` category.  Then any in the `+1` category will randomly use extra values for the `n_splits-classes_counts%n_splits` hole values.  And the `-1` category will randomly drop a value for its `classes_counts%n_splits` values.  Doing this strategy minimizes the number of repeated values and dropped values, while allowing this class label preservation property.  If it does not then slight modification to the strategy might be needed but the goal of minimizing the spurious values is not so complicated.  @jnothman what do you think of the idea?  Probably the issue will come up every so often without doing some best-try approximation solution like this and adding the feature flag.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I'd rather not make things more complicated in this space without very
clear justification

events.author: GregoryMorse
events.comment:
1. This would not change the existing code which is very good right now.  The refactoring is excellent and should not be changed as its certainly an improvement over the old algorithm.  I cannot think of any good argument for the old code though perhaps it is preserving the class sizes and not the test sizes (and should be also allowed via parameter).  Both can be argued as data science theoretically justified depending on what your priority is.  But its such a small point that I don't think anyone would ever care, and the old code is the most awkward.
2. Admittedly this does make things complicated.   Well the only clear justification is doing vectorized operations so a computation can be done on all train/test folds simultaneously.  Because you cannot construct an ndarray or matrix of them without them being equal class sizes.  Over enough data, the fact that a very small amount of missing rows or duplicated rows is present is statistically insignificant and the convenience of vectorized operations outweighs this cost.  I am doing axis-based calculations on data for example, its the slowest place in my code and I cannot optimize with the current stratification algorithm and am stuck with for-loops or list comprehensions or such.

3. Why not make StratifiedKFold totally comprehensive of all possible desirable details in terms of stable test/train sizes, stable class value sizes.  Even a mode parameter could easily allow all variations of functionality.

Mode 1: test/train size equivalent as in v0.22.
Mode 2: class label proportions equivalent (I am not sure if this was true in v0.21?)
Mode 3: test/train size equivalent and class label sizes equivalent.  This introduces either missing rows, duplicated rows or a mixture of the two theoretically adding 3 submodes of operation.
    Submode 1: minimize missing rows/duplicated rows using some simple algorithm along the lines of what I highlighted.
    Submode 2: increase the train/test size to make sure only duplicated rows are added and no rows are missing.
    Submode 3: decrease the train/test size to make sure no duplicated rows and only rows dropped.

At least we can at least discuss this here, as I cannot think of any further complication that could ever be justified.  Granted my situation might be a narrow use case, but is there harm in trying to include it?
