creator: rth
title: Change default copy value from True to None
text:
A fair amount of estimators currently have `copy=True` (or `copy_X=True`) by default. In practice, this means that the code looks something like,
```py
X = check_array(X, copy=copy)
```
and then some other calculations that may change or not X inplace. In the case when the following operations are not done inplace, we have just made a wasteful copy with no good reason.

As discussed in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/13923, an example is for instance `Ridge(fit_intercept=False)` that will copy X, although it is not needed. ~~Actually, I can't find any inplace operations of `X` in `Ridge` even with `fit_intercept=True`, but maybe I am missing something.~~ (found it)

I think in general it would be better to avoid the,
```py
X = check_array(X, copy=copy)
```
pattern, and instead make a copy explicitly where it is needed. Maybe it could  be OK to not make a copy with `copy=True` if no copy is needed. Alternatively we could introduce `copy=None` by default.

Adding a common test that checks that `Estimator(copy=True).fit(X, y)` doesn't change `X`.

events.author: amueller
events.comment: Actually we have test with read-only X which probably will enforce that we don't change X by default.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> Actually we have test with read-only X which probably will enforce that we don't change X by default.

Very good point. I made #13987 to address this issue in preprocessing (e.g. `StandardScaler`).

For future reference, to find estimators that potentially have this issue, one can use a common test that checks that an exception is raised when one tries to use an estimator with `copy=False` on read-only array. If it is not raised, it is likely that with `copy=True` a copy is not actually necessary (though there are false positives).
```py
@ignore_warnings(category=(DeprecationWarning, FutureWarning))  
def check_transformer_extra_copy(name, transformer):    
    X, y = make_blobs(n_samples=30, centers=[[0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1]],  
                      random_state=0, n_features=2, cluster_std=0.1)  
    X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)  
    X -= X.min()  
  
    X, y = create_memmap_backed_data([X, y])  
  
    estimator = clone(transformer)
    sig = signature(transformer.__class__.__init__)
    if "copy" in sig.parameters:
    	estimator.set_params(copy=False)  
  
    	assert_raise_message(ValueError, "is read-only", estimator.fit, X, y)
```

It's not reliable enough to add it to common tests, but as a detection method, it works reasonably well. The same could be done for classifiers etc.

Also, it should be noted, that for more complex estimators with numerous options it is sometimes hard to decide whether a copy is needed (e.g. `Birch.fit`). In that case, it's probably better to keep the copy to be safe, particularly when the performance gained by avoiding the copy is negligible with respect to the fit or transform time.

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
awesome. though that will "only" detect spurious copies if there's a ``copy`` parameter (and that copy parameter is what causes the spurious copy).
I'm sure there's many other spurious copies that don't fulfill these requirements.

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment:
I think I'd worry about not copying even if the user explicitly says so. Imagine you have a live system which is updating some matrix on the go, and every now and then does some training using a snapshot of the data. In that case, the user would probably want to have the model to use a copy of the data instead of the data which is changing in another thread as the model trains.

That said, I'd say the user should probably not do what I just described, which means it's pretty okay to avoid those copies if not needed, and probably raising an error if `copy=True` and it's not needed, instead of silently not creating a copy?

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> I think I'd worry about not copying even if the user explicitly says so. Imagine you have a live system which is updating some matrix on the go, and every now and then does some training using a snapshot of the data. In that case, the user would probably want to have the model to use a copy of the data instead of the data which is changing in another thread as the model trains.

My point is that instead of using `copy=True` and making a copy when it's not needed, the default should be `copy=None` so that a copy is only made when the data is changed inplace. From the user perspective, this shouldn't change anything (if they didn't rely on scikit-learn to make that copy for his user code). The problem is that ideally, this would involve changing the default of the `copy` parameters in estimators.

For instance take `StandardScaler()` the copy parameters (default: True) says,
> If False, try to avoid a copy and do inplace scaling instead. This is not guaranteed to always work inplace; e.g. if the data is not a NumPy array or scipy.sparse CSR matrix, a copy may still be returned.

While actually, currently after https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/13987 even with `copy=True` no copy will be made (if this doesn't change the data), and that's actually not a good behavior . That should be the behavior for `copy=None`.

So the questions is do we,
 - change the default `copy=True` to `copy=None` without a deprecation warning, considering this a bugfix since copying the data for the user is outside of the responsibility of estimators IMO, the only thing estimator should do is either pass the data through unmodified (default) or modify it inplace if `copy=False`.
 - the default `copy=True` to `copy=None` with a deprecation warning. This will pretty be annoying for the user as most estimator will then raise a warning.

Neither is ideal, but at the same time I feel this is something that we need to fix, as when you have a pipeline with N estimators, the overhead of copying the data N time even when it's not necessary can become non-negligible.

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment:
The whole `copy` semantics is kinda not clean at the moment IMO, and I like your proposal. So it'd be:

- `None`: only copy if there is going to be a change in the data, avoid _inplace_ modificatoins.
- `True`: always create a copy before doing anything, no matter what.
- `False`: do not copy and do modifications in place. With the side note that we still create copies because some operations create a copy, or some modules require the data in a specific dtype (like float64), and therefore we still create a copy, even though we're trying to fix them?

events.author: rth
events.comment:
Agreed. Any ideas how we should change the default value?

> True: always create a copy before doing anything, no matter what.

To make matters more complicated, the above should be true for transformers, but say `estimator.fit` doesn't need to copy the data (if no inplace modifications happen) even with `copy=True`.

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment:
> To make matters more complicated, the above should be true for transformers, but say estimator.fit doesn't need to copy the data (if no inplace modifications happen) even with copy=True.

But that's why we want to introduce `None`, isn't it? Why would we give the same behavior to `True` if we have `None` for it?

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> But that's why we want to introduce None, isn't it? Why would we give the same behavior to True if we have None for it?

We need `copy=None` to avoid needless copies in `estimator.transform`.

For `estimator.fit(X)`, the only case when the user may want to copy the data is if `X` is stored as a private attribute of the estimator (e.g. brute force nearest-neighbors). For other cases, if no inplace operations happen, it doesn't really make sense to guarantee that a copy will be made internally IMO.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: I think I had just assumed that copy=True meant copy=None. I'd prefer `copy='on-write'` or something...

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> I think I had just assumed that copy=True meant copy=None. 

That is another possibility to avoid a deprecation cycle, but then we need to clearly state it in the docstring.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
> I'd prefer copy='on-write' or something...

I am +1 on this idea. People with a slight CS background can quickly understand "copy-on-write" over `None`.

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment: @jeremiedbb we probably should fix this one first, and then we would know what to show the user in case of failure in #14481

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
I hadn't seen this discussion before, my 2c are in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/14481#issuecomment-515548671

I don't think there's three options that we care about. I think the two options that we care about on estimator level is "allow in-place operations" and "don't allow in-place operations".

I think maybe part of the confusion is that the ``copy`` keyword of ``check_array`` means something different from the ``copy`` parameter of an estimator.

The copy parameter of ``check_array`` says whether to force a copy, the copy parameter of an estimator says whether to allow inplace operations in X.

We could deprecate the ``copy`` in all estimators and rename it ``inplace`` to make the meaning more clear? I think for ``check_array`` the ``copy`` keyword makes sense: it's whether to make a copy or not.

```python
X = check_array(X, copy=self.copy)
```
on the other hand makes little sense really.

When you say you want to add ``copy='on-write'``, is that for ``check_array`` or for estimators? Or for both?
Right now, I think for estimators, the (only sensible) meaning of ``True`` is ``'on-write'``.

creator: amueller
title: Add non-strict mode to check_estimator
text:
Right now the common tests have two different use-cases: checking internal sklearn estimators, and checking 3rd party estimators via ``check_estimator``.

The common tests are very strict to a degree that's not really reasonable for 3rd party estimators, in particular in checking for particular error messages.
Furthermore, the required error-messages are not documented anywhere (see also #10082).

I think it would be good to add a ``strict=False`` argument to check_estimator to not require exact messages, and possibly not even the exact error types. That would make it much easier for people to use ``check_estimator``.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
It's true that having a way to differentiate common tests used internally for scikit-learn and those intented to run on 3rd-party packages would be very useful. Related to #6715 . Maybe using something like,
```py
if estimator.__module__.startswith('sklearn.'):
    # run some scikit-learn specific check
```
in common tests would be better? For the examples you provide they should never apply outside of scikit-learn and this would avoid passing this parameter everywhere..

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
I would rather give the user the control rather than being magic about it. It would add the parameter in a lot of places.
On the other hand, we would have to add your snippet in a lot of places as well (though not in the signatures).
Maybe someone wants to have error messages consistent with sklearn?
I'm not entirely decided but right now tending towards a parameter.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: I'm happy with strict=False param...

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment: I think not having the exact error message is good. Now...are we okay with not even checking the types when `strict=False`?

events.author: amueller
events.comment: Or strict could be ``'message', 'type' or False``? Not sure if that's necessary though.

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment: Since this seems to be the place, do we want to have a deprecation cycle for certain API changes in `check_estomator`? Seems reasonable to me. Certain checks can then move from non-strict to strict with a deprecation cycle (related: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/14241#issuecomment-517383733)

creator: ShakesB33r
title: Linear regression unnecessarily slow
text:
TLDR so far: sklearn uses SVD which is more numerically stable, but perhaps it should default to something quicker such as suggested below unless SVD is needed. Later post contains detailed suggestion.

Standard linear regression implementation seems unnecessarily slow, at least in many cases. May extend to other linear estimators e.g. Ridge.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```py
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import numpy as np
import time

def mylin(X,Y):
    CXX = np.dot(X.T,X)/X.shape[0]
    CXY = np.dot(X.T,Y)/X.shape[0]
    return np.linalg.solve(CXX,CXY).T
    
X = np.random.normal(size=[500000,40])

lin.fit(X,Y)

t = time.time()
coef = mylin(X,Y)
print('Time to fit analytic linear regression solution:', time.time()-t)

print('Correlation between solutions:', np.corrcoef(coef.flatten(), lin.coef_.flatten())[0,1])
```

events.author: rick2047
ShakesB33r
events.comment:
The scipy/sklearn version will in fact be much more numerically stable and accurate in cases when you have near-singular (or even singular) X covariance matrices, as it uses SVD. In fact, if you try to do an SVD in python via `coefs = np.dot(np.linalg.pinv(X), Y)`,  it runs a little slower than sklearn/scipy implementation. 

Perhaps the default behaviour could be to calculate the X covariance matrix (CXX), and if that is ill conditioned then to fall back on scipy implementation, otherwise to proceed as above (or something similar). To be more precise, calculate CXX, calculate its condition number `cond = np.linalg.cond(CXX)`, and if that is above some (perhaps user-specified) threshold, e.g. 1e4, then revert back to other solution method. You could also make use of a kwarg that allows you to prefer such a solution method.

New code snippet for comparison below. If you decrease N (to e.g. 20), you will see that the SVD solution stays much closer to the sklearn one, since the conditioning of the sample covariance matrix worsens on average with fewer samples.

```
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import numpy as np
import time

def mylin(X,Y):
    CXX = np.dot(X.T,X)/X.shape[0]
    CXY = np.dot(X.T,Y)/X.shape[0]
    return np.linalg.solve(CXX,CXY).T
    
N = 500000

X = np.random.normal(size=[N,40])
Y = np.random.normal(size=[N,10])

lin = LinearRegression(False)

t = time.time()
lin.fit(X,Y)
print('Time to fit sklearn linear:', time.time()-t)

t = time.time()
coef = mylin(X,Y)
print('Time to fit analytic linear regression solution with matrix inversion:', time.time()-t)

print('Deviation from sklearn solution:', np.std(coef.flatten() - lin.coef_.flatten()))

t = time.time()
coef2 = np.dot(np.linalg.pinv(X), Y).T
print('Time to fit analytic linear regression solution with SVD:', time.time()-t)

print('Deviation from sklearn solution:', np.std(coef2.flatten() - lin.coef_.flatten()))

CXX = np.dot(X.T,X)/X.shape[0]
print('Condition number of X covariance:', np.linalg.cond(CXX))
```

events.author: rth

> sklearn seems to add a 5-10x overhead on top of the solution itself, at least on my machine.

That should not be happening, refactoring your benchmarks a bit below 

<details>

```
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.utils import check_X_y
import numpy as np
import time
from neurtu import timeit, delayed


def simple_linear_regression(X, Y):
    X, Y = check_X_y(X, Y, multi_output=True)
    CXX = np.dot(X.T, X) / X.shape[0]
    CXY = np.dot(X.T, Y) / X.shape[0]
    return np.linalg.solve(CXX, CXY).T


N = 500000

X = np.random.normal(size=[N, 40])
Y = np.random.normal(size=[N, 10])


benchmarks = []

for name, estimator_fit in [
    ("LinearRegression", LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit),
    (
        "Ridge(alpha=1e-9, solver='cholesky')",
        Ridge(alpha=1e-9, solver="cholesky", fit_intercept=False).fit,
    ),
    ("np.linalg.solve(CXX,CXY)", simple_linear_regression),
    ("np.linalg.pinv(X) @ Y", lambda X, y: np.dot(np.linalg.pinv(X), Y).T),
    ("condition number", lambda X, y: np.linalg.cond((X.T @ X) / X.shape[0]))
]:
    benchmarks.append(delayed(estimator_fit, tags={"name": name})(X, Y))


df = timeit(benchmarks)

print(df)
```
</details>


I get roughly comparable performance for `Ridge(1e-9, solver="cholesky")` and `np.linalg.solve(CXX, CXY).T`, particularly once `check_X_y` is added (run on a laptop),


creator: AbhilashMathews
title: Error when computing the gradient of a derivative with Gaussian process regression in scikit
text:
Gaussian process regression in scikit-learn provides a conditional mean and variance, (y_*,\sigma_*^2), based upon the observed data, (y,\sigma^2). But given (y_*,\sigma_*^2), how can you compute the variance of \frac{dy_*}{dx_*} in scikit-learn? The formula for doing this is given by [equation (9.1)](http://www.gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW9.pdf), although when applying this method in the below code, I receive erroneous results. Here is a working example:  

    import numpy as np
    from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
    from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
    from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF, ConstantKernel as C
    def f(x):
        """The function to predict."""
        return 1.5*(1. - np.tanh(100.*(x-0.96))) + 1.5*x*(x-0.95) + 0.4 + 1.5*(1.-x)* np.random.random(x.shape)
    
    X = np.array([0.803,0.81,0.82,0.827,0.83,0.84,0.845,0.861,0.875,0.892,0.905,
                    0.91,0.92,0.925,0.935,0.941,0.947,0.96,
                    0.974,0.985,0.995,1.0])
    X = np.atleast_2d(X).T
    
    # Observations and noise
    y = f(X).ravel() 
    noise = 0.6/y
    y += noise
     
    kernel = C(1.0, (1e-10, 1000)) * RBF(100, (1e-4, 1e4))
    gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=kernel, alpha=noise ** 2,
                                  n_restarts_optimizer=50)
    
    gp.fit(X, y)
     
    x = np.atleast_2d(np.linspace(0.8, 1.02, 1000)).T
    y_pred, sigma = gp.predict(x, return_std=True)
    
    plt.figure() 
    plt.errorbar(X.ravel(), y, noise, fmt='k.', markersize=10, label=u'Observations')
    plt.plot(x, y_pred, 'k-', label=u'Prediction')
    plt.fill(np.concatenate([x, x[::-1]]),
             np.concatenate([y_pred - 1.9600 * sigma,
                            (y_pred + 1.9600 * sigma)[::-1]]),
             alpha=.1, fc='k', ec='None', label='95% confidence interval')
    plt.xlabel('x')
    plt.ylabel('y')
    plt.xlim(0.8, 1.02)
    plt.ylim(0, 5)
    plt.legend(loc='lower left')
    plt.show()
    
provides me with the expected result for (y_*,\sigma_*^2):

[![y][1]][1]

But now I would like to compute \frac{dy_*}{dx_*} and its associated error. I try this via 2 approaches:

**1)** I know that k(x_*,x_*) = \sigma^2_*, so if I simply take the gradient of \sigma^2_* with respect to x_* twice, then I should recover \frac{d^2k(x_*,x_*)}{dx_*^2}, which is exactly equal to the expression in (9.1). When I do this: 

    dkdx = np.gradient(sigma**2.,x[:,0])
    d2kdx2 = np.gradient(dkdx,x[:,0]) 
    dydx = np.gradient(y_pred,x[:,0])
    d2kdx2_old = d2kdx2*1.
    d2kdx2[d2kdx2 < 0.] = 0.01
    inds_new = np.where(d2kdx2 >= 0.) #I set all negative errors to 0 for plotting purposes
    cov_grad_used = d2kdx2[inds_new]
    x_plot = x[inds_new]
    dydx_err_plot = np.sqrt(cov_grad_used)
    dydx_plot = dydx[inds_new]
    
    plt.figure()  
    plt.plot(x_plot, dydx_plot, 'k-', label=u'Prediction')
    plt.fill(np.concatenate([x_plot, x_plot[::-1]]),
             np.concatenate([dydx_plot - 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot,
                            (dydx_plot + 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot)[::-1]]),
             alpha=.1, fc='k', ec='None', label='95% confidence interval')
    plt.xlabel('x')
    plt.ylabel('dy/dx (using sigma)')
    plt.legend(loc='lower left')
    plt.show()

[![dy/dx v1][2]][2]

the output looks almost right, but when I compute `np.min(d2kdx2)`, or, equivalently, `np.gradient(dkdx,x[:,0])`, I get a negative quantity! Yet we know that the variance of \frac{dy_*}{dx_*} should be purely positive! 

**2)** When I try an alternative but supposedly equivalent approach of evaluating the trained covariance kernel directly via `gp.kernel_` and trying to take the second derivative of the values along the diagonal, I get simply zero. This is displayed below:
    
    i = 0
    just_k = []
    while i < len(x):
        kern_eval = gp.kernel_(np.array([x[i][0]]).reshape(1,-1),np.array([x[i][0]]).reshape(1,-1))[0][0]
        just_k.append(kern_eval)
        i = i + 1
        
    just_k = np.array(just_k)
    K_used = just_k
    dkdx_kern = np.gradient(K_used,x[:,0]) #derivative of kernel (along diagonal) evaluated for the radial profile
    d2kdx2_kern = np.gradient(dkdx_kern,x[:,0]) #second derivative, which would correspond to error on dy/dx
    
    inds_new_kern = np.where(d2kdx2_kern >= 0.)
    cov_grad_used_kern = d2kdx2_kern[inds_new_kern]
    x_plot_kern = x[inds_new_kern]
    dydx_err_plot_kern = np.sqrt(cov_grad_used_kern)
    dydx_plot_kern = dydx[inds_new_kern]
    
    plt.figure()  
    plt.plot(x_plot_kern, dydx_plot_kern, 'k-', label=u'Prediction')
    plt.fill(np.concatenate([x_plot_kern, x_plot_kern[::-1]]),
             np.concatenate([dydx_plot_kern - 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot_kern,
                            (dydx_plot_kern + 1.9600 * dydx_err_plot_kern)[::-1]]),
             alpha=.1, fc='k', ec='None', label='95% confidence interval')
    plt.xlabel('x')
    plt.ylabel('dy/dx (using kernel)')
    plt.legend(loc='lower left')
    plt.show()

[![enter image description here][3]][3]

where `np.min(np.gradient(dkdx_kern,x[:,0]))` and `np.max(np.gradient(dkdx_kern,x[:,0]))` both equal zero; or equivalently, `d2kdx2_kern` is zero everywhere! This makes sense mathematically since I am applying a stationary kernel, but given (9.1), I thought this quantity was supposed to represent the variance of my derivative, so something appears off here.

Essentially these are two examples of codes trying to compute the variance associated to the derivative of y_*. But why do I get negative values for the derivative's variance using the first approach (i.e. via the second derivative of the conditional variance), and only zero using the second approach (i.e. via the second derivative of `gp.kernel_`)? What step(s) are necessary to compute the variance of \frac{dy_*}{dx_*} properly using scikit-learn's Gaussian process framework?

  [1]: https://i.stack.imgur.com/lkLHa.png
  [2]: https://i.stack.imgur.com/L0UGr.png
  [3]: https://i.stack.imgur.com/AtNWr.png

events.author: plgreenLIRU
events.comment:
Hi @AbhilashMathews I've had a look at your question. There's quite a lot going on in there so I'll start with a few questions about your example:

- Firstly, I can see that you are using the alpha parameter to tell the GP about the noise that is corrupting the observations. I don't think this is the correct way of doing this - alpha puts a 'ridge' on the GP covariance matrix (making sure we can find it's inverse without numerical errors) but alpha isn't included in the predictive equation, so it doesn't fulfil the role of 'noise variance'. I think this is actually a problem with the docs and have raised  #15990  as a result. Discussion is ongoing so I could still be wrong!

- I notice the 'noise' term being applied actually isn't random? Also, it's a function of so it isn't constant variance? If the noise variance changes with x then we would need to use something called a Heteroscedastic GP which, as far as I'm aware, is not something that sklearn has. Again, I think the docs are a bit misleading on this point (also an ongoing discussion).

- I can see there's a random number being used in the function f. Why is this there? I would usually expect f to be deterministic and then for the observation noise to be treated as random? 

Long story short, a more suitable example for you to test your method is probably something like this:

[pete.txt](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/files/4356070/pete.txt)

Final thing - why are you interested in calculating GP gradients? Not a criticism, just interested :)

title: Feature Request: DummyRegressor Per Category
text: The current [DummyRegressor](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.dummy.DummyRegressor.html) supports mean, median etc. for the whole dataset. What would be a very convenient addition is, if there was an argument that the DummyRegressor uses for grouping. I often encounter the situation where I want to build a model per some group or category and this would really help.

events.author: albertcthomas
events.comment: +1. I implemented a similar estimator for work. More generally a meta estimator learning one model per group could be useful. Using this meta estimator with DummyRegressor will give you what you want and you could also apply this meta estimator with other baseline estimators. This requires that all the groups are present in the training set.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
The grouping variable is a feature at fit and at predict time? I don't think this kind of thing is so easy to describe or identical across usages, and so might not be worth creating a standard component for it.

Is that basically a shallow tree built on a single feature?

events.author: r0f1
events.comment:
> More generally a meta estimator learning one model per group could be useful.

I like the idea too. Actually more than the idea of giving the DummyRegressor extra arguments. 

> ... so might not be worth creating a standard component for it.

I have written such a meta estimator once for a regression task. The constructur expects a model, feature columns and a grouping column (not sure if every component would be needed in a standard component). Say there are k different values in the grouping column. `fit()` fits the k models, and `predict()` uses those k models. 

Here it is: 

```python
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator
from sklearn.base import RegressorMixin
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

class ModelPerCategoryWrapper(BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin):  
  
    def __init__(self, model_class, model_columns, groupby, model_args=None):
        self.groupby = groupby
        self.model_class = model_class
        self.model_args = {} if model_args is None else model_args
        self.model_columns = model_columns
        self.models = dict()
        
    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        for group, frame in X.groupby(self.groupby):
            self.models[group] = self.model_class(**self.model_args)
            self.models[group].fit(
                  frame[self.model_columns]
                , y.loc[frame.index]
            )
        return self
    
    def predict(self, X, y=None):
        y_pred = pd.Series(np.nan, index=X.index)
        for group, frame in X.groupby(self.groupby):
            model = self.models.get(group, None)
            if not model: continue
            y_pred.update(
                pd.Series(
                      model.predict(frame[self.model_columns])
                    , index=frame.index
                )
            )
        return y_pred
    
    def score(self, X, y=None):
        y_pred = self.predict(X)
        return r2_score(y, y_pred)
```

#### Description
<!-- Example: Joblib Error thrown when calling fit on LatentDirichletAllocation with evaluate_every > 0-->
In ``_log_marginal_likelihood`` of BayesianRidge, some of the constant terms seem to be omitted.
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/17a253b0c748cd2ea0f64f8aa2911daf129ddff8/sklearn/linear_model/bayes.py#L351-L358
This code only calculates ![texclip20190510122056](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40843206/57500366-1c265c80-731e-11e9-86bb-1fc5989495d7.png) of the constant terms, which is a bit incorrect and confusing.

This problem is not really important, but I think it would be better to fix it.
Please let us know what you think.

#### Exact expressions
<!-- Example: No error is thrown. Please paste or describe the expected results.-->
The reference (Tipping, 2001) contains equations for log marginal likelihood (eq. 36, 38 and 40),
but there is no expression of constant terms.

So, I derived the formula as follows, 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/40843206/57502732-fe5df500-7327-11e9-8901-06c0e26d34e9.png)
where N is ``n_samples``, M is ``n_features`` and mu is ``coef``. (The red terms are currently omitted.)

events.author: albertcthomas
events.comment:
I strictly followed the paper when I fixed the formula of the `scores_` atttribute and I kept the `n_samples/2*ln(2*pi)` term that was in the previous formula. I agree that it is strange to have the `n_samples/2*ln(2*pi)` term if the other constant terms are not in the formula.
Why adding the others and not just remove the `n_samples/2*ln(2*pi)` term then?

Besides, `_log_marginal_likelihood` is also not a very good naming from my part as the method implements the product of the log of the marginal likelihhood and priors. We might want to change that (it's a private method so it should have no consequences for the users) and the description of the `scores_` attribute as well.

events.author: c56pony
events.comment:
> Why adding the others and not just remove the ``n_samples/2*ln(2*pi)`` term then?

If you only want to maximize, the constant terms are not needed.
But in my opinion, they are needed when comparing various models with different numbers of features and hyper-parameters.

>``_log_marginal_likelihood`` is also not a very good naming
We might want to change...the description of the ``scores_`` attribute

In this case, the product of the marginal likelihood (integrated out w) and the prior is apparently the same as the marginal likelihood integrated out w, alpha and lambda(, except that the point estimate of ``alpha`` is replaced with the expectation value of alpha, ``E[alpha]`` and so on).
So, the name ``_log_marginal_likelihood`` is not necessarily wrong, but I agree that it's confusing and not good.
How about changing to ``_log_likelihood`` simply?
In fact, L above is the log likelihood for ``alpha_1``, ``alpha_2``, ``lambda_1``, ``lambda_2``

events.author: albertcthomas
events.comment: I'm +1 to update the score with the constant terms. And I also think that it might be good to update the `scores_` description and the name of the method that implements it.

creator: thomasjpfan
title: Add Hypothesis Testing
text:
It may be beneficial to add hypothesis testing to some of our tests. Hypothesis testing allows for us to verify mathematical properties such as commutativity: 

```python
from hypothesis import given
import hypothesis.strategies as st

@given(st.integers(), st.integers())
def test_ints_are_commutative(x, y):
    assert x + y == y + x
```

This allows the CI to look for edge cases for us. This would be useful testing metrics. https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

events.author: rth
events.comment:
I think hypothesis is quite interesting, however, in my experience, it makes tests run significantly longer (when compared to  pytest.parametrize with a couple of options), and our tests suite is already quite slow.

Also, I really see the usefulness of hypothesis for testing edge cases of functions taking in int, str, etc (as the example above). For scientific computing when the input is arrays it more challenging. For instance, all invariance etc assumptions are valid as long as we don't reach floating point precisions issues, and it's relatively easy to reach those when generating random unbound floats. 
 
> This would be useful testing metrics. 

What kind of things did you have in mind? Possibly related https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/8589

creator: gwerbin
title: ColumnTransformer doesn't accept some valid Pandas column names
text:
#### Description

Pandas columns can be tuples, or in the case of a MultiIndex, can be accessed using a tuple. `ColumnTransformer` does not support this. It seems to be an oversight in the data validation, specifically in how [`_check_key_type()`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/compose/_column_transformer.py#L560-L588) is used.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

columns_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([('a', 1), ('a', 2), ('b', 0)])

d1 = pd.DataFrame([
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6]
], columns=columns_index)

ct = ColumnTransformer([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler(), [('a', 1), ('a', 2)])
])

d2 = ct.fit_transform(d1)
```

#### Expected Results

`ColumnTransformer` accesses columns `('a', 1)` and `('a', 2)`, and sends them to the `StandardScaler` instance.

#### Actual Results

```
ValueError: No valid specification of the columns. Only a scalar, list or slice of all integers or all strings, or boolean mask is allowed
```

events.author: gwerbin
events.comment:
> @gwerbin We had many discussions in the original ColumnTransformer PR, but I _think_ we limited the allowed types on purpose, and not by oversight (or at least for scalar types (eg also no floats, timestamps, etc work), MultiIndex tuples I am less sure about).
> 
> Which doesn't mean we can't relax the restriction now with good arguments for certain cases of course!
> 
> So currently it is strictly limited to ints and strings or list / slice of them (+ boolean mask). And the integers are always interpreted as positional, although they could also be column names in pandas. I think for that reason, we decided to just stick with strings, at least for the initial implementation, which is the most common case.

Hi, I forgot about this issue.

Yes, I think specifically accepting _tuples_ to support multiindex columns is a useful thing to support, because multiindexes are a really useful advanced pandas feature.

I think for the most part people tend to avoid numbers, booleans, tuple literals, etc. as column names, because they have questionable built-in support in Pandas anyway. So you definitely don't need to (and probably shouldn't) support various other general cases like that.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
> I'm under the impression that https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/13790 was closed as this feature were not accepted for inclusion.

Looking over the PR, I think that `tuple` was too permissive https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/13790#issuecomment-490141672. 

Looking at this now, I think we can support MultiIndex selection if we become restrictive and require the MultiIndex itself. Here is my proposed API:

```python
ct = ColumnTransformer([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler(), pd.MultiIndex([('a', 1), ('a', 2)]))
])
```

Essentially, we do no processing when a pandas Index object is used for selection. (We can have the same semantics for `pd.Index`.) With that in mind, I think we can leave this issue open.

@gwerbin Would the proposed API of passing the `MultiIndex` directly work for your use case?

REF: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/13790#issuecomment-491506336

events.author: gwerbin
events.comment:
It is a bit verbose, but I understand the desire to avoid confusion over "sequence" types. Maybe at least you could allow a specification like this: `[('a', 1), ('a', 2)]`, which shouldn't be confusing or ambiguous as far as I can tell.

The problem with both is that neither specification allows you to select a _single_ multiindex'ed column. Maybe that's fine and it's just a limitation/tradeoff to avoid the interface confusion. It's certainly better than nothing.

Note that Pandas and Numpy already do not treat lists and tuples interchangeably, so I imagine that moderately-experienced Pandas users should find this interface intuitive, or at least consistent with what they are already familiar with.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
> The problem with both is that neither specification allows you to select a single multiindex'ed column.

Here are all the use cases I am thinking of:

```python
import pandas as pd

columns_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([('a', 1), ('a', 2), ('b', 0)])

df = pd.DataFrame([
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6]
], columns=columns_index)

# Select on the first level
df[pd.Index(["a"])]

# Select a single column
df[pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("a", 1)])]

# Select multiple columns.
df[pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([("a", 1), ("a", 2)])]
```

I think using the mulitindex can specify a single column. Is there another use case I am missing?

events.author: gwerbin
events.comment:
> I think using the mulitindex can specify a single column. Is there another use case I am missing?

This produces a "single column", but if you use it with `DataFrame.loc` it returns a `DataFrame` of one column, rather than a `Series` representing that one column.

The difference isn't that big, and the only cost is that it might require you to write a wrapper for your transformer that converts between `DataFrame` and `Series`. So it's a question of making the "sub-transformers" more complicated in order to make the "top-level transformer" interface less confusing.

creator: kyle-pena-nlp
title: calling ComplementNB.predict_proba with sparse X converts feature_log_prob_ to sparse
text:
<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description

*Surface Level*: `ComplementNB.predict_proba` is slow when you call predict_proba with a sparse X - far slower than if you call predict_proba with a dense X.

*Deeper Problem Description*: `ComplementNB` converts `ComplementNB.feature_log_prob_` to a sparse matrix on every call to predict_proba, which is expensive and wasteful.

Ideally, when BaseNB calls `safe_sparse_dot`, it should do so with matrices that are either both sparse, both dense, or if they are not both the same "kind", then the matrix that gets converted should be cheap to do so.

The unfortunate reality is the current implementation results in the usually large `feature_log_prob_` matrix getting converted to sparse and then thrown away, on every predict_proba call.

Some suggested fixes:

1. Call safe_sparse_dot with the mathematically equivalent `safe_sparse_dot(self.feature_log_prob_, X.T).T` in `_joint_log_likelihood`, which results in X.T getting converted to a dense matrix rather than self.feature_log_prob_ getting converted to a sparse matrix.  This results in a speedup when `X` is much smaller than `feature_log_prob_`

2. Represent `feature_log_prob_` both densely and sparsely, using one or the other for safe_sparse_dot depending on whether X is sparse or dense, or perhaps other considerations  (for example, I noticed that sometimes it is just faster to densify X)

3. Create separate APIs for working with dense vs. sparse X.

Note on 2: There are some technicalities with logsumexp that would need to be resolved.  Calculating logsumexp isn't supported on a sparse matrix because the "log-sum-exp" trick basically makes all entries non-zero, albeit temporarily.  Surely there's a workaround to get logsumexp to work on sparse matrices, I just haven't thought of a solution yet.

Details:
- When the developer calls `Complement.predict_proba`, this calls `BaseNB.predict_log_proba`, which calls `ComplementNB._joint_log_likelihood`, which in turn calls `safe_sparse_dot` on the sparse X and the dense `ComplementNB.feature_log_prob_`
- In `safe_sparse_dot`, if the first argument is sparse and the second is dense, the second argument is converted to a sparse matrix.
- `ComplementNB.feature_log_prob_`  can be expected to be very wide (vocab) and tall (classes) for CBOW-type problems.  
- Thus, the conversion to CSR is very time consuming and costly
- Thus, predict_proba is far slower than it needs to be.

My work-around is to densify X before calling predict_proba.   This works for when len(X) is reasonably small.

However, isn't supporting sparse matrices a major selling point of the sklearn Naive Baye's implementation, and kind of essential for being a good solution?

I've spent some time looking into changing the representation of `MNB.feature_log_prob_` to sparse in my own implementation.  What it comes down to is that a dense/dense multiplication is going to be faster for smaller X but doesn't scale well,, whereas a sparse/sparse multiplication is going to be slower than it needs to be for smaller problems but scales well in both speed and memory.

Moreover, there are technical problems with scipy.special.logsumexp (particularly, getting the "log-sum-exp" trick to work in a sparse context) that I just don't have the time to solve completely.  I do wonder if the log-sum-exp trick is truly necessary in this use case.

Perhaps feature_log_prob_ should be represented both ways and _joint_log_likelihood should choose the multiplication thought to be best give some heuristic?

Or, better yet, perhaps we should fork the naive bayes implementations into ones that support sparse and dense?

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Train a ComplementNB model with a large (100's of thousands vocab, ~500+ classes) vocabulary.  Call predict_proba using a sparse X with a single row. Note the execution time.

Call predict_proba with a dense X with a single row.  Note the vastly reduced execution time.

#### Expected Results
<!-- Example: No error is thrown. Please paste or describe the expected results.-->

Acceptable performance when X is sparse.




#### Actual Results
<!-- Please paste or specifically describe the actual output or traceback. -->

- With an `X` of 1 x 250K, and a `ComplementNB.feature_log_prob_` of 503 x 250K , the combined cost of sparsifying `feature_log_prob_` and performing `safe_sparse_dot` on the result is in the neighborhood of 4 seconds. With dense X, 0.088 seconds.
- The sparsification of `ComplementNB.feature_log_prob_` is repeated on every call to `predict_proba`, rather than once or never.




#### Versions


<!--
Please run the following snippet and paste the output below.

creator: sdpython
title: Ambiguous way to store n-grams in TfidfVectorizer and CountVectorizer
text:
#### Description

I'm trying to convert TfidfVectorizer into ONNX and it is not always to possible to find the exact list of tokens which composes a n-grams. I'd like to store n-grams as tuple instead of strings to clear ambiguities in ``vocabulary_``. The notebook explains it all: 
https://github.com/sdpython/mlinsights/blob/master/_doc/notebooks/sklearn/traceable_ngrams_tfidf.ipynb

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
https://github.com/sdpython/mlinsights/blob/master/_doc/notebooks/sklearn/traceable_ngrams_tfidf.ipynb

#### Expected Results
No change except in interval members vocabulary_.

#### Versions
< 0.21

events.author: rth
events.comment:
I agree that concatenating ngrams into one string is a non-reversible operation and using a tuple of strings might be more general.

However, at present, it is difficult to change it due to backward compatibility. Also in Python  manipulating `vocabulary_ : Dict[str, int]` is easier than `Dict[Tuple[str, ...], int]`.

In ONNX can't one concatenate ngrams parts into a single string?

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> I'd like to store n-grams as tuple instead of strings to clear ambiguities in vocabulary_

Any other opinions on this @jnothman @ogrisel ? Otherwise I'm afraid we might have to close this as a "wontfix".

events.author: mitar
events.comment:
> Also in Python manipulating vocabulary_ : Dict[str, int] is easier than Dict[Tuple[str, ...], int].

What would that be true? Both `str` and `Tuple` are in Python immutable, so manipulation is very similar.

+1 for fixing this.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> Both str and Tuple are in Python immutable, so manipulation is very similar.

What I meant is that the vocabulary of "this sentence" being `['this', 'sentence']`, is conceptually simpler than `[('this',), ('sentence',)]` because there is one less container object.

More importantly though is the question of backward compatibility. Changing the type of vocabulary would break (or require changing) a lot existing code. If that is to happen IMO a compelling case should be made why making this this change would be important in practice.

Also, the operation is indeed not reversible but in the end I'm not sure it's a bug or a feature. From an above linked notebook,
> As you can see, the original 30th n-grams 't is  the' is a little but ambiguous. It is in fact ('t is', ' the') as the TraceableTfidfVectorizer lets you know. The original form could have been ('t', 'is  the'), ('t is', '  the'), ('t is ', ' the'), ('t is  ', 'the'), ('t', 'is  ', 'the')... The regular expression gives some insights but not some information which can be easily used to guess the right one.

Does it really makes sense to represent the substring 't is  the' as 5+ different objects (all of which map to this substring exactly) for the ML model that would be applied to this? In other words, with this change, for a given tokenizer and a value of `ngram_range`,
  - would we only get only one of the above forms anyway? In that case, this change would not make a practical difference, except for inteprerability.
 -  would we always get the same multiple forms when that is possible? In this case we would be creating redundant variables which is probably not that great.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I don't get why this is necessary for ONNX support. What's the goal? If
ONNX is trying to replicate CountVectorizer.transform it obviously doesn't
need to make this distinction if we don't.

You're right that there's some ambiguity and that "t is the" can pass the
min_df threshold by mixing different forms. But I think the idea of taking
>1-grams of tokens containing spaces is a pretty strange thing to do.
What's the intention there?

But I'm okay for space_join to become a class attribute, maybe even a
parameter. This would allow the user to use json.dumps or
'MYDELIMITER'.join... but it is flexibility that is usually not needed.

(Also, please focus on CountVectorizer, not TfidfVectorizer which is just a
composition of CountVectorizer and TfidfTransformer.)

title: Strange behavior of label_binarize when there's only one class in y
text:
When there's only one class in y, label_binarize produces unexpected result
```

label_binarize([1, 1, 1], classes=[1])
# actual result [[0], [0], [0]]
# expected result [[1], [1], [1]]
```

```py
Out[13]:

In [14]: label_binarize([1, 1, 2, 5], classes=[3, 6])
```

events.author: cmarmo
events.comment: The [current main version](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/b6bc5599ae063a90c27c9c1fef1940d620b5a206) still has the same behavior.

events.author: Micky774
events.comment:
## Problem

Okay it looks like the key here is that it bases its problem type mainly off of `y` as can be seen here:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/e2d120981fa8e520a8bec85e9902530b0c7c15b5/sklearn/preprocessing/_label.py#L505

This causes a couple different patterns.

1. When there are at most 2 distinct elements in `y` and exactly 1 element in `classes`, we get that `label_binarize` treats it as a trivial binary encoding where it always returns `np.zeros(len(y))+neg_label`, where `neg_label=0` by default. Code here:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/e2d120981fa8e520a8bec85e9902530b0c7c15b5/sklearn/preprocessing/_label.py#L517-L524

2. When there are at most 2 distinct elements in `y` and exactly 2 elements in `classes`, `label_binarize` treats it as a binary encoding where it returns an array default populated with `neg_label` but indices corresponding to elements of `y` that actually have their corresponding classes found in `classes` get `pos_label`. I think one thing that contributes to the confusion is that it silently and implicitly handles _unexpected classes_ as just negative labels which actually has a different semantic meaning in a binary context (i.e. not a _lack_ of label, but an actual negative label).

## Proposed solution:
1. Calculate problem type based on the set union of `classes` and `y`. The number of columns in the output would still be dependent only on `classes`. The set union just paints a clearer picture of the problem context. This definitely would not be backwards compatible with some cases, but I'm inclined to see it as a bug-fix. This would not alter the behavior of `LabelBinarizer` since it sets `classes` based on the unique entries of `y`, hence analyzing the set union would lead to the same result as just analyzing `y`.

2. Instead of returning a trivial array of `neg_label` in the first case of a 1-class binary encoding problem, the output should be `pos_label` in indices corresponding to elements of `y` contained in `classes` -- essentially a membership test as is the general case for multiclass encoding.

events.author: lucyleeow
events.comment:
In the second case I would argue that it is not clear what the user wants and maybe we should issue a warning instead of making assumptions?

In the first case:

> Instead of returning a trivial array of neg_label in the first case of a 1-class binary encoding problem, the output should be pos_label in indices corresponding to elements of y contained in classes 

seems like a reasonable solution. Essentially we will either return an array of `neg_label` if `y` is not in `classes` or an array of `pos_label` if `y` is in `classes`?

creator: 66Antigravity
title: Support for Pandas DataFrames in kernels & heterogeneous kernel
text:
#### Description

Categorical features in datasets are commonly treated with One-Hot-Encoding. However, a Gram matrix of a dot kernel can be calculated much faster directly with:

```python
def nominal_gram_dot(X1, X2):
   gram_matrix = np.zeros((X1.shape[0], X2.shape[0]))
   for i in range(X1.shape[0]):
       gram_matrix[i, :] = np.sum(X1[i, :] == X2, axis=1)
   return gram_matrix
```

On heterogeneous data, which contain both, numerical and categorical features, the Gram matrix can be then computed with:

```python
def hetero_kernel(X1, X2):
   X1_cat, X1_num = split_data(X1, categoricals)
   X2_cat, X2_num = split_data(X2, categoricals)
   gram_cat = nominal_gram_dot(X1_cat, X2_cat)
   gram_num = np.dot(X1_num, X2_num.T)
   gram = gram_cat + gram_num
   return gram
```

This can be used as a combination not only for the linear kernel but also polynomial, RBF (while defining "categorical Euclidean distance"), etc..

#### Comparison

![runtime-comp-samp](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30484650/56349073-1ed2dd80-61c8-11e9-9d84-e2af0225bba6.png) In this graph I compare np.dot after one-hot-encoding versus my implementation. Done on synthetic data.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
n_features = 50
n_samples = range(300, 2400, 100)
cardinality = 10
np.random.seed(seed=21)

times_samp = list()
for samples in n_samples:
   df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randint(cardinality, size=(samples, n_features)))
   for col in df.columns:
       df[col] = df[col].astype('category')

   start = time.time()
   df_ohe = pd.get_dummies(df, dummy_na=True, sparse=False)
   gram_ohe = np.dot(df_ohe, df_ohe.T)
   t_ohe = time.time() - start

   start = time.time()
   gram_delta = ker.build_hetero_kernel(np.ones(n_features, dtype='bool'))(X, X)
   t_delta = time.time() - start

   np.testing.assert_array_equal(gram_delta, gram_ohe)
   times_samp.append([t_delta, t_ohe])

times_samp = np.array(times_samp)
```

This is how you can reproduce the results of the linked graph.

#### Versions

events.author: 66Antigravity
events.comment:
Yes @jnothman, there is a straightforward way. In my implementation, I used closure to "simulate" the callable kernel. It is depending on the number of parameters you put into the ```build_hetero_kernel``` function.

Look at this snippet, where I used closure for various (three) kernels:

```python 
def nominal_gram_dot(X1, X2):
    gram_matrix = np.zeros((X1.shape[0], X2.shape[0]), dtype=int)
    for i in range(X1.shape[0]):
        gram_matrix[i, :] = np.sum(X1[i, :] == X2, axis=1, dtype=int)
    return gram_matrix


def build_nominal_eucl_dist():
    def nominal_eucl_dist(X1, X2):
        gram_matrix = np.zeros((X1.shape[0], X2.shape[0]))
        for i in range(X1.shape[0]):
            gram_matrix[i, :] = 2 * np.sum(X1[i, :] != X2, axis=1)
        return gram_matrix

    return nominal_eucl_dist


def build_numerical_eucl_dist():
    def numerical_eucl_dist(X1, X2):
        K = euclidean_distances(X1, X2.T, squared=True)
        return K

    return numerical_eucl_dist


def build_hetero_kernel(categoricals, degree=None, coef0=None, gamma=None):
    def hetero_kernel(X1, X2):
        gram = np.zeros((X1.shape[0], X2.shape[0]))

        nominal_gram = nominal_gram_dot
        numerical_gram = np.dot

        if gamma is not None:
            numerical_gram = build_numerical_eucl_dist()
            nominal_gram = build_nominal_eucl_dist()

        if categoricals is None:
            X1_num = X1
            X2_num = X2
        else:
            X1_num = X1[:, [not i for i in categoricals]]
            X1_cat = X1[:, categoricals]
            X2_num = X2[:, [not i for i in categoricals]]
            X2_cat = X2[:, categoricals]
            gram += nominal_gram(X1_cat, X2_cat)

        gram += numerical_gram(X1_num, X2_num.T)

        if (degree is not None) and (coef0 is not None):
            gram = np.power(coef0 + gram, degree)

        if gamma is not None and degree is None and coef0 is None:
            gram = np.exp(-gamma * gram)
        return gram

    return hetero_kernel
```

I am not sure, how you want the kernel function to be "callable" in the constructor of e.g. [SVC](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.svm.SVC.html), how it takes the parameters from the ```__init__``` function?
If it can be redefined to take the parameters from the SVC constructor, using this kernel would be much more comfortable.

![runtime-big-1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30484650/58864662-6f899180-86b5-11e9-9cb9-d8298699e112.png)

What is surprising in this graph, that when I used ```kernel='linear'``` or ```'poly'``` or ```'rbf'``` while using SVC, fitted with larger datasets with possibly higher cardinality categorical features, numpy was doing much better than the libsvm implementation (which I suppose is taking care of the gram matrix in your implementation). OHE means one-hot-encoding. I fitted each dataset to the SVC 10 times and measured the time.

Anyways, is there a better way to implement the kernel, not using the closure? I am not sure, what you mean by "callable" and how is the given kernel function taking the right parameters from the constructor, when, i.e., doing a grid-search.

creator: mitar
title: Unclear behavior of max_train_size argument in TimeSeriesSplit
text:
#### Description

So I am trying to understand the behavior of [`TimeSeriesSplit`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit.html#sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit). Especially the `max_train_size` parameter. I was initially surprised that it is an absolute number and not a ratio like it is in other splitting operations.

I traced this parameter to issue #8249 and PR #8282 and I realized that it was added to support window-based splitting, as it is described [here](https://topepo.github.io/caret/data-splitting.html#data-splitting-for-time-series). This was very surprising for me because this is not really clear from documentation that this is happening. Moreover, I found parameters `initialWindow`, `horizon`, and `fixedWindow` much easier to understand, especially with that image.

I would suggest that:
* Documentation is improved here. Such visualization as shown in https://topepo.github.io/caret/data-splitting.html#data-splitting-for-time-series would really help a lot.
* We consider using or sample based parameters, like `initialWindow`, `horizon`, and `fixedWindow`, or ratio/fold based ones, but not both, because it is very confusing.

If we have splitting done by number of folds (which I prefer because it makes things adapt to different dataset sizes automatically), then also window size should be expressed in folds. In a way, parameters could then be:
* How many folds to do.
* Number of folds used in horizon, i.e., used in test data. It looks like this is currently fixed to 1 in this splitting operation and cannot really be configured. I suggest we allow this to be configured.
* Number of folds used in the window, i.e., training data. Default could be None, which would mean a non-fixed window and would mean to use all folds before the test data. Or you could fix it to get a sliding window.

#### Versions

Relates to how it is in sklearn v0.20.3.

creator: jeremiedbb
title: Common test for memmap when fitting estimators should use appriopriate dtype
text:
The common tests `check_classifier_train` and `check_regressor_train` with `readonly_memmap=True` use float64 data. However, all tree based estimators requires float32 data, leading to a copy and resulting in not actually testing on read-only memmap.

We could either run the tests with both dtypes, but it would make the test twice as long, or add a new estimator tag holding with dtype is copying.

creator: azrdev
title: Do not require lexicographic order of classes_ and assume max()=positive class
text:
I'm implementing a classifier[1] which does *concept learning*, i.e. unsymmetrical binary classification with a (sometimes user-defined) *target/positive class* and the learned model describing that class, while everything not matching the model is classified as the other "negative" class.

I'm stumbling across the documented[2] assumption that `classes_` be sorted lexicographically and the positive class has to be the last entry, which is clearly at odds with my background.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/4450#issuecomment-86298663 gave me the idea to wrap the classifier and translate class values, which works, but I consider it a workaround: Therefore the request to drop that assumption.


maybe related: #8100
sklearn v0.20.3

---

[1] <https://github.com/azrdev/sklearn-seco/>
[2] Here it went into the glossary: <https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/9517/files#r152116415>

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Is the problem that you want to define decision_function such that the
greater value corresponds to the positive class? Otherwise I can't see any
real problem maintaining the convention but asking the user to specify
which class is to be considered positive (perhaps with a pos_label
parameter as we do in metrics).

>

events.author: azrdev
events.comment:
I have such a parameter, but if the user specifies [the equivalent of] `pos_label=min(classes_)`, then my decision_function returns `>0` for it, which breaks the assumption that `predict(X) == classes_[decision_function(X) > 0]` (e.g. the test <https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/utils/estimator_checks.py#L1733..L1735>)

Edit:

For multiclass the problem is that the assumption forces me to break ties using argmax, i.e. the lexicographic order of classes; I'd rather order classes by their size in the training set, i.e. err towards those with a larger probability of occurrence.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Yes, you're right we would need to establish a new convention here. Options
include: force the user to make the positive class the greatest; output a
2d decision_function; or output the decision_function corresponding to
pos_label

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
> For multiclass the problem is that the assumption forces me to break ties using argmax,

can you explain that? Is that enforced in a test? Then that test is not good. I think you should do tie-breaking any way you want.


I'm not sure I understand how your model doesn't fit into our current framework.
It sounds like it's a standard binary classification task?

events.author: amueller
events.comment: Can you maybe give some examples of what ``y_train`` and ``y_pred`` and ``decision_function`` would look like in your ideal setting?

events.author: azrdev
events.comment:
> > For multiclass the problem is that the assumption forces me to break ties using argmax,
> 
> can you explain that? Is that enforced in a test?

Yes, in [check_classifiers_predictions](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/utils/estimator_checks.py#L1741).

---

> I'm not sure I understand how your model doesn't fit into our current framework.
> It sounds like it's a standard binary classification task?

Except that it treats the two classes differently. I'm learning rules (a variant of the algorithm is RIPPER/JRip which you might know from weka), e.g.
~~~
rule1: (feature1 <= 3) => positive class
rule2: (feature1 >= 10) and (feature2 == category1) => positive class
...
default rule: (always true) => negative class
~~~

which are (in the binary, "concept learning" case) evaluated sequentially, i.e. only if none of the normal rules (which always predict the positive class) fires/matches, then the negative class is predicted.

Example:

~~~python
est = SeCo(pos_label='pos')
est.fit(X=[[0], [1]], y=['pos', 'neg'])
assert est.classes_ == ['pos', 'neg']  # not sorted because of pos_label
# assert est.theory_ == [  # for illustration
#    ([feature0=[0]], class='pos'),
#    ([], class='neg') ]
assert est.predict([0, 1]) == ['pos', 'neg']
decision = est.decision_function([0, 1])
assert decision == [9000, 0]
assert est.classes_[decision > 0] == ['neg', 'pos']  # != predict(), fails check_classifiers_predictions
~~~
The last line fails because of the assumption `pos_label == est.classes_[-1]`, which is not true (line 3).
My proposed fix still is to drop the requirements to have `classes_` sorted lexicographically and the positive class as `classes_[-1]`. Probably this means `decision_function` always needs to return a 2d array with one column per class.

Above example would then have to use the same code as in multiclass cases, i.e.
~~~python
assert est.classes_[np.argmax(decision, axis=1)] == ['neg', 'pos'] == est.predict(...)
# argmax is not forcing a certain tie breaking here, because I can reorder classes_
~~~

I'm however not sure about the implications, i.e. where/how does the rest of sklearn build upon these assumptions, and what is gained by the special binary case of `decision_function`?


---

As for the **multiclass** case, imagine:
~~~python
...
>>> est.classes_
array(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'])
>>> decision = est.decision_function(X); decision
array([
[0,0,0,0],
[1,2,3,4]])
>>> np.argmax(decision, axis=1)
array([0, 3])
>>> est.classes_[np.argmax(decision, axis=1)]
array(['a', 'd'])
~~~
If I want to break that tie using e.g. sizes of classes in the training data, i cannot do so here.
My approach now is to wrap my classifier in a reordering `LabelEncoder`, as proposed in #4450.

creator: jamesmyatt
title: Shuffled GroupKFold
text:
I agree that it's right for GroupKFold to try to balance the folds, since it's mandatory for certain scenarios. However, since this is done deterministically, it makes repeated GroupKFold impossible, since even if you shuffle the groups, the folds you get might be the same, for example, sizes of 5, 4, 3 in 2 folds will always be assigned (5, ) and (4, 3).

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/model_selection/_split.py#L506

My idea would be, rather than selecting the largest each time and assigning it to the lightest fold, select a random group, weighted by size, so large groups are more likely to be assigned first and less likely to be in the same fold as each other.

It might also be interesting to have an unbalanced option for GroupKFold for cases when you know that your groups are of similar sizes.

What do you think?

There was a previous feature request for this: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/13148. It's also kind of similar/related to https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/9297.

events.author: jamesmyatt
events.comment: I'm hoping to get some time to try this in a few weeks.

events.author: onacrame
events.comment:
Hi any update on this one.  I’ve achieved this in a hacky way by assigning a random number to each group and using that random number as the actual “group” to split on.

There are real world uses where this comes into play.  I work in finance where a lot of the data is panel data such as a customer’s loan payment history.  In my case smaller customer IDs in how long the customer has been on the company’s books or it could mean the loan was acquired from another lender.  Deterministic splitting doesn’t work here using the customer ID because you’re effectively splitting by time or some other implicit credit profile (in the case of acquired loans). 

Randomising the allocation of groups would solve this issue.

As mentioned above, assigning a random label to each group will not have
any effect if the groups have different sizes. There has been little work
here. Perhaps it just needs a confident champion.

events.author: laqua-stack
events.comment:
Hi, 
I came across this issue and would like to share a skeleton of my solution.

Actually, this is a minor change of the GroupKFold implementation. Instead of distributing the current relative largest group to the lightest fold, a random group is drawn from the current remaining groups weighted by their frequency and mapped to the relative lightest fold. It would be straightforward to wrap a repeated version around ShuffleGroupKFold by providing different `random_seed` s. 
Folds should be nearly equally sized, unless there are some very silly group distributions.


```
class ShuffleGroupKFold(GroupKFold):
    def __init__(self, n_splits='warn', random_state=None):
        if n_splits == 'warn':
            warnings.warn(NSPLIT_WARNING, FutureWarning)
            n_splits = 3
        super(GroupKFold, self).__init__(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)

    def _iter_test_indices(self, X, y, groups):
        if groups is None:
            raise ValueError("The 'groups' parameter should not be None.")
        groups = check_array(groups, ensure_2d=False, dtype=None)

        unique_groups, groups = np.unique(groups, return_inverse=True)
        n_groups = len(unique_groups)

        # Get RandomState
        rng = check_random_state(self.random_state)

        if self.n_splits > n_groups:
            raise ValueError("Cannot have number of splits n_splits=%d greater"
                             " than the number of groups: %d."
                             % (self.n_splits, n_groups))


        # Weight groups by their number of occurrences
        n_samples_per_group = np.bincount(groups)

        # Distribute the most frequent groups first
        indices = np.argsort(n_samples_per_group)[::-1]
        n_samples_per_group = n_samples_per_group[indices]

        # Init already distributed groups
        groups_to_distribute = np.ones(groups.shape, dtype=bool)

        # Total weight of each fold
        n_samples_per_fold = np.zeros(self.n_splits)

        # Mapping from group index to fold index
        group_to_fold = np.zeros(len(unique_groups))

        # Distribute samples by randomly drawing out of the remaining groups for the lightest fold
        while groups_to_distribute.any():
            # take an index from the not distributed indices (intrinsically weighted by relative frequency)
            index = rng.randint(0, np.count_nonzero(groups[groups_to_distribute]), size=None)
            group_to_distribute = groups[groups_to_distribute][index]

            # get lightest fold to fill next
            lightest_fold = np.argmin(n_samples_per_fold)

            # fill lightest fold
            n_samples_per_fold[lightest_fold] += n_samples_per_group[group_to_distribute]
            group_to_fold[group_to_distribute] = lightest_fold
            groups_to_distribute = np.where(groups == group_to_distribute, False, groups_to_distribute)

        indices = group_to_fold[groups]

        for f in range(self.n_splits):
            yield np.where(indices == f)[0]
```


Unfortunatly, I am currently too busy for writing a proper pull request. Sorry in advance.
Maybe someone can look at the code and implement the tests he or she finds suitable.

creator: nogilnick
title: BaggingClassifier uses Class Label as Index to Array when Voting
text:
<!--
If your issue is a usage question, submit it here instead:

- Mailing List: https://mail.python.org/mailman/listinfo/scikit-learn
For more information, see User Questions: http://scikit-learn.org/stable/support.html#user-questions

<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description
<!-- Example: Joblib Error thrown when calling fit on LatentDirichletAllocation with evaluate_every > 0-->
BaggingClassifier uses Class Label as Index to Array when Voting

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Provide a base estimator to _BaggingClassifier_ that does not define the function _predict_proba_. This results in _BaggingClassifier_ resorting to voting. It appears the code for performing voting uses class labels as array indices instead of looking up the index of the class label in the _classes__ member.

Example:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier

class Foo:
    
    def __init__(self):
        pass
    
    def fit(self, X, Y, W=None):
        return self
    
    def predict(self, X):
        return np.full(X.shape[0], True, np.bool)
    
    def score(self, X, Y):
        YH = self.predict(X)
        return (Y == YH).mean()
    
    def get_params(self, deep=True):
        return {}
    
    def set_params(self, **params):
        for k, v in params:
            setattr(self, k, v)
        return self
    
# %%
A = np.random.rand(10, 4)
Y = np.random.randint(2, size=10, dtype=np.bool)
bc = BaggingClassifier(Foo())
bc.fit(A, Y)
YH = bc.predict(A)
print('BaggingClassifier Voting Result: ')
print(YH)
print('Ensemble Member Predictions: ')
for Ei in bc.estimators_:
    print(Ei.predict(A))
```

#### Expected Results
<!-- Example: No error is thrown. Please paste or describe the expected results.-->
In the above code snippet, _BaggingClassifier_ should return an array of _True_ since it is the majority prediction of all ensemble members.

#### Actual Results
<!-- Please paste or specifically describe the actual output or traceback. -->
_BaggingClassifier_ returns an array of False. This issue only occurs when the base estimator does not define the function _predict_proba_.

The issue appears to be due to lines 137 and 140 in ensemble/bagging.py.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/e14ac6d36d9dd069cc7fc2e51e4973514a003591/sklearn/ensemble/bagging.py#L137

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/e14ac6d36d9dd069cc7fc2e51e4973514a003591/sklearn/ensemble/bagging.py#L140

The predictions of the ensemble members are directly used as indices into the original array. I'm guessing the prediction labels need to be converted into class labels using _estimator.classes__.

#### Versions

executable: C:\Users\XXXXXX\Anaconda3\pythonw.exe

creator: qinhanmin2014
title: The default value of some parameters make little sense
text:
See #13541 
Seems that we've decided that all parameters should have a default. (Can someone tell me why? I don't like it.) For some parameters, the default value makes little sense (e.g., n_clusters in KMeans, eps in DBSCAN), I think we should have a way to recommend users to set these parameters manually.
My proposal is to define a DefaultMeaninglessWarning and raise it when these parameters are not set manually.

events.author: jeremiedbb
events.comment:
I don't know if it was the original reason, but common tests run with defaults parameters of estimators.
It will cause a whole bunch of new warnings in tests.

> My proposal is to define a DefaultMeaninglessWarning and raise it when these parameters are not set manually.

So you would replace the default values by 'auto' which falls back to the current default with a warning ?

events.author: qinhanmin2014
events.comment:
> but common tests run with defaults parameters of estimators. It will cause a whole bunch of new warnings in tests.

If we decide to do so, we can easily solve the problems in the common tests.

> So you would replace the default values by 'auto' which falls back to the current default with a warning ?

I'd rather use a specific string (e.g., "default-meaningless"). "auto" might be a valid option for many parameters.

events.comment:

but in that case, would it fall back to the current default value ?

Yes, we need to maintain backward compatibility.

events.author: NicolasHug
qinhanmin2014

I've not read through the code of estimator tag. Seems that it's a better way (if it's possible).

> then do something about it (e.g. warn) in base classes.

Ideally we'd be able to also point user to where they could find information on how to set those parameters. Something like "There's no good default value for this parameter, please consult the literature such as blah blah as an example", maybe?

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment: Also, going down this path we'd probably introduce a lot of warnings. We can give and easy way to the users to disable all such warnings so that we don't have to care about the surge of sudden new warnings introduced maybe.

events.author: qinhanmin2014
events.comment:
> Ideally we'd be able to also point user to where they could find information on how to set those parameters. Something like "There's no good default value for this parameter, please consult the literature such as blah blah as an example", maybe?

It's definitely useful, but I think it's acceptable to only raise a warning.

> Also, going down this path we'd probably introduce a lot of warnings. We can give and easy way to the users to disable all such warnings so that we don't have to care about the surge of sudden new warnings introduced maybe.

We'll define a new warning based on UserWarning so CIs won't complain. For users, I think it's acceptable to let them see the warning. They can easily get rid of the warning through setting these parameters manually.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
> the default value makes little sense (e.g., n_clusters in KMeans

At least for KMeans, initially running it with around 10 clusters, and then adjusting that number if needed, depending on the output seems a fairly common approach. I'm not sure that asking the users `n_clusters` before running KMeans would help usability.

Should we go with this option ? If so let's start a list of such parameters and maybe ask for new contributors to do it.
