creator: amueller
title: Machine readable definition of parameters
text:
Related to #5004.
For automl purposes and automatically using scikit-learn more programmatically, it would be helpful for some to specify allowed parameters in a machine-readable format. Right now they are only available via the documentation, which doesn't allow us to actually test them and might be hard to parse.

Considerations are how to specify hyper-parameters. We could use the Python type system, but I think we would need to define custom types for strings with a fixed number of options.

It might also make sense to have possible ranges for integer and float parameters.

Finally, it might be interesting to annotate whether a parameter influences algorithm results, algorithm speed and/or memory consumption.

Not all options influence the result and I've seen people grid-search optimization options while evaluating only on accuracy. There might be fuzzy cases, though, like different solvers might yield slightly different results but it's mostly a time/memory issue.

Another question is whether it's in scope of doing this inside scikit-learn at all, or whether it should live outside - but it will be hard to keep in sync.

Being able to test for different options (not in standard CI but maybe in cron?) might be a good motivation. However, only some combinations of parameters are valid and actually specifying valid combinations (which would be required for testing) is more tricky than just specifying valid values.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
This broad goal of enabling Auto ML is not something we have on our roadmap
iirc, and probably should be. Another aspect of parameter use that might
deserve machine readable annotation is which parameters can be varied for
warm_start (and in what order).

events.author: mitar
events.comment:
In the [d3m](https://gitlab.com/datadrivendiscovery/d3m) project we have a [language to describe parameters using Python classes](https://gitlab.com/datadrivendiscovery/d3m/blob/devel/d3m/metadata/hyperparams.py). We have decided not to use Python typing because of its strange focus on using `Type[Arg]` syntax which means that everything is a class and not an instance so then you have to program with metaclasses and so on. It just becomes another tricky thing to manage. So we just use regular Python instances.

We already parsed docstrings for many sklearn functions and also hand-curated them to fix some things. 

We do differentiate between "params" (state of an estimator which is being changed during fitting) and "hyper-parameters" (parameters which control what the estimator is doing). For first we just record their type (using Python typing), for the latter we define the whole search space, in which context they could probably be used (tuning, resource use, controlling the logic itself). I think sklearn already has something like that with its differentiation between params with `_` suffix and without. One tricky thing is that it is tricky to know the whole "params" (state) in sklearn because some attributes are set outside of constructor. One thing sklearn could improve also is make sure all instance attributes are set in the constructor and not outside.

See example of our description of "params" and "hyper-parameters" for random forest [here](https://gitlab.com/datadrivendiscovery/sklearn-wrap/blob/dev-dist/sklearn_wrap/SKRandomForestClassifier.py#L28).

I think it would be great to have such machine-readable format as source which would then generate docstrings. (You could use a Python metaclass to do that automatically.)

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Our convention is to set those "parameters" attributes during the fit
method. I don't see how it would be an improvement to change that rather
than, say, add the type annotations for them like those you have
constructed, and enforce them in tests.

events.author: mitar
events.comment: So how would one automatically inspect an estimator? It seems that currently the idea is that you create an instance of the estimator, provide hyper-parameters, and then read what are params/state ... how? So if flags are dynamic and depend on hyper-parameters, params are as well. But I am not sure if I want to fit the estimator just to figure out what state it might have and populate the AutoML database.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: What do you use the parameter annotations for?

events.author: mitar
events.comment: The idea is that you can have more insight into what the state is and be able to inspect how, what, and how much changes during fitting. It is an ongoing research area. But I agree that those "params" in our view (state) is not as important as "hyper-parameters" in machine readable format.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Right. So it might allow your auto ml engine to learn which "hyper"
parameters actually affect the fit. Interesting, although prediction should
often tell you that too.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
Here is an API proposal for defining machine readable parameters: 

```py
class LogisticRegression(..., BaseEstimator):
    valid_params = {
        "penalty": Enum("l2", "l1", "elasticnet", "none"),
        "dual": TypeOf(bool),
        "tol": Interval(float, 0, None, lower_inclusive=False),
        "C": Interval(float, 0),
        "fit_intercept": TypeOf(bool),
        "class_weight": Union(TypeOf(dict), Enum('balanced', None)),
        "random_state": TypeOf(int, RandomState, type(None)),
        "solver": Enum("newton-cg", "lbfgs", "liblinear", "sag", "saga"),
        "max_iter": Interval(int, 0),
        "multi_class": Enum("ovr", "multinomial", "auto"),
        "verbose": Interval(int, 0, tags=["control"]),
        "warm_start": TypeOf(bool, tags=["control"]),
        "n_jobs": Union(Interval(int, 1, None), Enum(-1, None), tags=["resource"]),
        "l1_ratio": Union(Interval(float, 0, 1), Enum(None))
    }

    def fit(self, X, ...):
        self._valid_params()

class BaseEstimator:
    def _validate_params(self):
        ...
```

This introduces a four parameter types:

1. `Enum` - Collection of options
2. `TypeOf` - Specifying types
3. `Interval` - Numerical interval
4. `Union` - Union of above parameter types

There is also a `tags` parameter that adds metadata for each hyperparameter.

There will be estimator tests to make sure `valid_parameters` and the parameters in `__init__` match up.

events.comment: TLDR: We believe that JSON Schema is a good choice for a machine readable representation for hyper-parameter specifications.  We have explored this in our open source project Lale [[1]](#myfootnote1). JSON Schema is a widely used specification language for JSON [[2]](#myfootnote2). As part of the open source Lale (https://github.com/ibm/lale) project we use JSON Schema for our specifications, and it seems to work well. In particular, we have wrappers for many scikit-learn classes that provide schemas for hyper-parameters (and input/output), and would be excited to integrate them more directly with scikit-learn.   In Lale, we gain a number of benefits from using these schemas: - Automation: given a pipeline of operators that come with schemas we automatically generate search spaces for a number of AutoML tools, including GridSearchCV, Hyperopt, and SMAC. - Documentation: We auto-generate documentation about the hyper-parameters based on the schemas.  See for example: https://lale.readthedocs.io/en/latest/modules/lale.lib.sklearn.logistic_regression.html A goal could be to enhance the text descriptions sufficiently so that original scikit-learn documentation for the operators is auto-generated and thus always in sync with the machine description. - Error checking: We check that the hyperparameters passed to an operator conform to the schema (this is just JSON Schema validation). In addition to simple schema constraints (such as enumerations and ranges), we also use JSON Schema's rich logical connectives to support side-conditions.  For example, our schema for logistic regression encodes that 'The newton-cg, sag, and lbfgs solvers support only l2 penalties.' as a constraint [[3]](#myfootnote3), which is validated automatically. Additionally, our search generator takes these constraints into account when generating a search space for AutoML tool. We support additional fields in a JSON Schema allowing the schema writer to specify a distribution for numeric ranges, as well as some other enhancements oriented towards AutoML tools.  For example, some fields can be marked as not relevant for optimization [[4]](#myfootnote4).  Other fields can have one variant marked as relevant for the optimizer, while still allowing others.  For example, specifying the class_weight as a dictionary is valid, but not necessarily the best choice for an AutoML tool [[5]](#myfootnote5). creator: thomasbridi
title: Smarter BaseSearchCV memory management
text:
In a search made to optimize a `Pipeline` the pipeline is copied with a **deep** copy. The deep copy has the problem that can copy multiple times things that should be shared between two objects. This problem happens during a scikit-learn search if you want to share information contained in one transformer to another. E.g.
```
class StandardizeTransformer():
    def fit(self, X):
        self.divisor = X.max()
    def transform(self,X):
        return X / self.divisor
    def anti_transform(self,X):
        return X * self.divisor

class AntiTransformer():
    def __init__(self, transformer):
        self.transfromer = transformer
    def transform(self,X):
        return self.transformer.anti_transform(X)
st = StandardizeTransformer()
pipe = Pipeline[('standardize', st), ... , ('destandardize', AntiTransformer(st))]
gs = GridSearchCv(pipe,...)
```

In this case, during the `GridSearchCv`, `st` is copied two times in two different address. This result in an unfitted `st` into the `AntiTransformer`

Solving this problem would add much more possibilities to scikit-learn e.g.
- destandardized metrics
-  possibility of pre-train and fine-tune approaches in a grid search
and much more

I suppose that this can be solved by implementing in the right way the `__deepcopy__()` in the BaseSearchCV as mentioned in the python's copy documentation:

> The difference between shallow and deep copying is only relevant for compound objects (objects that contain other objects, like lists or class instances):
 A shallow copy constructs a new compound object and then (to the extent possible) inserts references into it to the objects found in the original.
 A deep copy constructs a new compound object and then, recursively, inserts copies into it of the objects found in the original.
Two problems often exist with deep copy operations that don’t exist with shallow copy operations:
 Recursive objects (compound objects that, directly or indirectly, contain a reference to themselves) may cause a recursive loop.
 Because deep copy copies everything it may copy too much, such as data which is intended to be shared between copies.

events.author: thomasbridi
events.comment:
I can add an example to make the thread more clear:

Suppose to have to make a Sklearn Pipeline with a parameter optimization made by the GridSearchCV. The pipeline has to get the best model for several different entities implementing a pre-train and then fine-tune approach: pre-train all the entities together and the fine-tune (starting from the weights of the pre-trained network) every single element and returns a model for each entity. These are the constraint of the pipeline:

- Pre-train and fine-tuning have to be in the same pipeline because both the model has to `fit` the same data in each GridSearchCV's fold.
- The pre-train model has to pass its weights to the fine-tuning model.

In the following code you can see:

A Sklearn Transformer (with a regressor in it) that takes a data-frame with all the entities in input and fit itself.
A Sklearn Regressor that splits the whole data-frame in one data-frame for each entity and fit a Keras model for each entity.
If you try to pass the model weights from the regressor contained into the transformer to the regressors contained in the LoopTransformer this is not possible due to the problem in the deep copy.
Here is the code:

```
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import random
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from keras.models import Model
from keras.layers import Dense, Input
import copy

class MyRegressor(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    def __init__(self, neurons, featInput, featOutput):
        self.neurons = neurons
        self.preTrain = None
        self.featInput = featInput
        self.featOutput = featOutput

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X_train = X[self.featInput]
        y_train = X[self.featOutput]

        inputLayer = Input(shape=(len(self.featInput), ), name='INPUT')
        hidden = Dense(self.neurons, name='HIDDEN')(inputLayer)
        outputLayer = Dense(len(self.featOutput), name='OUTPUT')(hidden)

        self.model = Model(inputLayer, outputLayer)
        self.model.compile(loss='mse', optimizer='rmsprop')

        if self.preTrain is not None:
            self.model.loadWeights(self.preTrain)

        self.model.fit(X_train, y_train)

        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.model.predict(X[self.featInput])

    def transform(self, X):
        return X

    def score(self, X, y=None, sample_weight=None):
        y_true = X[self.featOutput]
        y_pred = self.predict(X)
        return mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)


class LoopTransformer(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    def __init__(self, columns, component):
        self.columns = columns
        self.component = component
        self.components = []

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        for index, idx in X[self.columns].drop_duplicates().iterrows():
            entityDf = X[(X[self.columns] == idx).sum(axis=1) == len(self.columns)].copy()
            self.components.append({'id': idx, 'component': copy.deepcopy(self.component)})
            self.components[-1]['component'].fit(entityDf, y)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        results = []
        for comp in self.components:
            entityDf = X[(X[self.columns] == comp['id']).sum(axis=1) == len(self.columns)].copy()
            res = comp['component'].predict(entityDf)
            results.append(res)
        dfRes = pd.concat(results)
        return dfRes

    def score(self, X, y=None, sample_weight=None):
        results = []
        for comp in self.components:
            entityDf = X[(X[self.columns] == comp['id']).sum(axis=1) == len(self.columns)].copy()
            if len(entityDf) > 0:
                results.append(comp['component'].score(entityDf))
        return np.average(results)


#create the input dataframe: 3 entities
dataFrame = pd.DataFrame([], columns=['entityId', 'input', 'output'])
for entity in range(3):
    x = np.arange(random.randint(10, 20))
    y = x * (entity + 1)
    tempDf = pd.DataFrame(np.array([x, y]).T, columns=['input', 'output'])
    tempDf['entityId'] = entity
    dataFrame = pd.concat([dataFrame, tempDf], sort=False)
dataFrame = dataFrame.reset_index(drop=True)

#create the pipeline
neurons = [5, 10]
preTrainTransformer = MyRegressor(neurons=neurons[0], featInput=['input'], featOutput=['output'])
myPipe = Pipeline([('preTrain',
                    preTrainTransformer),
                   ('fineTuning',
                    LoopTransformer(['entityId'],
                                    MyRegressor(
                                        neurons=neurons[0],
                                        featInput=['input'],
                                        preTrain=preTrainTransformer.model.get_weights(),
                                        featOutput=['output'])))])

#pre-train and fine-tuning has to have always the same number of neurons
params = [{
    'preTrain__neurons': [neurons[0]],
    'fineTuning__component__neurons': [neurons[0]]
}, {
    'preTrain__neurons': [neurons[1]],
    'fineTuning__component__neurons': [neurons[1]]
}]

gs = GridSearchCV(myPipe, params, verbose=1, cv=3)

gs.fit(dataFrame, dataFrame)
score = gs.score(dataFrame, dataFrame)
print(score)
```

creator: rth
title: TST check_transformers_unfitted not run on some transformers
text:
Currently, there seem to be no common tests that ensure that calling `transform` of estimators without a fit raises a `NotFitedError`. 

One instance of this issue is https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/12959

There is a common test for `predict` and some other methods in [`sklearn/utils/estimator_checks.py:check_estimators_unfitted`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/2955129128341ba3f2187c5a6619084f312bca88/sklearn/utils/estimator_checks.py#L1586). It might be worthwhile to extend that also to the transform method (if it is present).  

Though we probably want to enforce this only to a subset of estimators (maybe estimator tags) would have been useful here.

events.author: rth
events.comment:
Actually, there is also a `check_transformers_unfitted` check but it should have failed on `RandomTreesEmbedding` due to #12959 and it didn't.

This issue aims to investigate why (and whether this could apply to other estimators)

events.author: finnoshea
events.comment:
When transform is called for PCA, it inherits the method from _BasePCA, which calls check_is_fitted to ensure a fit has been performed (line 125 of decomposition/base.py):

>raise NotFittedError(msg % {'name': type(estimator).__name__})
sklearn.exceptions.NotFittedError: This PCA instance is not fitted yet. Call 'fit' with appropriate arguments before using this method.

When transform is called for TruncatedSVD, the failure is similar to that in #12959 in that it simply says it doesn't have an attribute that is called by the transform:

>AttributeError: 'TruncatedSVD' object has no attribute 'components_'

(lines 209 and 210 of decomposition/TruncatedSVD.py) Do not show a check_is_fitted call, so based on the three examples so far, the inelegant failure isn't surprising.  The method inverse_transform has the same problem.

Both classes inherit from TransformerMixin and BaseEstimator, neither of which define a transform method (so does ExtraTreesEmbedding through BaseForest and then BaseEnsemble).  In any case, none of these cases use check_transformers_unfitted.  Here is a list of other elegant and inelegant failures of the transform and inverse_transform methods I have found (if the latter exists):

**check_is_fitted**:
FactorAnalysis
FastICA
KernelPCA (transform only, inverse_transform is custom)
NMF
SparsePCA (no inverse_transform)
MiniBatchSparsePCA (inherits from SparsePCA)

**No check**:
RandomTreesEmbedding (see #12959)
TruncatedSVD

**Custom check**:
LatentDirichletAllocation
KernelPCA (inverse_transform only)

All of those but ExtraTreesEmbedding are in decomposition.  There does not appear to be a consistent use of checking for a fit and the most popular check is `check_is_fitted`.  Assuming the methods you reference function (I haven't checked), I think the simplest fix is to consistently apply one to all calls of TransformerClass.transform or .inverse_transform.  Maybe update the style guide as well?

events.author: finnoshea
events.comment:
Using the all_estimators tool I've found 19 transformers and estimators that do not call check_is_fitted within transform, inverse_transform or predict.  Most of those have a custom message of some kind and a few have nothing at all and fail inelegantly.

The root problem appears to be that the pytest files for almost all estimators do not contain a test to make sure that NotFittedError is raised.  This was fixed in #12279 for NearestNeighbors calling the `kneighbors_graph` and `radius_neighbors_graph` methods by adding a straightforward test.

Fixing the 19 above functions is an easy task, but going through all 156 estimators looking for functions that should call check_is_fitted and adding an appropriate set of tests is going to take a fair bit of time.  grep of the test files shows that only 10-15 test files even import NotFittedError (I don't know if they use it).  So there is potentially 140 test files to modify.

Is copying the structure (not the code) in the NearestNeighbors graph solution the way to go?  From `/cluster/tests/test_neighbors.py`:

>def test_not_fitted_error_gets_raised():
    X = [[1]]
    neighbors_ = neighbors.NearestNeighbors()
    assert_raises(NotFittedError, neighbors_.kneighbors_graph, X)
    assert_raises(NotFittedError, neighbors_.radius_neighbors_graph, X)

events.comment:

I think estimators tags (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/8022) should make this task easier. That PR will hopefully be merged very soon, so maybe we could wait for that before addressing this issue.

creator: ErikDeSmedt
title: RadiusNeighborsRegression is inconsistent when extrapolation occurs
text:
#### Description
The behavior of `RadiusNeighborsRegression` is inconsistent when extrapolation occurs. The behavior depends on the chosen weight-function. 

-`weight="uniform"` will return `[NaN]`.
-`weight="distance"`will raise an error
-`weight=lambda d: d`will raise an error


#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
```python
from sklearn.neighbors import RadiusNeighborsRegressor

X = [[1],[2],[3],[4]]
y = [1,2,3,4]

X_predict = [[-100]]

model = RadiusNeighborsRegressor(radius=1.0, weights = "distance")
fitm = model.fit(X,y)

# raises ZeroDivisionError
result = fitm.predict(X_predict)  
```

#### Expected Results
No error is raised and `[[NaN]]` is returned. 

#### Actual Results
```
 File "c:/test.py", line 12, in <module>
    result = fitm.predict(X_predict)
  File "C:\...\anaconda3\lib\site-packages\sklearn\neighbors\regression.py", line 296, in predict
    for (i, ind) in enumerate(neigh_ind)])
  File "C:\...\anaconda3\lib\site-packages\sklearn\neighbors\regression.py", line 296, in <listcomp>
    for (i, ind) in enumerate(neigh_ind)])
  File "C:\...\anaconda3\lib\site-packages\numpy\lib\function_base.py", line 1158, in average
    "Weights sum to zero, can't be normalized")
ZeroDivisionError: Weights sum to zero, can't be normalized
```

#### Versions
```
Windows-8.1-6.3.9600-SP0
Python 3.6.5 |Anaconda, Inc.| (default, Mar 29 2018, 13:32:41) [MSC v.1900 64 bit (AMD64)]
NumPy 1.14.3
SciPy 1.1.0
Scikit-Learn 0.19.1
```

events.author: nixphix
events.comment: can you test it in latest sklearn version? I could run the code without any error in version `0.20.0` and the predicted result is `array([-9223372036854775808])` though I'm not sure if the result is correct.

events.author: adonizetti
events.comment:
Hi, this issue seems to exist even in version `0.21.3`. 
The code doesn't raise any error nor warning, but the output values are clearly wrong (as the one shown in the previous comment). To be precise, the behavior is now consistent for the different choices of `weight` (should I open a new issue?), but it's still different from the expected results mentioned above (which would totally make sense to me). 

This is the code version I'm referring to: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/c1ba7bfe43c2157a3fbb0acc1a49c9f14363f49c/sklearn/neighbors/_regression.py

I think the issue is coming from line 346: empty_obs = `np.full_like(_y[0], np.nan)`.
Whenever there are no neighbors within the specified radius, line 356 will get the `empty_obs`, except that the values returned won't be `np.nan` as one could expect.

```
import numpy as np   # Version 1.17.4

y = [1,2,3,4]

curr_implementation = np.full_like(y, np.nan)
print(curr_implementation)
print(np.isnan(curr_implementation))  # [False False False False]

new_implementation = np.full_like(y, np.nan, dtype=np.double)
print(new_implementation)
print(np.isnan(new_implementation))  # [True True True True]
```


NaN values would be easy to catch and handle, but that's currently not possible and it's not always easy to understand when the output value is "clearly" wrong, which makes it hard to use the predict() method as is. 

Possible proposals: 
 - enforce the specification of dtype value in line 346, so that the output would really be an array of `np.nan` - I'm sorry but I don't know if this can cover all the possible use-cases
 - let users specify a default value to use in line 346 instead of `np.nan` - this wouldn't really solve the issue but it would still be quite an improvement in terms of usage and error handling 

Hope it helps a little! :)

creator: jarednielsen
title: Naive Bayes Classifier with Mixed Bernoulli/Gaussian Models
text:
#### Description
I suggest allowing mixed datasets (half binary variables, half real-valued variables) into the Naive Bayes classifier. Currently the `GaussianNB` and `BernoulliNB` classes handle one case or the other, but not combined. I'd be happy to write the code for this, so I'm curious if this has been explored before and if it would be helpful!

For example, on the Titanic dataset, gender is a bernoulli variable while age is real-valued. Passing both into a Naive Bayes classifier would improve it.

This is related to this currently pending PR: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/12569

creator: dirkpadfield
title: Implementing partial_fit for NearestCentroid
text:
#### Description
The NearestCentroid classifier (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.neighbors.NearestCentroid.html) does not currently have a partial_fit method, but it would be very useful when running the algorithm in an online fashion.  The math for implementing it is simple; it's just a matter of updating the centroids weighted by the number of samples.  The implementation could be similar to the partial_fit method of the GaussianNB classifier (except for the obvious mathematical differences).  I'm happy to submit an implementation of this, but I wanted to gather input first to see if others have already done this and whether others would find this useful. 

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Look at NearestCentroid classifier code and notice that it has not partial_fit method.

There should be a partial_fit method.

There is no partial_fit method.

We can store the "true centroid" and "true variance" as new member variables.  Then we can update both of these with each iteration of partial data similar to how it is done in GaussianNB.  Then, we can compute the shrunken centroids real-time from these values.

title: Using pre-fitted GradientBoostingRegressor init estimator
text:
<!--
If your issue is a usage question, submit it here instead:

<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description
Scikit-learn allows to put a base estimator for some models like gbm by using an init parameter. But base estimator is again fitted inside the parent gbm model irrespective of whether the base estimator is already fitted or not. If i want to fit a base estimator where the target is modified version of the target (for ex logarithm of target for regression) but parent gbm model should train on the actual target then I get erroneous values as it tries to refit the base estimator again. We need a flag in the wrapper to check if we want to refit it again. Otherwise we have to write the entire fit function in the init base estimator class
#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
from sklearn.utils import check_array


class GBR_Init(GradientBoostingRegressor):
    def predict(self,X):
        X = check_array(X, dtype=np.float32, order='C', accept_sparse='csr')
        return np.expm1(self._decision_function(X))
#here i am training base estimator with log of the target

events.author: baluyotraf
events.comment: Looks like it has something to do with the multiprocessing since an n_jobs=1 removes the warning.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: Yes, I'm guessing that somehow joblib is not maintaining the warnings environment across processes correctly. (@tommoral?)

events.author: yihengli
events.comment:
I forgot to mention this in my original description. 

I also tested this script in a Jupyter notebook, and warnings can be suppressed as expected. I was wondering if the warning or joblib mechanism is different from Jupyter and vanilla python

events.author: baluyotraf
events.comment: Jupyter will print it to the terminal you used after you close the notebook.

events.author: tomMoral
events.comment:
Yes the warning environment is reset when starting new workers with `'spawn'` or `'forkexec'` instead of `'fork'`. This is actually the way it is implemented in `python`.  I see no way to suppress the warning currently without changing the internals of worker spawning. If this is critical to your application, I guess you could use the `multiprocessing` backend by using `paralell_backend('multiprocessing')` in your script. Note that the main drawback of this solution is that you would revert to `start_method='fork'` which is known to cause bad interaction with third party library, in particular on OSX.

```python 
import warnings
from sklearn.utils import parallel_backend
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np


x = np.random.normal(0, 1, (100, 100))
y = [0] * 50 + [1] * 50

if __name__ == "__main__":
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
    clf = LogisticRegression()
    clf = RandomizedSearchCV(clf, {"C": [1,2]}, n_jobs=-1)
    with parallel_backend('multiprocessing'):
        clf.fit(x, y)
        clf.predict(x)
    print("done")
```

The warning management could be changed for the `loky` backend directly by sending `warning.filters` to the spawned workers. My two concerns would be that it would differ from the behavior in `multiprocessing` and only the filters set before the spawning of the worker would be taken into account. This means that if they change later, new workers would not have the same warning policy.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
At what point is the worker spawned? I think only transferring filters when
spawning might be a reasonable caveat and an improvement on the current
behaviour

events.author: hermidalc
events.comment:
@yihengli @tomMoral @jnothman

In Python you can easily set warning filters that work for any spawned worker by setting the `PYTHONWARNINGS` env var dynamically in your code. `loky` workers will pick this up:
```python
os.environ["PYTHONWARNINGS"] = "ignore::UserWarning"
```
Though since this applies globally until you unset it in your code then you want to be more specific:
```python
os.environ["PYTHONWARNINGS"] = "ignore:Liblinear failed to converge:UserWarning:sklearn.svm.base"
```
You can specify multiple warning filters this way (https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html#describing-warning-filters)

I did see that there is an issue with Python currently that you cannot easily specify custom (subclass) warning categories this way (see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/42495641/filtering-based-on-custom-warning-categories and https://bugs.python.org/issue22543).  There is a workaround that is described there by specifying `PYTHONPATH`, but that didn't work when I tried it:
```python
import sklearn.exceptions
os.environ["PYTHONPATH"] = os.path.dirname(sklearn.exceptions.__file__)
os.environ["PYTHONWARNINGS"] = "ignore::exceptions.ConvergenceWarning:sklearn.svm.base"
```
Maybe I did something wrong but it follows exactly what was described.  I even tried it from command line and still didn't work.

events.author: e3vela
events.comment:
If you are using logs, a workaround would be using the `logging` module to [capture warnings](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.captureWarnings) and set a filter:

```python
import logging

logging.captureWarnings(capture=True)

# Get logger for warnings
logger = logging.getLogger("py.warnings")

# StreamHandler outputs on sys.stderr by default
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
logger.addHandler(handler)

# Set rule to ignore warnings
logger.addFilter(lambda record: "ConvergenceWarning" not in record.getMessage())
```

Other types of warnings will be printed on the console.

events.author: JoElfner
events.comment: Any news on this? This reduces the usability of `RandomizedSearchCV`, since it hides useful information... Setting `PYTHONWARNINGS` works, but seems like a quite clumsy workaround...

from sklearn.utils import parallel_backend

with parallel_backend("multiprocessing"):

```

creator: chuanren
title: sklearn.cluster.bicluster.BaseSpectral._svd: n_discard eigenvectors from svds
text:
#### Description

The function sklearn.cluster.bicluster.BaseSpectral._svd incorrectly uses the parameters svd_method = 'arpack' and n_discard.

The function _svd should discard the eigenvectors with largest eigenvalues, but the function svds used when svd_method=='arpack' returns the eigenvectors with ascending eigenvalues. This behavior is different with that of the function randomized_svd used when svd_method=='randomized'.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Thanks for the report.

It would be useful to either present a snippet of code that fails your assumptions or link to the error in the code (https://help.github.com/articles/creating-a-permanent-link-to-a-code-snippet/). 

But a pull request fixing the issue, ideally with a test, is also welcome.

events.author: chuanren
events.comment:
Code is presented.

The issue is that: the order of eigenvalues computed in the two conditions (randomized and arpack) are different.

A simple fix would be reorder the eigenvalues after the computation. This will also avoid future errors if more parameter choices are included.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/8d7e849428a4edd16c3e2a7dc8a088f108986a17/sklearn/cluster/bicluster.py#L132-L162

events.author: gykovacs
events.comment:
I can confirm the bug:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn import cluster

A= np.array([[-2, -4, 2], [-2, 1, 2], [4, 2, 5]])

sc= cluster.bicluster.SpectralCoclustering(n_clusters= 2, 
                                           svd_method='randomized')

sc.fit(A)
print(sc.column_labels_)
```
gives
```
[0 0 1]
```
, but
```
sc= cluster.bicluster.SpectralCoclustering(n_clusters= 2, 
                                           svd_method='arpack')
sc.fit(A)
print(sc.column_labels_)
```
gives
```
[0 0 0]
```

Checking the arpack docs it clearly states that the singular values are returned in ascending order.
https://www.caam.rice.edu/software/ARPACK/UG/node136.html#SECTION001210000000000000000

I just submitted a pull request #12898 fixing the issue. https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/12898

         return (safe_sparse_dot(X, self.feature_log_prob_.T) +
                 self.class_log_prior_)

+    def _additive_smoothing(self, alpha):
+        smoothed_fc = self.feature_count_ + alpha
+        smoothed_cc = smoothed_fc.sum(axis=1)
+        return np.log(smoothed_fc) - np.log(smoothed_cc.reshape(-1, 1))
+
+    def _simple_goog_turing(self, fc):
+        N = fc.sum()
+        # Get the frequencies of frequencies
+        n = dict()
+        for r in fc:
+            if r == 0:
+                continue
+            n[r] = n.get(r, 0) + 1
+
+        # The probability of unseen samples
+        P_0 = n.get(1, 0)/N
+
+        # Compute the Z values
+        r = np.array(sorted(n.items(), key=lambda keyval: keyval[0]), dtype='int')[:, 0]
+        n = np.array(sorted(n.items(), key=lambda keyval: keyval[0]), dtype='int')[:, 1]
+        Z = dict()
+        Z[r[0]] = 2*n[0] / r[1]
+        Z[r[-1]] = n[-1] / (r[-1] - r[-2])
+        for (idx, j) in enumerate(r):
+            if idx == 0 or idx >= len(r) - 1:
+                continue
+            i = r[idx-1]
+            k = r[idx+1]
+            Z[j] = 2*n[idx]/(k-i)
+        Z = np.array(sorted(Z.items()))[:, 1]
+
+        # Compute S using linear regression
+        log_r = np.log10(r).reshape(-1, 1)
+        log_Z = np.log10(Z).reshape(-1, 1)
+        reg = LinearRegression().fit(log_r, log_Z)
+        a, b = reg.intercept_, reg.coef_[0]
+        S = np.power(10, a+b*np.log(np.arange(1, np.max(r)+2)))
+
+        # Compute r*
+        cease_x = False
+        r_star = np.zeros(len(r))
+        for i in range(len(r)):
+            y = (r[i]+1)*(S[r[i]]/S[r[i]-1])
+            if i >= len(r) - 1 or r[i+1] != r[i] + 1:
+                cease_x = True
+            if cease_x:
+                r_star[i] = y
+                continue
+            x = (r[i]+1)*(n[i+1]/n[i])
+            threshold = 1.96*np.sqrt(((r[i]+1)**2)*(n[i+1]/n[i]**2)*(1+(n[i+1]/n[i])))
+            if np.abs(x-y) <= threshold:
+                r_star[i] = y
+                cease_x = True
+                continue
+            r_star[i] = x
+
+        # Compute the probability of each frequency
+        N_prime = np.inner(n, r_star)
+        p_r = (1-P_0)*(r_star/N_prime)
+
+        # Calculate probability of each feature
+        total_unseen = np.count_nonzero(fc == 0)
+        unseen_prob = P_0/total_unseen
+        prob = np.zeros(fc.size)
+        for i in range(len(p_r)):
+            idx = np.where(fc == r[i])
+            prob[idx] = p_r[i]
+        prob[np.where(fc == 0)] = unseen_prob
+
+        return np.log(prob)
+
```

This is what I have so far. The notation is the same as in the paper linked in the references. 

Since Good-Turing uses raw counts, the code won't work if the input is transformed using, for example, [TfidfTransformer](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfTransformer.html). Would throwing an error be a reasonable solution when the input is not raw counts?

Below are some other smoothing algorithms from [Enhancing Naive Bayes with Various Smoothing Methods for Short Text Classification](http://www.ntu.edu.sg/home/gaocong/papers/wpp095-yuan.pdf) that might be worth considering.

```python
def jelinek_mercer(fc, alpha):
    mle = fc.sum(axis=0)/fc.sum()
    return np.log((1-alpha)*(fc/fc.sum(axis=1).reshape(-1,1)) + alpha*mle) 

def dirichlet(fc, alpha):
    mle = fc.sum(axis=0)/fc.sum()
    smoothed_fc = fc + alpha*mle
    smoothed_cc = smoothed_fc.sum(axis=1)
    return np.log(smoothed_fc) - np.log(smoothed_cc.reshape(-1, 1))

def absolute_discounting(fc, alpha):
    mle = fc.sum(axis=0)/fc.sum()
    count_unique = np.count_nonzero(fc, axis=1).reshape(-1,1)
    cc = fc.sum(axis=1).reshape(-1,1)
    return (np.log(np.maximum(fc - alpha, 0) + alpha*count_unique*mle) - 
            np.log(cc))

def two_stage(fc, lam, mu):
    mle = fc.sum(axis=0)/fc.sum()
    smoothed_fc = fc + mu*mle
    smoothed_cc = smoothed_fc.sum(axis=1)
    return np.log((1-lam)*(smoothed_fc/smoothed_cc) + lam*mle)
```

title: LogisticRegressionCV failure when not all classes appear in each fold
text:
#### Description

When not all classes appear in each CV fold, LogisticRegressionCV fails when trying to collect the coefficient array.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegressionCV

xtmp, ytmp = make_classification(n_samples=2500, n_informative=10, n_classes=6)

# remove all but 2 instances of class 3, in order to make class 3 not-appear in at least one fold
remove = np.where(ytmp == 3)[0][2:]
keep = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(ytmp), dtype='int'), remove)

lr = LogisticRegressionCV(multi_class='multinomial', cv=KFold(5)).fit(xtmp[keep], ytmp[keep])

Indeed, Kfold is splitting your dataset without taking into account the group information. Then, as you see, you get folds where the 3rd group is not represented.
Instead, StrafitiedKfold (the default one in case of classification in any CV estimator in scikit-learn) makes that every groups are present in the folds. Then, the expected shape of the estimator output is really filled.

Do you expect that Kfold yields the same none error that StrafitiedKfold ?

events.author: gwerbin
events.comment:
@phypho I would expect the coefficient matrices in `multi_coefs_paths` to be re-aligned before combining, like what `CalibratedClassifierCV` does.

IMO this should be a part of scikit-learn anyway: a routine to re-align matrices when models are fit using only a subset of classes. The basic method is straightforward:

1. Get an ordered sequence of "all classes", and an ordered sequences of classes in the data you're using to fit the model
2. Create a dictionary mapping the position of one to the position of the other
3. When a coefficient matrix or prediction matrix is generated, reorder it to match the order in the "all classes" sequence, inserting `0` or `np.nan` (as appropriate) when that class doesn't appear in the training data

This would be very helpful when working with highly-imbalanced classes in multivariate problems. As it stands right now, several other parts of the scikit-learn codebase fail in this scenario as well (e.g. `log_loss`).

I have my own wrapper class that does this label aligning, and it works very well for me so far. I can share it if there is interest.

Hi all, sorry for the long absence.

I dug up my old code for this task and posted the core of it as a Gist here: <https://gist.github.com/gwerbin/3e095a63169042de88c80410ceca8705>. As you can see, it's mostly docstrings and error checking; the logic itself is not complicated. I used a [Bidict](https://pypi.org/project/bidict) to maintain the label correspondence because that's what made sense to me at the time. ​As @jnothman pointed out, you could do it using `LabelEncoder`.

I had also written my own `Model` class, which is akin to `TransformedTargetRegressor` (which either didn't exist or was brand-new at the time) or a hypothetical `TransformedTargetClassifier`. `Model.fit` runs `get_positional_correspondence` on the target and stores the result. `Model.fit_and_score` does pretty much what you'd expect, with the added feature that classification targets are re-aligned using the stored correspondence before trying to compute the scores.

Note that this _still_ didn't solve the original problem, because `LogisticRegressionCV` internally is unaware of all this machinery. Therefore I ended up writing my own cross-validation/resampling framework, which uses `Model.fit_and_score` at each resampling step.

The ultimate solution might be to add some kind of `align_before_scoring=True` option to the various `*CV` estimators and meta-estimators, which would then apply this column realignment before scoring in multi-class and multi-label tasks. Or maybe it should be an option in `make_scorer`.

CC @cvanelteren.

@gitDawn: you have to write your own loop over `ParameterSampler`/`ParameterGrid`, something like this:
```python
def fit_cv(estimator, sampler, cv, score_func, x, y):
    best_score = None
    best_estimator = None

    y_unique = np.unique(y)

    for p, params in enumerate(sampler):
        for ix_train, ix_test in cv.split(x, y):
            x_train = x[ix_train]
            y_train = y[ix_train]

            x_test = x[ix_test]
            y_test = y[ix_test]

            y_test_unique = np.unique(y_test)
            column_mapping = get_positional_correspondence(y_test_unique, y_unique)

            estimator_ = estimator.clone().fit(x_train, y_train)
            proba_test = estimator_.predict_proba(x_test)

            proba_test_aligned = reorder_matrix_columns(proba_test, column_mapping)
            score = score_func(y_test_aligned, proba_test_aligned)

            if best_score is None or score > best_score:
                best_score = score
                best_estimator = estimator_

    return best_score, best_estimator
```

creator: oleksandr-pavlyk
title: Plea to not use datasets with duplicate samples in SVC tests
text:
#### Description
Support vector classification solves a quadratic programming problem, see [sklearn's user guide secion on SVC](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/svm.html#svc). 

The quadratic form Q[i, j] is constructed from kernel function values at pairs (i, j) of input samples. 

Duplicate samples thus cause quadratic form to have zero eigenvalues. In such a case the solution of the quadratic problem is not unique. 

It is important for SVM code to handle such cases, and libSVM resorts to use of regularization parameter `tau` (see [src/libsvm/svm.cpp#L89](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/svm/src/libsvm/svm.cpp#L89)). So any eigenvalues smaller than `tau` are replaced with `tau`, essentially resolving the non-uniqueness in a machine arithmetic fragile way.

A change in implementation may result in a different set of support vectors found.

Inputs with duplicates are pervasive in sklearn's test suite. 
Duplicates arise from use of grouped data, members of groups being represented by the same value. In iris dataset, the length and width of petals are only recorded with single decimal place precision, creating duplicates

```
In [17]: iris.data[[101, 142]]
Out[17]:
array([[5.8, 2.7, 5.1, 1.9],
       [5.8, 2.7, 5.1, 1.9]])
``` 

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Consider an subset of 0-1 targets of iris, where we introduce a duplicate on purpose:

```
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sparse

perm = np.array([18, 8, 18, 93, 77, 81, 81])
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
X = load_iris().data[perm]
y = load_iris().target[perm]
```

Define function to evaluate quadratic programming objective function:

```
import sklearn
import sklearn.svm

def compute_obj_func(clf, X, y):
    y_c = y.copy()
    y_c[y==0] = -1
    Kmat = sklearn.metrics.pairwise.rbf_kernel(clf.support_vectors_, gamma = clf._gamma)
    # support coefficients is alpha * y
    dc = clf.dual_coef_
    if sparse.issparse(dc):
        dc = dc.toarray()
    ys = y_c[clf.support_]
    assert np.all(dc * ys >= 0)
    assert np.all(dc * ys <= clf.C), "{}, {}".format(dc * ys, clf.C)
    assert np.allclose( np.dot(dc, np.ones_like(clf.support_)), 0)
    aQa = np.dot(np.dot(dc, Kmat), dc.T)
    eTa = np.dot(dc, ys)
    return (0.5 * aQa - eTa)
```

Now run

```
idx = np.arange(len(y))
pos_all = np.arange(len(y))
rng = np.random.RandomState(1234)

kw_args = {'gamma': 0.12682018203120274, 'tol': 1e-10, 'decision_function_shape': 'ovo'}

for i, p in enumerate([pos_all]):
    ii = idx[p].copy()
    XX = X[p].copy()
    yy = y[p].copy()

    clf_sp = sklearn.svm.SVC(**kw_args).fit(sparse.csr_matrix(XX), yy)
    clf = sklearn.svm.SVC(**kw_args).fit(XX, yy)

    if not (len(clf.support_) == len(clf_sp.support_) and
            np.allclose(clf.support_, clf_sp.support_) ):
        print("failed for index {}. Supports: {} and {}, objective functions: {}".format(
                i, ii[clf.support_], ii[clf_sp.support_], (compute_obj_func(clf, XX, yy).tolist(),
                 compute_obj_func(clf_sp, XX, yy).tolist()) ))
```

With run with `daal4py` [patches](https://github.com/IntelPython/daal4py/pull/15) the dense result is computed by Intel DAAL, while sparse result is computed by libSVM. 

DAAL find `[0 1 2 3 4 6]` as support vectors, libSVM gives `[0 1 2 3 4 5 6]`, with objective functions being 
``([[-2.249185019516638]], [[-2.2491850195166347]])`` respectively.

As you see, objective function on DAAL's solution is several machine epsilons (`14*np.finfo(np.double).eps` to be exact) lower than libSVM's objective function, and hence are essentially equivalent.

#### Expected Results

I hope to have convinced the community to either not use inputs with duplicate samples for SVC tests, or modify that test to compare values of the objective function at the solutions, or the result of 
`predict`.


#### Versions

I used scikit-learn `0.20.1`  with Numpy 1.15.4 on 64-bit Linux machine.
I also used Intel DAAL 2019.1

text:
It would be nice to have 'tangent distance' as a possible metric in nearest neighbors models.

It is not a [new concept][1] but is [widely cited][2]. It is also relatively standard, the [Elements of Statistical Learning][4] covers it.

Its main use is in patter/image recognition where it tries to identify invariances of classes (e.g. the shape of '3' regardless of rotation, thickness, etc). 

![tangent distance](https://i.imgur.com/8s8rwmu.png)

I have looked for other ways to implement it in python, but [I did not find anything yet][3].

Would be happy to contribute but do not really know how to do it.

Maybe I am misunderstanding how this calculation works?

Here is a test example. To run it we need to have `tangentDistance.py` and `ts.so` [from the quoted project][1] in the same directory where we run the script.

creator: pkomiske
title: BallTree assumes samples can be added component-wise
text:
I am using BallTree with a custom metric and am running into the following issue: BallTree seems to assume in lines 71-92 of [this file](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/neighbors/ball_tree.pyx) (possibly elsewhere also) that the sample vectors can be added component-wise. 

For my custom metric, this does not necessary produce a valid sample, i.e. the points cannot be averaged component-wise because this makes no sense for the space they live in, and thus BallTree is invalid.

Instead of averaging the samples, for cases like mine it would seem like BallTree should be restricted to using a representative central element for the dataset (a "medoid" rather than a mean). It would be great to either have this functionality implemented or for the documentation to specify that BallTree makes an explicit (in principle unnecessary) assumption that it makes sense to average samples component-wise.

substantial proposal

creator: amueller
title: Use working_memory in mlp.predict_proba etc
text:
Running predict with lots of data can blow up the ram, even on tiny models.
See https://github.com/amueller/introduction_to_ml_with_python/issues/67

It might be nice to use ``working_memory`` to restrict the size of batches used during prediction.

events.author: sagarkar10
events.comment:
Hi @amueller  Can I pick this up as my first issue!
If yes, I will need a little more description of the issue!

events.author: sagarkar10
events.comment:
From what I understand, we can use `get_chunk_n_rows` function to get the optimal number of rows to process at a time.
```python
def get_chunk_n_rows(row_bytes, max_n_rows=None,
                     working_memory=None):
    """Calculates how many rows can be processed within working_memory
    Parameters
    ----------
    row_bytes : int
        The expected number of bytes of memory that will be consumed
        during the processing of each row.
    max_n_rows : int, optional
        The maximum return value.
    working_memory : int or float, optional
        The number of rows to fit inside this number of MiB will be returned.
        When None (default), the value of
        ``sklearn.get_config()['working_memory']`` is used.
    Returns
    -------
    int or the value of n_samples
    Warns
    -----
    Issues a UserWarning if ``row_bytes`` exceeds ``working_memory`` MiB.
    """

    if working_memory is None:
        working_memory = get_config()['working_memory']

    chunk_n_rows = int(working_memory * (2 ** 20) // row_bytes)
    if max_n_rows is not None:
        chunk_n_rows = min(chunk_n_rows, max_n_rows)
    if chunk_n_rows < 1:
        warnings.warn('Could not adhere to working_memory config. '
                      'Currently %.0fMiB, %.0fMiB required.' %
                      (working_memory, np.ceil(row_bytes * 2 ** -20)))
        chunk_n_rows = 1
    return chunk_n_rows

```
For more usability we can pass an argument to `predict_proba` or even to `mlp_classifier` to override the default config.
Then we can add this function call to the `predict_proba` method inside `mlp_classifier` class
to take into account the chunk of rows at a time.
```python
    def predict_proba(self, X):
        """Probability estimates.

        Parameters
        ----------
        X : {array-like, sparse matrix}, shape (n_samples, n_features)
            The input data.

        Returns
        -------
        y_prob : array-like, shape (n_samples, n_classes)
            The predicted probability of the sample for each class in the
            model, where classes are ordered as they are in `self.classes_`.
        """
        check_is_fitted(self, "coefs_")
        # changes here, calculate optimal number of rows
         y_pred = self._predict(X)
        # modify this to iterate over each chunk and collate results 

        if self.n_outputs_ == 1:
            y_pred = y_pred.ravel()

        if y_pred.ndim == 1:
            return np.vstack([1 - y_pred, y_pred]).T
        else:
            return y_pred
```
If you think my approach is fine, I can make the edits and raise a PR. Please let me know your thoughts!

creator: xiaoxionglin
title: LDA covariance shrinkage 'auto' bug
text:
<!--
If your issue is a usage question, submit it here instead:
- StackOverflow with the scikit-learn tag: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/scikit-learn
- Mailing List: https://mail.python.org/mailman/listinfo/scikit-learn
For more information, see User Questions: http://scikit-learn.org/stable/support.html#user-questions
-->

<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description
<!-- Example: Joblib Error thrown when calling fit on LatentDirichletAllocation with evaluate_every > 0-->
The current implementation of shrinkage 'auto' is to calculate ledoit-wolf shrinkage factor separately for each matrix. 

The within-class covariance matrices are calculated with different shrinkage factors, then summed together to be S_w. Because shrinkage factor depends largely on sample size, the shrinkage factor of every within-class covariance matrix will be much larger than that of the total covariance matrix, meaning diagonal entries are weighted more in S_w than in S_t. This will result in negative diagonal entries for the between-class covariance matrix $S_b=S_t-S_w$

negative variance then leads to weird behavior of eigen-value decomposition, including 1) wrong/meaningless explained_variance 2) questionable eigenvectors

this problem can be resolved by calculating the ledoit-wolf shrinkage factor first and pass it as an argument to the LDA decoder.

I'm not sure whether this is an intended feature or a bug.

If it's the former case, how should we interpret the eigenvectors?

creator: jnothman
title: pairwise_distances(X) should always have 0 diagonal
text:
In the case of euclidean distances, we explicitly set the diagonal of unary pairwise distances to 0: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/e170d479acff31aadd9d2ab404952b23f7994aab/sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py#L257 as well as in pairwise_distances_chunked: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/e170d479acff31aadd9d2ab404952b23f7994aab/sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py#L1279. We also do so for cosine distances: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/e170d479acff31aadd9d2ab404952b23f7994aab/sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py#L550.

We should zero the diagonal of the output for all metrics through pairwise_distances and pairwise_distances_chunked (where `Y is None or Y is X`) to reduce the effect of imprecision during distance calculation.

That is, for all `metric` we eventually want:
```py
assert not np.any(pairwise_distances(X, metric=metric)[np.diag_indices(X.shape[0])])
```
and a similar assertion for `pairwise_distances_chunked`

I say eventually because I propose that:

* if current output satisfies `np.allclose(pairwise_distances(X, metric=metric)[np.diag_indices(X.shape[0])], 0)`, we just set it to 0
* if current output does not satisfy that condition, we only raise a FutureWarning saying that "The specified metric is not a valid dissimilarity metric; it does not return metric(x, x) == 0 for some values. In version 0.23, the diagonal of pairwise_distances(X) will be set to 0." We do this because at the moment we do not strictly require that the metric be a valid dissimilarity measure.
* we do the same for `pairwise_distances_chunked`

events.author: eamanu
events.comment:
And should be delete the  `distances.flat[::distances.shape[0] + 1] = 0.0 ` for euclidean and cosine distances right?

I want to work on this

events.author: jeremiedbb
events.comment:
I don't think so because you can use `euclidean_distances` instead of `pairwise_distances` and you still want 0s on the diagonal in that case.

Btw, `np.fill_diagonal(array, 0)` does the job and is more readable :)

events.author: eamanu
events.comment: So, the change must be added on the `pairwise_distances()` and whole metrics distances.

events.author: jeremiedbb
events.comment: Yes. However we rely on scipy's one for many of them, which are already consistent, so there shouldn't be too many to update

creator: mojones
title: Should cross validation shuffle by default?
text:
Apologies if issues is the wrong place for this, but it didn't seem like a usage question...

Recently I was teaching a bunch of clinical scientists how to use scikit-learn by having them build classifiers for their datasets. Several of them ran into problems with cross validation giving terrible results with some classifiers (decision trees/random forests seem particularly bad), because their datasets were ordered, either by class or by one of the features. This led me to wonder: is there a reason why the various cross-validators (KFold, etc.) do not shuffle the data by default? It seems like this would avoid problems for novice users with real-world datasets (which are often at least partially ordered). Is there a drawback that I'm not seeing? I did a quick test with the iris dataset and couldn't see any performance cost.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Iirc, This has indeed been discussed several times before, on the mailing
list and in this issue tracker.

The issue is not performance. I think the default is open for debate, and
perhaps you're right that shuffling would be better especially since most
users just to cv=10 or similar. Sometimes shuffling inappropriately
inflates scores if sample order is meaningful (e.g. temporal)...

I think this could probably be documented more clearly. PR welcome.

We could also consider whether there is a nice way to make "shuffled
10-fold" simpler to express to a cv parameter.

We could also consider whether *SearchCV (and perhaps cross_validate)
should raise a warning when variance across splits is high. I'm not sure
how to define "high" for this purpose.

events.author: mojones
events.comment:
Thanks for such a quick and thoughtful reply to a question you've obviously heard before!

From my point of view, shuffle-by-default would definitely be better, as it would be one less thing for novices to worry about. But of course, I know that my use case is just one of many. 

I'd be happy to take a stab at putting something in the docs. Maybe it would be appropriate to have it in a red warning box, [similar to the section here](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#obtaining-predictions-by-cross-validation)?

It would certainly be simpler if `shuffle` were an argument to `cross_val_score` and co., rather than having to be passed to the constructor for one of the cross-validator classes. I.e. if we could call

`cross_val_score(clf, iris.data, iris.target, cv=5, shuffle=True)`

That would open up the option of leaving `False` as the default, but having `True` in the examples to assist the copy-and-paste brigade (myself and my students included).

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I think the place to warn about it is in documenting the cv parameter. I'm
not sure if it needs to be in red, but you can, say, italicise *not* in
"not shuffled" to make it stand out.

I'm not sure what the right API is.

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
I think one of the reasons to not shuffle was that our reasoning is that it's better to show wrongly deflated results than wrongly inflated results. The intuition is that if there's correlation in your data, you should be made aware of it.

If you're using cv=5, we're using stratification for classification, which kind of solves the problem of ordered classes. If we changed to a form of stratification for regression as well, that would also solve the problem - though it would also kind of invalidate the original reason for not shuffling.
Another reason I'm not a big fan of the non-shuffling these days is that I usually suggest that people have an outer split with train_test_split, which does shuffle. So even if there was correlation in the data, it's destroyed there, and so using ``train_test_split`` has a non-obvious side-effect. If your clinical scientists used ``train_test_split`` before running cross-validation, their results would be much better for a reason that's hard to figure out imho.
If we shuffle by default, it would be harder to control the random state, though, unless we add it to all the things taking a ``cv`` argument.
Also this would be a tricky to implement change unfortunately - I'm not sure if the current deprecation of the cv default would make this easier or harder?
I'm not opposed to revisiting this.

events.comment:
You're right about random_state. Maybe cv=int is just bad design... :(

creator: Joao-M-Almeida
title: PLSRegression incompatibility with MultiOutputRegressor
text:
#### Description
<!-- Example: Joblib Error thrown when calling fit on LatentDirichletAllocation with evaluate_every > 0-->

It seems that PLSRegression doesn't work with MultiOutputRegressor. This is not usually needed, but if you want to analyze what is the influence of doing multi output fitting with PLS it is needed.

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
I got the error on my own code, but was able to reproduce it based on the Scikit-learn example availble on: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/ensemble/plot_random_forest_regression_multioutput.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-ensemble-plot-random-forest-regression-multioutput-py

I just replaced all Random Forest Models with PLSRegression(n_components=1).

Here it is:

```

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.multioutput import MultiOutputRegressor

# Create a random dataset
rng = np.random.RandomState(1)
X = np.sort(200 * rng.rand(600, 1) - 100, axis=0)
y = np.array([np.pi * np.sin(X).ravel(), np.pi * np.cos(X).ravel()]).T
y += (0.5 - rng.rand(*y.shape))

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, train_size=400, test_size=200, random_state=4)

max_depth = 30
regr_multirf = MultiOutputRegressor(PLSRegression(n_components=1))
regr_multirf.fit(X_train, y_train)

regr_rf = PLSRegression(n_components=1)
regr_rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Predict on new data
y_multirf = regr_multirf.predict(X_test)
y_rf = regr_rf.predict(X_test)

# Plot the results
plt.figure()
s = 50
a = 0.4
plt.scatter(y_test[:, 0], y_test[:, 1], edgecolor='k',
            c="navy", s=s, marker="s", alpha=a, label="Data")

creator: rth
title: sqeuclidean metric is much slower than euclidean in pairwise_distances
text:
Currently, passing `metric='sqeuclidean'` to `pairwise_distances` falls back to scipy pairwise distance calculations instead of using the fast (and less accurate) implementation in scikit-learn. As a result, it can be up to 10x slower in some cases,

```py
In [1]: from eucl_dist.cpu_dist import dist                                                                                                                  
    ... import numpy as np                                                                                                                                   
In [2]: rng = np.random.RandomState(1)                                                                                                                        
    ... a = rng.rand(1000, 300)                                                                                                                              
    ...b = rng.rand(1000, 300)
In [3]: %timeit pairwise_distances(a, b, metric='euclidean')**2                                                                                             
21.5 ms ± 804 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)

In [4]: %timeit pairwise_distances(a, b, metric='sqeuclidean')                                                                                              
212 ms ± 2 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

this is particularly confusing because people who would use `sqeuclidean` will mostly do it for performance reasons,  I think,  to save one square root computation with repsect to `euclidean`.

events.author: jeremiedbb
events.comment:
This is just a matter of documentation because you can use sklearn's implementation with
```python
pairwise_distances(a, b, metric='euclidean', metric_params={'squared': True})
```

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I suppose this is similar to the fact that we use different implementations
for euclidean and minkowski,p=2... should we be trying to resolve aliases?

creator: cottrell
title: LinearSVC check fails on sparse succeeds on dense
text:
Minor issue

```
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
import scipy.sparse
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.utils import shuffle
import numpy as np
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=10, n_features=100, n_informative=30, n_classes=3, random_state=1)
y = np.atleast_2d(y).T
y_sparse = scipy.sparse.lil_matrix(y)

# works
svc.fit(X, y)

# fails

```
Yields

ValueError: Found input variables with inconsistent numbers of samples: [10, 1]

I looked at the code and there are a number of switches like "accept_large_sparse" and other sparse checks so it's not clear what was meant there or where the right place is to make the change in the shared utils/.

Basically looks like while in dense case it just throws the usual warning about y should be 1d, in sparse it throws. 

This comes up in when you use the MultiOutputClassifier for example.

events.author: amueller
events.comment: So you'd want a better error message here? I don't think it makes a lot of sense to support this. If you use ``MultiOutputClassifier``, having the ``y`` be dense won't change anything, right? The models will not be able to exploit ``y`` being sparse anyway (there is not really any semantics in that).

events.author: cottrell
events.comment: If it is not obvious where the bug is to you, it is definitely not worth spending time on. I just thought there was a switch missing to do the to_dense conversion without erroring. creator: mikkelam
title: ColumnTransformer with array of dicts
text:
Love the new columntransformer and using it.

However i'd like to be able to use it in a production environment with arrays of python dicts or similar so i dont have to install pandas in production, this does not seem possible currently, are there any plans to support it?

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
We kinda decided against supporting it (in the first version) because we didn't think there would be a big use-case. Do you want arrays of dicts or dicts of arrays?
Either will be hard to slice: one will be hard to slice along columns, one will be hard to slice along rows. I think we want to avoid having additional logic in cross-validation.
Have you thought about using structured arrays? https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy-1.15.0/user/basics.rec.html

I don't think we're supporting structured arrays now, but these might be easier to support.
Is there a specific reason you don't want to use pandas?

An array of dicts will probably be incredibly slow btw, and doesn't really seem a good idea to me.

events.author: mikkelam
events.comment:
Yeah both ways would be fine. I didn't know about structured numpy arrays, which would be totally fine in my use case.

I'm serving my pipeline in an AWS lambda instance, and there's a very strict max size of these packages. My API endpoint is basically 1-row-at-a-time predictions, and it hurts to have to include 25 MB of pandas just to wrap a dict in a DataFrame. I'm already bundling numpy of course, so that would be cool if it worked with structured arrays.

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
Right now this doesn't work:

events.author: jorisvandenbossche
events.comment:
> I think we want to avoid having additional logic in cross-validation.

Yes, I think this was the main reason we decided not to support a dict or arrays, as such a data structure is not compatible with the rest of scikit learn (splitting in cross-validation, passing such data directly to transformers, ..)

I don't fully recall any more the reason for not supporting structured arrays. 
But one problem is that structured arrays are a bit a different "data model". For example, it is 1D (like a 1D array of "structs"), and that is actually the reason the above example code breaks.

@mikkelam there is actually special code in cross-validation to handle pandas dataframes. I added it because I felt it was a very common use-case that's important to support.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I think there is some behaviour around `partial_fit` that is poorly documented if not buggy:

* partial_fit [breaks after a single iteration](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/a028416609a347c93bcd27b052cf4ad2c8b82a21/sklearn/neural_network/multilayer_perceptron.py#L556) rather than performing up to max_iter iterations
* the `n_iter_no_change` is essentially disregarded in `partial_fit` despite `_no_improvement_count` not being reset between `partial_fit` calls, because the update on the `partial_fit` batch is done prior to checking that criterion.
* I'm not convinced from the code that the lbfgs solver really works with `partial_fit`
* It seems that `warm_start=True` is [treated like partial_fit](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/a028416609a347c93bcd27b052cf4ad2c8b82a21/sklearn/neural_network/multilayer_perceptron.py#L976) on non-initial fits, meaning only a single iteration is performed. I'm not sure this behaviour is intended/expected.
* I've not looked into how any of the behaviours above may or may not be tested.

This certainly deserves further investigation and, at a minimum, improved documentation.

events.comment:
I believe the following generated data reproduces the problem. (Let me know if this does not look the same as your problem in some way.) Otherwise, I am still investigating.
```
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

y_pred2 = mlp2.predict(x_test)

print('Using `partial_fit`:')
print(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred2))

events.comment:
@jnothman Yes the above code reproduces the problem with one exception. y is multi-label in my case, meaning that more than 1 class can be positive at a time. The following would generate similar multi-label data. 

```

events.author: samwaterbury
events.comment:
Alright. For reference, I am using variations of this code snippet in my experiments:

```
from sklearn.datasets import make_multilabel_classification
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

X, y = make_multilabel_classification(n_samples=1000, n_features=10,
                                      n_classes=5, n_labels=2,
                                      allow_unlabeled=False, random_state=1)
X_train = X[:500]
x_test = X[500:]
y_train = y[:500]
y_test = y[500:]

mlp1 = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(200, ), max_iter=200, random_state=1)
mlp1.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred1 = mlp1.predict(x_test)

mlp2 = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(200, ), max_iter=200, random_state=1)
mlp2.partial_fit(X_train, y_train, classes=list(range(y_train.shape[1])))
y_pred2 = mlp2.predict(x_test)

print('Using `fit`:')
print(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred1))

print('Using `partial_fit`:')
print(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred2))
```

First, I can definitely confirm that the poor performance with `partial_fit` comes from the fact that it breaks after a single iteration. This is clear from the code, and by setting `max_iter=1` you can see that the score will be identical for both `fit` and `partial_fit`. This probably makes sense, since its use in reinforcement learning is when the number of iterations is unknown at first and so it would be called some variable number of times depending on the situation.

Second, given that the model has been fitted for at least one round already, `warm_start=True` is treated as equivalent to `partial_fit` (i.e., it breaks after one round). In my opinion, this does not make sense; the documentation states that `warm_start=True` uses the existing weights as initialization and says nothing about only running for one round. I think that this is not reasonable behavior and inconsistent with the way other classes use the `warm_start` parameter. It’s a relatively easy fix, although it would obviously change the behavior of the class.

This `warm_start=True` behavior is especially unintuitive because if you set `max_iter=K` and then call `fit` twice, it will be fitted through K+1 rounds. The first call to `fit` will run for K rounds and the second call will run it for 1 round.

Some other notes:
1. There is currently no difference between (a) setting `max_iter=1`, `warm_start=True` and calling `fit` N times and (b) calling `partial_fit` N times.
2. The class currently throws an `AttributeError` if `partial_fit` is run with LBFGS. The only explanation I can find for this is that it is not a stochastic optimizer. However, I can remove the lines of code that throw this error and then `partial_fit` runs fine with LBFGS. After enabling LBFGS, the behavior is once again as described in note 1.
3. It is true that `n_iter_no_change` is disregarded in `partial_fit`. However, due to the above, it is also disregarded in `fit` when `warm_start=True`, which I think is even more problematic.

If nothing is changed in the code, at a minimum I would recommend changing the following in the documentation:
* The documentation for `partial_fit` does not mention that it is incompatible with LBFGS.
* It is not explained that `warm_start` will limit each `fit` call to 1 round.
* As a side note, technically `partial_fit` is a `@property` function which returns `_partial_fit`. This has the effect of making `partial_fit` show up strangely in the documentation (see what I mean on the doc page [here](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.neural_network.MLPClassifier.html#sklearn.neural_network.MLPClassifier)). I'm not sure if there's an easy way to fix this, but it causes `partial_fit` to not appear in the list of class methods.

Beyond that, I think the following changes would make this class behave in a more reasonable way:
1. I think that the limit of a single iteration for `warm_start=True` should be changed/removed. It doesn't make sense in my opinion, and it allows for the strange behavior where the initial call to `fit` results in multiple rounds of fitting but subsequent calls result in only one round. Removing this limit would also implicitly resolve note 3.
2. Unless anyone knows why LBFGS is not allowed with `partial_fit`, I don't see why we shouldn't allow it. As described in note 2, LBFGS + `warm_start=True` + `max_iter=1` achieves the same as LBFGS + `partial_fit` would.
3. **Edit:** I also found out that the `shuffle` argument is ignored, so that should be fixed.

The first change would obviously cause regressions. I'll leave it up to others to decide what's the right course to take. If we want to make changes, I would be happy to work on this.

Also, I can provide the exact code to show any of the behaviors I described in this post. Most of them can be shown with variations of the snippet I posted above.

events.comment: Thank you @samwaterbury for digging into this. I would much prefer a working partial_fit method over the warm_start. Seems like this would be more intuitive. Would the max_iter need to be set in order to run the partial fit data more than once or will it always only run once?

...produces the output:

events.comment:
@christinebuckler Yes, that is because the random seed is used for other things before each iteration when `partial_fit` is used, but not with `fit` since it does all the iterations in a single loop.

In addition, I just found something else. The `shuffle` parameter is completely ignored by this class; the batch is always shuffled even if you pass `shuffle=False`. That's another thing that should be fixed.

events.comment: I'm going to open a PR to address the documentation issues and the bug with `shuffle`, and then we can figure out whether to make the additional changes from there.

events.comment:
I think documenting the partial_fit behaviour (i.e. exactly 1 iteration
