creator: pierreglaser
title: New feature: correlation matrix generation
text:
I was thinking it might be a good idea to enrich the positive-definite matrix generation part, by adding correlation matrix generation.

**Interest of covariance matrices**: Covariance and correlations matrices are cool because from them we can generate multi-variate data sampled from specific laws (example, mutltivariate gaussian)

 **Why correlation matrices**:  Now we can generate covariance matrices (that are symmetric positive definite matrices) from `sklearn.datasets.make_spd_matrix`. However, covariance coefficients are dependent on the variable's variances, and do not give a clear, intuitive information about variables dependencies. Correlation matrices inform us about this intrinsic dependency through scaled coefficients.

**The feature**: I think that would be cool to say for example: I want a 4x4 correlation matrix with c<sub>12</sub> low, c<sub>23</sub> high and c<sub>34</sub> high. More generally, we can even replace "low" and "high" with any value between -1 and 1;  the algorithm will try to match them (but within the complex space of correlation matrices)

**How**: Of course, generating a correlation matrix C is not as simple as simply filling a matrix with 1's on the diagonal and c<sub>ij</sub><1. Most of them won't work. Methods exist on the literature (-> [Onion Method Generation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047259X09000876), sorry for non-academic wifi users...) for uniform and/or more complex sampling behaviors and it may be a good idea to implement one of them.



If this generates any interest, we can discuss it together, and I am fine with implementing a batch of functions to generate such objects.

Let me know guys!

events.comment: I suggest that before taking any actions, we should assess whether or not there is an actual demand for such a feature. If yes, kamathhrishi I appreciate the help,  but the code is already written, as I needed it on other projects.

events.comment: I think this would be very useful for many users.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: Sounds interesting, but it's certainly not my area. Within scikit-learn, we only seem to use make_spd_matrix in testing GMMs. Would you see a more generic correlation matrix generator as being used to present an example of some machine learning technique, or test some machine learning technique? Try to clarify how it fits into the needs of ML practitioners.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: Also have you searched for FOSS implementations of such algorithms?

events.author: pierreglaser
events.comment:
The purpose of all of this is the further generation of data following a structure that the user will 
be able to specify. The user should end up with a n-dimensional input dataset X following a correlation matrix M, as well as an output y with a correlation vector V linking y to X. M and V will try to fit the user needs in terms of data structure (paragraph "The Feature" in the original post)

Testing ML models on data that follow quantifiable and modifiable behavior is pretty useful when studying the scope of practice of ML models. A practical example would be for the user to study how a specific ML model incorporates a feature F with little (but non-zero) correlation to the output. 
There are more specific and less easily-explainable uses of this, however, they (and even the first use) probably more belong to the research field than the everyday ML practitioner actions. 

FOSS implementations exist for generation of correlation matrices given specific distributions, but so far, I have not found a function that incorporates quantifiable correlations like in my first post (e.g create a correlation matrix C with c12=0.4 etc..)

creator: naught101
title: Standard attribute for model completion status
text:
At the moment, there is no way to know why a model stopped fitting (aside from exceptions). It may be because convergence was reached (below a tolerance), or because a hard limit on iterations was hit, or possibly some other condition was met. It would be excellent if Scikit-learn models had some kind of flat attached after fitting. Perhaps `model.fit_status_` or similar. This could then be reported during usage.

For example, I'm hitting [a problem with MiniBatchKMeans clustering](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/304404/dealing-with-unassigned-clusters-in-minibatchkmeans), where some clusters are not assigned. The only think I know is that the `max_iter` was not met, but I don't know if it's due to the `max_no_improvement` flag, because the `tol` is too high (not in my case). It would be great if the model reported this in a standard way.

creator: atorch
title: Feature request: include mean absolute error (MAE) as scorer in sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNetCV
text:
<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description
<!-- Example: Joblib Error thrown when calling fit on LatentDirichletAllocation with evaluate_every > 0-->

In scikit-learn v0.19.0, ElasticNet minimizes the objective function:

> `1 / (2 * n_samples) * ||y - Xw||^2_2`
> `+ alpha * l1_ratio * ||w||_1`
> `+ 0.5 * alpha * (1 - l1_ratio) * ||w||^2_2`.

In words, the objective function is mean squared error (MSE) loss on the predicted variable, plus regularization terms.  My feature request is to include an argument (with 'mse' as its default value) that would allow the user to switch to mean absolute error (MAE) loss on the predicted variable.  For the equivalent in R, see https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/glmnet/glmnet.pdf, particularly the documentation for cv.glmnet:

> type.measure="mae" (mean absolute error) can be used by all models except ... "cox"

It would be great to also allow this functionality in sklearn.

Edit:  as @agramfort pointed out below, glmnet only supports MAE for cross-validation, but not for model fitting.  My request is to add an option for MAE in sklearn ElasticNet model fitting.  This already exists in sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor (loss='quantile' and alpha=0.50), if I am reading the documentation correctly.  There's also a linear-regression-with-MAE-loss option in sklearn.linear_model.HuberRegressor.html, if epsilon=0.0 ("The Huber Regressor optimizes the squared loss for the samples where `|(y - X'w) / sigma| < epsilon` and the absolute loss for the samples where `|(y - X'w) / sigma| > epsilon`").

creator: jnothman
title: warm_start for GridSearchCV and RandomizedSearchCV
text:
In practice it is useful to search over some parameter space and then continue the search over some related space. We could provide a `warm_start` parameter to make it easy to accumulate results for further candidates into `cv_results_` (without reevaluating parameter combinations that have already tested).

Issues:
* What do we do when the parameter space is reduced rather than expanded; do we delete former results?
* I'm not sure that this is identical semantics to other uses of `warm_start`. Do we let things change other than the parameter space? The set of scorers for instance?
* Given that calling split multiple times on a cv splitter does not guarantee identical splits, this means we would need to store the first cv split indices and reuse them in subsequent warm started fits. This in turn means that we cannot use warm start in a way that allows us to change the CV splitter (which I think @ogrisel mentioned as a potential use of grid search a while ago).
* Does calling `RandomizedSearchCV(n_iter=10, warm_start=True)`'s fit twice mean that it should do 10 iterations for each call, or 10 in total (0 in the second call)?
* Is this unnecessary complexity to add to GridSearchCV when users can just concatenate the multiple `cv_results_` dataframes?

events.author: adrinjalali
events.comment:
Just brainstorming, in case you find it useful.

- One way to look for model hyperparameters is to start with a coarse grid, and then refine the grid in areas which may look promising. With this strategy, you'd always _reduce_ the parameter space at each step, but you won't want to forget about the previous ones. (I may have understood a different thing from _reduce_ than what you mean here).
- To me, it makes sense to _erase the state_ of the search once anything other than the parameter space is changed, _i.e._ CVs, scorers, etc. Therefore something like the CV would be a part of the _state_.
-  If the goal is to accumulate the parameter CV scores, I think some documentation would be enough  (if not done explicitly yet) how the user can accumulate the results and how they should easily interpret it.

However, all this reminds me of some thoughts I had when I was frequently using `RandomizedSearchCV`. The first time I encountered the class, my assumption was that the search in the search space is rather dynamic. By that, I mean a sample would be taken from the large search space, with some coarse samples from the grid, get the scores, and get the next batch of parameters depending on the results of the first batch, _i.e._ to sample with a higher probability around the places where you get higher scores. I was proven wrong when I saw [this](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/model_selection/_search.py#L696)

 ```
            def evaluate_candidates(candidate_params):
                candidate_params = list(candidate_params)
                n_candidates = len(candidate_params)
```
which implies that the sample is taken from the search space at the beginning of the process, then it's processed. Although `ParameterSampler` is a generator, and in principle it could generate new samples based on the results of the previously tested parameters, it's converted into a `list` at the beginning of `evaluate_candidates`.

This also means, if you ask me, `RandomizedSearchCV(n_iter=10, warm_start=True)` would explore 10 hyperparameter values on the first call, and 10 other ones on the second call.

Of course you could also include different `ParameterSampler`s which implement different strategies of sampling from the space.

The user could then start the search, run for a few batches, then change the grid values if they want, and _continue_ the process. Alternatively, they could plug in their own `ParameterSampler` to the `RandomizedSearchCV`, which would have access to the `cv_results_` of the search machine and produce batches, or generate new parameter sets.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Regarding the conversion from iterator to to list: as long as we store all
the candidates in the results, there's little benefit to not materialising
them.​

The new _run_search interface can potentially facilitate manual search
space tuning too...

text:

<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description
Poor results always obtained when using sklearn.semi_supervised.LabelPropagation (or LabelSpreading) with any (callable) kernel other than the predefined "knn", "rbf", or sklearn.metrics.pairwise.rbf_kernel

#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Example:
```python
from sklearn.semi_supervised import LabelPropagation, LabelSpreading
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import pairwise_kernels, rbf_kernel

def my_kernel(X, Z):
        # This works good :
	return rbf_kernel(X, Z)
        # This seems to always work bad for any choice of metric (and parameters), except for "rbf" :
	return pairwise_kernels(X, Z, metric="cosine")

h = LabelSpreading(kernel=my_kernel, n_neighbors=7, alpha=0.2).fit(X_labelled+X_unlabelled, Y_labelled+[-1 for _ in X_unlabelled])
print "Result:", 100*accuracy_score( Y_test, h.predict(X_test) )
```

Here is a complete other example using the optical digits dataset:
```python
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
from sklearn import datasets 
from sklearn.semi_supervised import LabelPropagation, LabelSpreading
from sklearn.utils import shuffle
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import pairwise_kernels, rbf_kernel

def my_kernel(X, Z):
	# return rbf_kernel(X, Z, gamma=0.1) # works good
	return pairwise_kernels(X, Z, metric="cosine")  # works bad
	
if __name__ == "__main__":
	digits = datasets.load_digits()
	X, Y = shuffle( list(digits.data), list(digits.target) )
	Lx = X[:50]; Ly = Y[:50]; Ux = X[50:]; Uy = Y[50:]
	
	print Ly
	h = LabelSpreading(kernel=my_kernel, n_neighbors=7, alpha=0.2).fit(Lx+Ux, Ly+[-1 for _ in Ux])
	print "Result:", 100*accuracy_score( Uy, h.predict(Ux) )
```

#### Expected Results
I expected kernels such as: sigmoid, polynomial, poly, linear, cosine (tested with various parameters) to perform reasonably good, but all of those give extremely poor results.

#### Actual Results
Only kernel = "knn", or "rbf" (or a callable corresponding to an rbf kernel) gives good results.

#### Versions

``` Python
	digits = datasets.load_digits()
	X, Y = shuffle( list(digits.data), list(digits.target) )
	Lx = X[:50]; Ly = Y[:50]; Ux = X[50:]; Uy = Y[50:]
	
	for kernel in ['rbf', 'sigmoid', 'cosine', 'linear', 'laplacian']:
		clf = LabelSpreading(kernel=lambda X, Z: pairwise_kernels(X, Z, metric=kernel), n_neighbors=7, alpha=0.2).fit(Lx+Ux, Ly+[-1 for _ in Ux])
		print kernel, 100*accuracy_score( Uy, clf.predict(Ux) )
		
	# ---------------------------------------------------
	print "\n----------- Artificial dataset:"
	X, y_true = datasets.make_classification(n_classes=3, n_informative=5, n_samples=200)
	y = y_true.copy()
	y[::3] = -1
	for kernel in ['rbf', 'sigmoid', 'cosine', 'linear', 'laplacian']:
		clf = LabelSpreading(kernel=lambda X, Z: pairwise_kernels(X, Z, metric=kernel), max_iter=5000).fit(X, y)
		print kernel, 100*accuracy_score( y_true, clf.predict(X) )
```

creator: tomMoral
title: Rationalize metric argument in T-SNE
text:
The API of T-SNE have a `metric` argument to allow changing the metric in the input space. The original paper was developed using only the euclidean distance and changing the metric might change a bit the math. 

The main issue is to understand what is going on with the computation of the conditional probabilities. The original paper states that if `d_ij` is the euclidean distance between `x_i` and `x_j`, then the conditional probability is given by
``` 
p(x_j | x_i) = exp{ d_ij^2 / sig_i} / Z
```
where Z is a normalization constant and `sig_i` is a parameter, computed to fix the perplexity of the model. _If `d_ij` is not the euclidean distance, does it make sense to use this formula?_ 
The current implementation for other metric than the euclidean uses the formula without the square, so
``` 
p(x_j | x_i) = exp{ d_ij / sig_i} / Z
```
If it is fine, this should be documented. Else, shall we change it to use the square or another distribution? Another solution is to deprecate the `metric` argument.

A second point is the use of `init='pca'`. It is a very natural initialization for the euclidean metric but should be benchmarked for other to see if it gives an interesting starting point or not.

This issue is a follow-up of #9623 .

events.author: amueller
events.comment: This is still open and we should at least document current behavior, right?

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Is sig_i negative? Presumably in order to get a probability you need to exp negative numbers.

It's mostly intuition, but I'm fairly sure this conditional probability definition (which is a softmax over squared distances) should apply just as well to other squared distances.

 I've not understood why it should be squared, but obviously distance matrices have certain properties defined by the definition of proper distance metrics, and so squared distances would too. 

I don't see why Euclidean should be distinguished. As far as I understand, for any distance matrix you can construct points in infinite-dimensional Euclidean space that have those distances.

So yes, we should be squaring other metrics IMO. How to make this change, and how to deal with precomputed, I'm not sure. So we should absolutely start with documentation.

events.author: Micky774
events.comment:
TL;DR Changes in metric _mostly_ still correspond to gaussian conditional probability, I think it's fine to "trust" the user with using a proper metric.

First we can discuss Euclidean distance as a special case of a family of distance metrics defined by matrices -- given a PSD matrix `P`, `d_P(x,y) = sqrt[ (x-y)^T P (x-y) ]`. Then the Euclidean distance is the case where `P=I`.  Consider a distribution of points in any Euclidean space. Scaling the points' coordinates arbitrarily (but consistently for all points), e.g. `x_i,j --> x_i,j * s_j`, acts as a change of metric, where the corresponding matrix goes from `I --> S = diag(s_1, s_2,...)` -- if `S` is PSD. This is already considered fair-game for `t-sne` and is already put on the user.

I think you can generalize the choice of metric for `t-sne` to account for the fact that `exp[ (-1/2)*d_P(x, m) ]` defines a gaussian pdf when `m` is the mean and `P` is the covariance matrix. Therefore any invertible mapping `f` that can be viewed as a change to the underlying metric, e.g. `x --> Ax` where `A` is invertible which changes the underlying matrix `P --> (A^T)P(A)`, also ensures that `t-sne` of `f(X)` is `t-sne` performed under _some_ gaussian conditional probability, albeit potentially ill-conditioned.

In that sense, I think it's safe to generalize the "acceptable" metrics from just Euclidean to any PSD-matrix induced metric. 

*Bonus: For a metric space `(X, d)` I'm pretty sure that any _injective_ mapping `f: X-->X` also properly defines a new metric `d_f(x, y) = d( f(x), f(y) )`

creator: NathanWycoff
title: LatentDirichletAllocation: Modernization of Inference
text:
Firstly, I'm rather new around here; I hope this is the correct place for proposing replacement of algorithms. If it isn't, it would be awful kind of someone to point me in the right direction.

#### Summary
LatentDirichletAllocation uses a very old (2003) algorithm to estimate its parameters. I tried using the sklearn function for my research, but found that it was unsatisfactory compared to newer algorithms. I have implemented some newer algorithms, and would be happy to get one of them in a format conforming to sklearn's requirments and contribute them. I only have experience in using batch estimation (so no online), but I'd be happy to look into newer online algorithms as well.

#### Proposed New Algorithm

--Collapsed Variational Bayes (Zeroth Order Taylor Expansion)--

Introduced in 2012 in [Asuncion et al](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.2662.pdf), the Zeroeth Order Taylor approximation to Collapsed Variational Bayes (often abbreviated CVB0) is a much more modern algorithm than the original variational bayes algorithm proposed in [Blei Ng Jordan, 2003](https://endymecy.gitbooks.io/spark-ml-source-analysis/content/%E8%81%9A%E7%B1%BB/LDA/docs/Latent%20Dirichlet%20Allocation.pdf). 

It is essentially a deterministic version of Collapsed Gibbs Sampling (not introduced in [Wilson and Chew, 2010](http://www.aclweb.org/anthology/N10-1070), but I find their description quite understandable), wherein the topic-word propensity matrix (called $\beta$ in Blei et al and sometimes called $\phi$ in newer articles) as well as the document-topic prevalence vector (called $\theta$ in Blei et al) are analytically integrated out. This results in a posterior only on the word-topic associations (called $z$ in Blei et al), over which a variational distribution is defined. Unfortunately, this cost function is not analytic, but taylor series approximations yield good empirical results.

#### Advantages of New Algorithm

Based on my personal experience and reviewing relevant literature, I see the benefits of the new algorithm as threefold:

1) **Considerably faster** -- Asuncion et al report a tenfold increase. I have observed much higher in practice on certain datasets (though, admittedly, I did not spend much time optimizing my cpp implementations of either algorithm).
2) **More accurate** -- Theoretically, the process of integrating out certain parameters results in a lower bound on the loglikelihood that is strictly better than the lower bound induced by traditional VB. Empirically, taylor approximations of this bound are still able to beat traditional VB.
3) **Increase in convexity of cost surface** -- This is something I have not seen in the literature, but have observed myself. It is very important in my research that running the algorithm twice should produce the same result, something which seems not to occur with traditional VB. The newer algorithm seems to be much better at avoiding multimodality of the cost surface.

\vspace{5em}

I've benefited very much over the last several years from using sklearn, both as an academic in research and classes, as well as during internships in industry. I feel an obligation to contribute, now that I can, should these improvements be desired. My implementation is in C, but I can easily create a python wrapper for it (or re-write in python, if that's desired).

events.author: NathanWycoff
events.comment:
Hi @amueller , I'm not proposing removing the variational approach, I'm proposing switching which variational approach we use;[ this great article ](https://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/1205/1205.2662.pdf) goes over a bunch of the differences between the algos. I propose switching from what they refer to as VB to what they refer to as CVB0.

It's been a while since this topic opened. I have implemented the CVB0 algo in both pure python and in cython, but I don't see the computational savings I was expecting: it is usually not much faster than the existing algo, and can potentially be slower. This contradicts the reported findings from the paper I link, as well as my results from pure C implementations of both variational algos (regular variational and CVB0). I'm not a cython expert, nor a python one for that matter, but my understanding is that for loops induce a lot of overhead in interpreted languages such as python. Since the CVB0 algo involves nested for loops where the actual operation within each loop is very cheap, I would imagine that I'm getting destroyed by overhead. Why this is still the case in Cython I'm not sure (though the Cython implementation is an order of magnitude faster than the pure Python one, it is still rather slow). I'd be happy to share my work if anyone else wants to take a shot at it.

If you're suggesting using Collapsed Gibbs Sampling (CGS) instead, that could be another approach. Some arguments in favor of CVB0 over CGS would be 1) evaluating convergence 2) computational expense (though, as I mention, I've not been able to realize the theoretical computational savings). CGS is closely related to CVB0 from an implementation perspective, so I imagine it would suffer from the same overhead concerns I've run into, though a better coder than I may be able to circumvent this.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Cython does little to automatically optimise your code. It only will make
optimisation where you specify static types, switch off bounds checking
when indexing into lists, etc. cython -a is your friend for finding out if
you've got slow code due to not static typing etc.​

events.author: joshuacwnewton
events.comment:
This enhancement was recently brought up in a meeting between a few of sklearn's core maintainers and students in the MLH Fellowship. @parthivc and I have expressed interest, and @thomasjpfan recommended some starting points for proposing API changes.

### Parameter changes

From what I can tell, replacing Variational Bayes (VB) with a collapsed Gibbs sampler (CGS) shouldn't require any additional parameters. <sup>[[See p.3]](http://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/teaching/4f13/1112/lect10.pdf)</sup> 

I've compared the current parameters in [`sklearn.LatentDirichletAllocation`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.decomposition.LatentDirichletAllocation.html) with the parameters used by @hannawallach in her excellent [Python 2.7 LDA implementation with Gibbs sampling](https://github.com/hannawallach/python-lda/blob/master/src/lda.py). (I believe this link is what was referred to earlier by @amueller.) I couldn't find any new parameters that need to be added, and I believe many existing parameters can be directly reused.

<details>
    <summary>Table hidden, click to show</summary>
  
**Note:** Certain parameters are used by sklearn, but are absent in hannahwallach's implementation. I've grouped these into 3 categories:

 1. Parameters that are specific to Variational Bayes, whether online or batch.
 2. Parameters that are related to sklearn’s use of perplexity for checking LDA model convergence.
 3. Parameters related to sklearn core functionality (e.g. partial_fit, random_state, parallel processing, output verbosity)
 
 I believe parameters of the 1st type are unnecessary for Gibbs sampling. Parameters of the 2nd and 3rd type, though, could be reused.

| Name (sklearn’s LDA w/VB)                               | Name (@hannawallach’s LDA w/Gibbs) | Description                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `n_components` (default: `n_components=10`)                                                | `T` (default: `T=100`)                                           | Number of topics.                                                                                                                     |
| `doc_topic_prior` (default: `doc_topic_prior=1/n_components`)                                               | `alpha` (default: `alpha=0.1`)                         | Prior of document topic distribution theta (θ). In [[link]](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/3902-online-learning-for-latent-dirichlet-allocation.pdf), this is called alpha (α).                                                   |
| `topic_word_prior` (default: `topic_word_prior=1/n_components`)                                            | `beta` (default: `beta=0.01`)                         | Prior of the topic word distribution beta (β). In [[link]](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/3902-online-learning-for-latent-dirichlet-allocation.pdf), this is called eta (η).                                                      |
| `learning_method`                                             | N/A <sup>[1]</sup>                            | Method used to update `_component`. (‘batch’ or ‘online’)                                                                             |
| `learning_decay`                                              | N/A <sup>[1]</sup>                            | A parameter that controls learning rate in the online learning method. In the literature, this is called kappa (κ).                   |
| `learning_offset`                                             | N/A <sup>[1]</sup>                            | A (positive) parameter that downweights early iterations in online learning. In the literature, this is called tau_0 (τ<sub>0</sub>). |
| `max_iter` (default: `max_iter=10`)                                                    | `S` (default: `S=1000`)                                           | “The maximum number of iterations.” (sklearn) // “The number of Gibbs sampling iterations." (@hannawallach)                                                     |
| `batch_size`                                                  | N/A <sup>[1]</sup>                            | Number of documents to use in each EM iteration. Only used in online learning.                                                        |
| `evaluate_every`                                              | N/A <sup>[2]</sup>                            | How often to evaluate perplexity.                                                                                                     |
| `total_samples`                                               | N/A <sup>[3]</sup>                            | Total number of documents. Only used in the partial_fit method.                                                                       |
| `perp_tol`                                                    | N/A <sup>[2]</sup>                            | Perplexity tolerance in batch learning. Only used when evaluate_every is greater than 0.                                              |
| `mean_change_tol`                                             | N/A <sup>[1]</sup>                            | Stopping tolerance for updating document topic distribution in E-step.                                                                |
| `max_doc_update_iter`                                         | N/A <sup>[1]</sup>                            | Max number of iterations for updating document topic distribution in the E-step.                                                      |
| `n_jobs`                                                      | N/A <sup>[3]</sup>                            | The number of jobs to use in the E-step.                                                                                              |
| `verbose`                                                     | N/A <sup>[3]</sup>                            | Verbosity level.                                                                                                                      |
| `random_state`                                                | N/A <sup>[3]</sup>                            | Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.                                                                  |
| `X`                                                           | `corpus`                                      | Document word matrix.                                                                                                                 |
| `weight` | N/A <sup>[1]</sup>                            | Weight, rho (ρ). Used internally by sklearn, and is a function of `learning_offset` and `learning_decay`.                                                                                                                      |


</details>

### R's implementation

As well, I've taken a look at R's implementation ([`lda.collapsed.gibbs.sampler`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/lda/versions/1.4.2/topics/lda.collapsed.gibbs.sampler)) to see if they've included any additional parameters. There are a few that seem useful to add, but they don't seem to be absolutely necessary.

<details>
    <summary>Table hidden, click to show</summary>



| Name | Description | 
| ---- | ----------- |
| `burnin` | A scalar integer indicating the number of Gibbs sweeps to consider as burn-in (i.e., throw away) | 
| `compute.log.likelihood` | A scalar logical which when TRUE will cause the sampler to compute the log likelihood of the words (to within a constant factor) after each sweep over the variables. The log likelihood for each iteration is stored in the log.likelihood field of the result. This is useful for assessing convergence, but slows things down a tiny bit. |
  
</details>

### Other details

There are a few API details I'm unclear on:
 * Whether to keep online/batch VB as an alternative. _(A parameter `method` could be added with options `{'bayes', 'gibbs'}` for backwards compatibility. Then, parameters specific to Variational Bayes could be left as optional keyword parameters. The descriptions for these parameters could be amended to specifically mention VB.)_
 * Default values for `n_components`, `max_iter`, and the priors. _(There are some differences between sklearn's LDA w/VB and hannahwallach's LDA w/CGS, as listed in the first table.)_
 * The discussion above mentions Cython, but @thomasjpfan mentioned in email the possibility of a pure Python/NumPy implementation.

I'd love to hear thoughts on this proposal before proceeding. Thanks! :)

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
We can use `learning_method='gibbs'` to trigger the new method.

I think we can keep `n_components` as out default of 10. As for `max_iter` it would need to be set to `'auto'`, as gibbs sample would need a lot more iterations for it to get enough samples to produce something meaningful. For Gibbs sampling, there is traditionally some burn in period and I think this should be a parameter.

> The discussion above mentions Cython, but @thomasjpfan mentioned in email the possibility of a pure Python/NumPy implementation.

I was thinking of maybe Python/NumPy when consider the collapsed gibbs sampler. The collapsed version is much simplier since you only need to sample from the indicator variables. This is different form standard gibbs sampling since we do not need to sample from the corpus-wide topic vocab distributions or the per-doc topic proportions. On the other hand, if we are doing full gibbs sampling, I think that would have more benefits in Cython.

creator: jnothman
title: Store initial random state on models?
text:
I've sometimes wondered how to reproduce a model (or an error) if I did not provide a fixed random state.

Something we could consider is for every randomised estimator (or at least where `random_state` is not an int), to store something like `random_state_tuple_ = rng.get_state()`. This makes any saved model reproducible given the same data.

Given a saved estimator `est`, one can do:
```
est2 = clone(est)
rng = np.random.RandomState()
rng.set_state(est.random_state_tuple_)
est2.set_params(random_state=rng)
```
to get an identical estimator. Not particularly user friendly, but at least this makes it possible.

An alternative is storing `intial_random_state_ = copy.deepcopy(rng)`, being more user-friendly, as long as the user doesn't then accidentally generate something from it and so change it.

What do others thing?

Related issue (I think): #9658

events.author: thechargedneutron
events.comment:
I am not confident in my claim but can we add a function in `utils` which takes the an estimators as parameters and returns the new having the same random state as the older one?
Something like:
```
def estimator_with_same_random_state(est):
    est2 = clone(est)
    rng = np.random.RandomState()
    rng.set_state(est.random_state_tuple_)
    est2.set_params(random_state=rng)
    return est2
```
And hence can be used as 
`est2 = estimatpr_with_random_state(est)` ??

This would be user friendly as they have to use only an additional line.
Correct me if I am wrong.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
well that wouldn't be sufficient if there are nested randomised estimators,
but yes, perhaps a parameter to clone could do this, with the caveat that
it only has effect for a fitted estimator that supports this feature.

This isn't the sort of thing that people raise issues about often, but I do
suspect it is a bit of a pitfall for beginners... Keeping track of the
global random state is also something that might be possible with a Jupyter
extension (capture the current state at the beginning and end of each cell,
and store the initial state as cell metadata if it was changed, with a
widget to restore it).

events.author: rth
events.comment: The motivation is appealing, but I wonder if given the cost of changing all the estimators, just spending time to re-run the estimator with different fixed random states until it fails wouldn't be enough. Also in tests, we are supposed to fix all random states.

creator: raamana
title: Feature addition: Pipeline comparison
text:
Hi There,

During our research, we keep having to compare different pipelines or feature sets, and comparing improvement in numerical accuracy is not the best way for few reasons. Testing for significance of improvement can be via non-parametric Friedman test and some postdoc analysis [[check our paper for real-world example of usage](http://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2017/07/31/170381)].

I will be adding such a feature to one of my projects [`neuropredict`](https://github.com/raamana/neuropredict), which is aiming to make machine learning like eating ice cream for those who can't code :), and am thinking it might be better to include it in scikit-learn and use it from there. If the following sounds useful and good inclusion to sklearn, I will be happy send in a PR - just wanted to make sure there is no one else working on it already.

The results will look like something presented in [recent scikit-learn benchmarks paper](https://crossinvalidation.com/2017/08/22/quantitative-comparison-of-scikit-learns-predictive-models-on-a-large-number-of-machine-learning-datasets-a-good-start/).

![screen shot 2017-08-26 at 10 22 04 am](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3196357/29742348-8f6c2c8c-8a4b-11e7-845e-1dec0e366e03.png)


Simple usage I envision is
```python
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn import Pipeline, compare_pipelines

X, y = get_dataset_placeholder()
pipe1 = Pipeline([('reduce_dim', PCA()), ('clf', SVC())])
pipe2 = Pipeline([('reduce_dim', PCA()), ('clf', RandomForestClassifier())])
signif_matrix, comparison_report = compare_pipelines([pipe1, pipe2], X, y)
```


Rough implementation would look like:
```python
def compare_pipelines(pipe_list, X, y, cv_choice=None, perf_metrics = None):
    """ Compares two pipelines and whether one is significantly better than other.

    Performs a non-parametric comparison of predictive performance of two pipelines
    evaluated from bootstrapped distributions of cross-validated performance.

    """

    num_pipelines = len(pipe_list)
    if num_pipelines < 2:
        raise ValueError('Atleast two pipelines are required for comparison.')

    if cv_choice is None:
        cv = ShuffleSplit(test_size=0.5, n_splits=250, random_state=1)

    if perf_metrics is None:
        perf_metrics = ['accuracy_score', 'balanced_accuracy', 'auc', 'f1_score']

    pipe_scores = np.empty([num_pipelines, 1])
    for counter, pipe in enumerate(pipe_list):
        # this would be replaced later by local implementation, wherein we control
        # which train/test sets pipelines will be trained and tested on for better estimation
        pipe_scores[counter] = cross_validate(pipe, X, y, 
                                    scoring = perf_metrics,
                                    cv = cv_choice)

    signif_matrix, comparison_report = non_parametric_friedman(pipe_scores, posthoc= 'nemenyi')
    
    return signif_matrix, comparison_report

```

cc @amueller @GaelVaroquaux

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
Firstly, I don't think we mean pipelines here. Just arbitrary estimators.

Secondly, I think it would be good for us to have measures of significance
between systems available in the library and their use as a tool explained
in an example. Taking advantage of multiple metrics seems like a reasonable
idea except that assuming they're all equally competent judges for any
(binary classification) problem is quite naive.

I don't think this is the right interface. I think we should start by
considering how we would offer and illustrate access to a
non_parametric_friedman
friedman function dealing with cross_validate output or cv_results_ in the
first place.

creator: datajanko
title: Feature Request: Pipelining Outlier Removal
text:
I wonder if we could make outlier removal available in pipelines.

I tried implementing it for example using the IsolationForest but so far I couldn't solve it and I know why.

The problem boils down to `fit_transform` only returning a transformed `X` this suffices in the vast majority of cases, since we typically only throw away columns (think of a PCA). However, using outlier removal in a pipeline, we need to throw away rows of `X` **and** `y` during training and do nothing during testing. This is not supported so far. Essentially, we would need to turn the `predict` function into some kind of `transform` function during training.

Investigating the pipeline implementation shows, that `fit_transform`is called if present during the fitting part of the pipeline, rather than `fit(X, y).transform(X)`. Particularly, in a cross validation `fit_transform` is only called during training. This would be perfect for outlier removal. However, it remains to do nothing in the test step. But to this end we can simply implement a "do-nothing" `transform`-function.

The most direct way to implement this, would be an API-change of the TransformerMixin-class,  unfortunately.

So my questions are:

Would it be interesting to contain feature removal in pipelines?
Are there other more suitable ideas of implementing this feature in a pipeline?

If the content of this question is somehow inapropriate (e.g. since I'm only an active user, not an active developer of the project) or at the wrong place, feel free to remove the thread.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
This is the right place. Sorry I've not fished out issue numbers, but certainly things like this have been raised before, particularly as regards resampling in pipeline. A few points:
1. It's not hard to implement something like this as your own metaestimator (and maybe it makes sense to have one specialised for outlier removal)
2. We'd rather avoid allowing transform to resize the data, but introducing a new method (I think imblearn uses resample) is a something I would like to see happen.

events.author: datajanko
events.comment:
Hey, I skimmed through some issues but didn't find a related topic. Sorry for that.

I fully understand that an API change is suboptimal. Resample is of course the right method name for imblearn, `reduce`might be good in this case, but it's an completey overloaded name ;) What about condense? 
But would this really be the right place to be put directly into sklearn or would a "contrib" package be preferred?

Concerning the meta estimator: how would such an estimator remove rows? I just don't see it at the moment and a small(!) hint is appreciated.

events.author: datajanko
events.comment:
I think I found one of the related [issues](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/3855)

And I think I understood how to use a meta estimator. Compared to bagging, the random part in bagging is replaced by the outlier free set and the many estimators are replaced by the estimator we are interested in. 

However, this means, that we can only remove outliers in the final step (or build further meta estimators out of transformer (which seems awkward)). I think in that case, a new method might be a better choice

datajanko
events.comment:
For me, (re)sampling always contains a strong random component. This is not directly fulfilled when outliers shall get removed.

Thanks for the metaestimator hint. I thought in a similiar direction. Additionally, the classifier can be a pipeline, so my previous comment on removing outliers only in the last step is wrong in some sense.

refusing to classify is interesting. The estimator could have an option to

either need a wrapper for outlier detectors, or need to add a fit_resample
method on each of them. Or we can just add a metaestimator like mine above
to make outlier removal in training practical.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
You might be interested in using the random sub-sampling from https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/9645. For 800000 samples and 137 features, there's a lot of calculation to do at each split.


Perhaps MAE could perhaps be made faster (needs investigation), as per @mcgibbon's [comment](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/9553#issuecomment-324484928):

> When "mae" is selected as a criterion, the performance is O(N^2), but this can probably be written to be O(N*log(N)). This would likely be done by making it so that when items are pushed onto the WeightedMedianCalculator (which keeps a sorted list of its values) the correct index is found in log(N) time, whereas currently this takes N time. It probably also requires the MAE being pre-computed and updated every time an item is pushed onto the WeightedMedianCalculator, since currently it is re-computed which requires N time. There may be other places that need to be changed, but these are the two main ones I've identified.

I personally had 2 million samples splitting on 5 features, and I was doubting the code would finish in my lifetime based on what I saw for scaling.

Even if it is re-written, the MAE would still be much slower than MSE, since it would scale with N*log(N) whereas MSE seems to scale with N.

events.author: mcgibbon
events.comment:
@SmokinCaterpillar I attempted to implement this, but my resulting solution failed unit tests (it was doing one calculation or another incorrectly). I was unable to configure any kind of Cython debugging to work with Anaconda, and I figured for other reasons that this probably won't impact my research, so in the end I gave up.

The real issue isn't in computing running medians, but in computing the mean absolute error in constant time at each step (you can update the MSE in constant time). [`WeightedMedianCalculator`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/tree/_utils.pyx#L455) needs to be modified to update the median in constant time, and also to keep running track of the MAE and also update that in constant time.

You can compute running medians by keeping the entries sorted, and keeping track of the middle entry (which is necessary because it's a weighted median). When an entry gets pushed or popped, you need to update the position of the middle entry, if necessary, and update the MAE if the position is updated. You can update the weighted MAE based on the sign of the change in the MAE. If it decreases, the absolute error is decreased by that amount for all lower samples, and increased by that amount for all higher samples. You also add in the contribution to the MAE based on the absolute error of the new sample.

After that, [`MAE.node_impurity`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/tree/_criterion.pyx#L1232) and [`MAE.children_impurity`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/tree/_criterion.pyx#L1254) need to be updated to use the new `WeightedMedianCalculator.get_mae()` function that you will write.

At least, all that is the solution I came up with.

I'm very surprised about the tree number scaling. You should try with a few more numbers of trees (between 1 and 20) and plot the scaling in log space. The code really does train the trees independently, and there are other reasons you might expect the scaling to be nonlinear (though probably not exponential).

Sorry for digressing this thread, but if anyone is interested here are my benchmarks and sample script, note that I ended up performing these tests using MSE as this enabled to produce a similar performance wrt large sample data set, but without having to wait too long to complete (as with MAE):


```
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
import numpy as np
import time
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

cores = 36
n_model_list = range(1, cores+1, 1)
time_list_mse = []

n_samples = 1024 * 1024 #8 #64
train_X = np.random.randn(n_samples, 20)
train_y = np.ravel(np.random.randn(n_samples, 1))

for n_model in n_model_list:

    start = time.time()
    random_forest = RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=n_model, n_jobs=cores,
        criterion='mse', warm_start=False,
        max_features='sqrt') #, random_state=531)
    random_forest.fit(train_X, train_y)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print('No Of Tree(s): ' + str(n_model) + '; {} seconds'.format(elapsed))
    time_list_mse.append(elapsed)

plt.plot(n_model_list, time_list_mse, label='mse')
plt.xlabel('Number of trees')
plt.ylabel('Training time (seconds)')
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

creator: julian-ramos
title: cohen's kappa can't handle single label cases
text:
cohen_kappa_score assumes that the data is going to have multiple labels, although most time's that is the case for training a classifier that may not always be the case for testing, like for example if you are just evaluating a classifier over many datasets and one of them only has one class data. Sure this evaluation is kind of useless but this will happen when running a classifier through unknown datasets where you are trying to estimate classification performance.

Here how the problem could be reproduced:

```
from metrics import cohen_kappa_score
cohen_kappa_score([0,0],[0,0])
```

The above results in a nan, when in reality it should throw an error, or return a 1 with a warning. The one is because after all the classifier we are evaluating in this case predicted perfectly.

@GhivvagoDamas : I don't have a solution, but I have a work-around: 

`if len(set(Annotations1 + Annotations2)) == 1:`

This happens frequently in the inter-coder agreement situation if a given file being annotated is not assigned tags by either annotator.  (At least it does in our case--we assign a default null tag to every token to which an annotator has not assigned a token.)

creator: JointEntropy
title: ParametersGrid parameters combinations representation
text:
**Description**
Trying to define parameter grid for GridSearchCV I collided into a problem of handy representation of all possible combinations of parameters.
List of dictionaries or simple dictionary look rather cumbersome and doesn't provide easy way to aggregate some parameters.
Even taking this [example](http://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/grid_search.html#exhaustive-grid-search) from documentation: 
```
param_grid = [
    {'C': [1, 10, 100, 1000], 'kernel': ['linear']},
    {'C': [1, 10, 100, 1000], 'gamma': [0.001, 0.0001], 'kernel': ['rbf']}
]
```
Why not make the following structure:
param_grid always will be a dictionary. Each key of this dictionary that starts with double underscore means  aggregated parameter, and value besides this key — list of tuples:
- first entry of  tuple - the value of the parameter on which the aggregation was performed
- second entry of tuple - dictionary of parameters allowed with this certain aggregation value.
So same example will look as  follows:
```
 param_grid = {
        'C': [1,10,100,1000],
        '__kernel': 
        [
            ('linear', {}),
            ('rbf', { 'gamma': [0.001, 0.0001] } 
        ]
    }
```
In order to solve the problem of duplication possible values because of  partial intersection,  we also can  combine the collections under the same keys that located  both inside and outside of  some group. Another example(based on example from 'Introduction to ML with Python') might look as follows:
```
# before
param_grid = [
    {'classifier': [SVC()], 'preprocessing': [RobustScaler(),StandardScaler(), None],
    'classifier__gamma': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],
    'classifier__C': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]},
    {'classifier': [LogisticRegression()],
    'preprocessing': [RobustScaler(), None], 'classifier__penalty':['l1','l2']}
]

# after
param_grid = {
    'classifier__C': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100],
    'preprocessing': [RobustScaler(), None],
    '__classifier': [
        (SVC(), { 'classifier__gamma': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]},
             'preprocessing':[StandardScaler()]),
        (LogisticRegression(),{ 'classifier__penalty':['l1','l2'] })
    ]
}
```

creator: jnothman
title: feature_importances_ should be a method in the ideal design
text:
This issue is not meant to be very practical, just a place to share my thoughts.

I believe `feature_importances_` should have been designed as `get_feature_importances()` (which is, perhaps, funny because I think the `get_feature_names` design is pretty broken too), for the following reasons:
* calculating feature importances can be costly, and should not (and is not in some cases) be calculated at `fit` time unnecessary
* there are often multiple ways to calculate feature importances (as simply as choice of norm for `coef_`), and (as long as they depend on the same sufficient statistics) the user may fairly not decide which is appropriate until after `fit`. Thus `get_feature_importances` could have parameters to choose its method. Meta-estimators such as `SelectFromModel` and `RFE` currently have parameters for how they should interpret `coef_` as feature importances, but really these are parameters that should be passed to the linear model's `get_feature_importances`; the model itself should know how to summarise its `coef_`, and doing so gets more complicated once we have multi-output `coef_`.
* it is semantically different from other attributes, not being a sufficient statistic upon which basis the estimator makes predictions

I don't think there is currently sufficient motivation to change, but I could be persuaded.

Ping @kmike?

events.author: kmike
events.comment: I agree with these points. A thing to consider: random forests (and other ensemble methods) may need an access to OOB samples (and thus X and y) for some of the feature importance measures, so get_feature_names may need `get_feature_names(self, method, X=None, y=None, **kwargs)` signature, which complicates the design, as X and y must be the same as used during `fit`.

events.author: amueller
events.comment: I agree with the points as well as with the conclusion of not changing anything now.

events.author: raamana
events.comment:
Somewhat related issue I just ran into is needing uniform access to `feature_importances_` from non-ensemble estimators, such as SVMs. Is this already possible, or something that might be considered in the future?

Context: I am trying to let users of my package https://github.com/raamana/neuropredict choose their estimator. Analyzing feature importance is important for interpretation in neuroimaging. Hence, lacking uniform access or way to compute feature importance for different classifier would be slightly limiting. I can of course implement hacky approaches for few selected classifiers, but I would rather stick to sklearn API/workflow as much as possible.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
What do you intend by feature importances for non-linear svm?

eli5 implements a generic wrapper that computes feature importance using a
data perturbation approach, but you should still expect it to be of limited
relevance for polynomial, RBF, etc decision functions.

events.author: raamana
events.comment: I meant linear SVMs. I agree not all classifiers have a native measure of feature importance. But when they do, it would be good to have uniform access to it e.g. using a method you suggested `estimator.get_feature_importance()`, which may return different types of importance measures (feature weights in case of linear SVMs etc) for different estimators, but there is a clear way to access it.

events.author: kmike
events.comment: @raamana eli5.explain_weights (see https://github.com/TeamHG-Memex/eli5) provides an uniform way to access feature importances for many sklearn (and non-sklearn) estimators. One of its goals is pretty much the same as you've described.

events.author: raamana
events.comment:
Thanks @kmike and Joel - interesting and useful package. I will look into it. Obtaining weights native to the classifier (rather than explaining weights) would suffice for my use case - atleast for now. 

from a very quick reading, it looks like its not a true permutation approach (as in random forests), but a similar idea: http://eli5.readthedocs.io/en/latest/blackbox/permutation_importance.html#algorithm

If its reasonably correlated with RF approach and is much faster, that'd very helpful.

events.author: kmike
events.comment:
The difference between permutation importances implemented in eli5 and permutation importances commonly used for RF is the following: in RF you often have OOB samples out of the box, as a part of training; in general case you don't.

eli5's PermutationImportance doesn't use existing OOB samples for random forests at the moment, so it is less efficient than it could be for RFs, and a bit more tricky. Nothing prevents special RF support from being implemented though.

events.author: kmike
events.comment: `eli5.explain_weights` gets weights native to classifier, figures out feature names, and puts it into an unified object. You can also use `eli5.explain_weights_df(estimator)` to get weights native to an estimator in pandas.DataFrame format.

events.author: raamana
events.comment: Thanks a lot - I will spend more time on learning `eli5`, could be very useful to me for neuropredict.

events.author: raamana
events.comment:
Also, am I correct in thinking the default value for feature_importance in Tree type estimators is zero, and is not configurable by the user? It seems to me that way digging into the code : https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/f3320a6f1ab2d060fd49c94a6e3386291a684ec7/sklearn/tree/_tree.pyx#L1066-L1067

This can interfere with proper interpretation, some features that may never have been selected for training would have a value 0, which has a legitimate meaning for importance. In my applications atleast, I need to be able to distinguish features by their selection frequency (atleast those that never got selected). Any suggestions to achieve it?

A better way to handle this would be set it to `nan`, or allow the user to set it. But this may not be trivial (requiring changes to be propagated in many places).

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
if you're talking about an ensemble not selecting some features for
training, there are other attributes to determine that, no?

events.author: raamana
events.comment:
Not to my knowledge - I don't think so, although I would like to be shown otherwise.

Although being able to establish which features were never selected for training (is helpful), but still does not solve the interpretability issue of importance values being zero - meaning of 0 is ambiguous is here and doesn't convey its true status..

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
feature_importances_ doesn't purport to tell you which features are most
important in a dataset, only which are most important to a model. It is
correct to say that a feature never considered by a model has no importance
to it, and that a feature rejected by a model has no importance to it. yes,
the 0 is ambiguous, but that doesn't mean that feature_importances_ is the
right place to help a user who is looking for more than importance in the
model to disambiguate.

events.author: raamana
events.comment:
I agree with you that feature_importances_ should not more than what its name implies, and what I meant to suggest is think about a way to remove the ambiguity! A good way IMHO is NaN.

Would that be something that might be possible? I can give it a try, but this requires deep changes in  the Tree class itself (which affects many models), so it's important to get it consulted widely.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
but there is only ambiguity if what you want is not what
feature_importance_ measures. Start a new issue clarifying exactly the sort
of enhancement you would like. give an example of the code and desired
output (a test case in essence) so that we can understand your needs. But
the present issue does not pertain.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment: #12326 is another example of needing to configure a norm for the `coef_`, where that configuration needs to be passed through a metaestimator (as in RFE and SelectFromModel also).

events.author: amueller
events.comment:
I'm not sure if having a ``get_feature_importances`` method will solve this.
Unless that function gets a callback somehow?

If I have a generic way to compute feature importances, say permutation importance, how will this be done with ``get_feature_importances``?
Or is that an orthogonal use-case?
Maybe ``SelectFromModel`` was not implementing the right abstraction? I think providing a ``score_func`` here as well might make sense.

It depends on whether the feature importances are model specific or not whether you want the logic to be in the model or not. I think not tightly coupling the model to any specific feature importance method would be good. We did some uncoupling with ``SelectFromModel``. But if we also provided ``abs_coef_importance`` or something like that as a ``score_func``, we would be more flexible.
It would put the burden on how to compute feature importances on the user. This has pros and cons for sure. I wouldn't mind having the user have to think a bit harder about this, though.

It looks to me that we're only using ``feature_importances_`` in ``SelectFromModel`` and ``RFE``.
Right now, RFE doesn't take a ``score_func`` but I don't see why it shouldn't be able to take one (though the univariate ones clearly make no sense).

I think the idea that there's one particular notion of feature importances for, say, random forests, is not a good notion. So I guess my ideal design would be to remove ``feature_importances_`` and not replace it and require the user to explicitly specify a way to calculate importances, say ``gini_importance`` or if we allow strings for convenience ``"gini-importance"``.

events.author: amueller
events.comment: (I made some edits to my last post as it wasn't entirely making sense)

events.author: raamana
events.comment:
You're proposing a solution similar to `eli5` as noted above, which is model agnostic!

I support uniform interface for estimating feature importances, with options to select score function and type of importance etc.

creator: DiegoRomeres
title: Tutorial on how to create a new kernel?
text:
I am trying to implement my own kernel for Gaussian Processes regression.

In order to do so I tried to reproduce the structure of the common kernels in sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels but with no success at the moment. When I try to do regression and optimize the hyperparameters, something like:

    import sklearn
    import my_own_kernel

    k = my_own_kernel(Parameters)
    # GP optimization
    gp = sklearn.gaussian_process(kernel=k, n_restarts_optimizer=0)
    gp.fit(Xtr, Ytr)

I have always a bunch of errors. 
I have looked for a tutorial that explains how to build a new kernel that is compatible with the GP regression routines especially for the optimization of the hyperparameters but I did not find any. Something like [http://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/contributing.html#rolling-your-own-estimator][1] but specific for kernels.

I am wondering if such tutorial exists and I missed it or if there is a reason why it is missing. In case it does not exist can it be made?

If this is not the right place to ask this kind of questions, please, point out where I should write. Thank you in advance for the help.


  [1]: http://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/contributing.html#rolling-your-own-estimator

events.author: jeh0753
events.comment: I made a start on this, but will need someone with more experience building custom kernels to take it from here.

events.author: DiegoRomeres
events.comment:
Thank you @jeh0753  for beginning it. Hopefully other experts will complete it. 
For being a complete tutorial more explanation should be given for each method and examples should be provided.
I think that other methods are mandatory such as:
`__init__() , __call__()`
but also important is that for each method it is explained what are the possible inputs and outputs and the format (also with examples).
Additional information should be provided, such as, how to define the hyperparameters so that they can be optimized by the solver or the dimensions and format required by the sklearn routines that interface with the custom kernel methods.
Finally, often it will be the case the new kernels will not be completely built from scratch but they will inherit an already existing kernel and develop it in some of its aspects. So it would be helpful to understand how to do that.

events.author: wushanyun64
events.comment:
Hi,

I'm not an expert on this either, but I think this page can be a help:
[Link1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/svm/plot_custom_kernel.html)

Basically, there are two ways to create a customized kernel. 

The first method which is shown in the page above is to create a kernel function such as `Kernel(X1,X2)` which takes in two X from the feature space and output a single number which corresponds to an element in the Gram Matrix Kij(Xi,Xj). Then you can simply pass this kernel function to your predictor function such as `clf = svm.SVC(kernel=my_kernel) `

The second way takes one step further, you can "precompute" the whole gram matrix and pass it to the predictor as a whole. see this question for more detials: [Link2](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26962159/how-to-use-a-custom-svm-kernel). I think this method should be more efficient than the first one, but I'm not sure on this part. Any experts here want to elaborate more?

text:

<!-- Instructions For Filing a Bug: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-bugs -->

#### Description
<!-- Example: Joblib Error thrown when calling fit on LatentDirichletAllocation with evaluate_every > 0-->

It looks like PLSRegression is fitting noise really well

I've put together a null dataset simulating of the noise that I'd typically expect out of my dataset.
(See here for [notebook](https://github.com/mortonjt/benchmarkThis/blob/master/ipynb/part10_null_pls.ipynb))

Specifically, I generated the following dataset

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4184797/28706554-ae1052be-7329-11e7-9ac3-c7acc3d75d53.png)

And I get the following PLS fit

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4184797/28706558-b5334b78-7329-11e7-9ddc-52c4a72138f9.png)

Note, that I have tested this on simulated dataset with known signal, and it was able to recover the real signal.  However, it seems like PLSRegression is very prone to overfitting when tested on pure noise.

This is well-known in the literature - so its probably not a problem with the code. events.author: JPFrancoia
events.comment:
Euh, I'm really not sure ```explained_variance_ratio``` should be the same for PCA and LDA.

PCA is unsupervised, LDA is supervised. The principal components are calculated differently since LDA needs a label (y) for each point (that's why ```lda.fit(X, y).transform(X)``` and ```pca.fit(X).transform(X)```).

Since LDA will find different principal components, I see no reason why ```explained_variance_ratio``` should be the same in both cases.

If I'm wrong please let me know, otherwise this issue should be closed because it's not a bug.

events.author: amueller
events.comment: It shouldn't be the same, but I would have expected PCA to have more explained variance since that's what it's optimizing, while LDA has other things it optimizes. But I didn't think deeply about what the ``explained_variance_ratio`` in LDA means. My intuition was that the first principal component should explain more variance than any other direction. But maybe the denominator is different for the two ratios?

events.author: ycpei
events.comment:
Update on 2018-12-07: I was wrong. So please ignore this comment.

I suspect the problem has to do with the fact that each feature is normalised individually before SVD (see [_solve_svd](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/discriminant_analysis.py#L347)):

    X = np.sqrt(fac) * (Xc / std)

This was later "rectified" with the following:

    scalings = (V[:rank] / std).T / S[:rank]

where V and S are calculated using svd

    U, S, V = linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)

I don't think this makes sense mathematically. It produces a different `scalings` from the following:

    X = np.sqrt(fac) * Xc
    U, S, V = linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
    scalings = V[:rank].T / S[:rank]

events.author: YangXiaozhou
events.comment:
> Euh, I'm really not sure `explained_variance_ratio` should be the same for PCA and LDA.
> 
> PCA is unsupervised, LDA is supervised. The principal components are calculated differently since LDA needs a label (y) for each point (that's why `lda.fit(X, y).transform(X)` and `pca.fit(X).transform(X)`).
> 
> Since LDA will find different principal components, I see no reason why `explained_variance_ratio` should be the same in both cases.
> 
> If I'm wrong please let me know, otherwise this issue should be closed because it's not a bug.

Adding on to @JPFrancoia 's comment, there is indeed no reason why the two ratios should be the same since they are computed based on different data. Therefore it might not be a bug.

In particular, while both are ratios of descending eigenvalues against the sum of the eigenvalues,  PCA computes eigenvalues from the entire data set, **X**, while LDA computes those from **W**^{-1}**B**, the multiplication of within-class variance and between-class variance calculated from **X** and **y**. For example, when **X** is fixed, PCA would produce the same eigenvectors and eigenvalues every time, thus the same ratio of variance explained. However, LDA would give different ratios (because of different projection directions found) for different sets of **y** even when **X** is the same.

creator: lmcinnes
title: NN-Descent/KGraph for approximate knn
text:
Efficient approximate kNN-graph construction, and efficient approximate kNN search using such a graph would be of significant potential benefit for scikit-learn. Such methods are independent of data dimension, and support generic similarity measures. The relevant papers, including benchmarks are:

Dong, Wei, Charikar Moses, and Kai Li. "Efficient k-nearest neighbor graph construction for generic similarity measures." Proceedings of the 20th international conference on World wide web. ACM, 2011.

Kiana Hajebi, Yasin Abbasi-Yadkori, Hossein Shahbazi, and Hong Zhang. 2011. Fast approximate nearest-neighbor search with k-nearest neighbor graph. In Proceedings of the Twenty-Second international joint conference on Artificial Intelligence - Volume Volume Two (IJCAI'11), Toby Walsh (Ed.), Vol. Volume Two.

Fu, Cong, Changxu Wang, and Deng Cai. "Fast Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search With Navigating Spreading-out Graphs." arXiv preprint arXiv:1707.00143 (2017).
 
Such methods are implemented by the kGraph library, and perform extremely well in the ANN-benchmarks:

https://github.com/erikbern/ann-benchmarks

The algorithms themselves are fairly straightforward. I have successfully implemented the kNN-graph construction algorithm in around 100 lines of cython (supported code for heaps no included). Performance, even for simple implementations such as mine is still very good. Is there interest in including an implementation of such techniques? If so I would be happy to provide code.

Ping @ogrisel @jnothman

We have classification problem with input state of dimension 1,000,000 (very large).
Current Decision Tree using greedy algorithm, it's impossible to get the optimal tree.

As input of Decision Tree, specify the sub-list of columns(ie feature), we want to use

```
level 0 node:    [0, 1,0,1,0, 1]   (only some columns are evaluated in greedy algorithms)
level 1 node:    [0, 1,0,1,0, 1]   (only some columns are evaluated in greedy algorithms)
```

events.comment:
This sounds very similar to research I did in defining a constraint graph to merge domain knowledge with data to learn large Bayesian networks (unsurprising since Bayesian networks and trees share a great deal of math). I think the correct solution when you're one-hot encoding a massive categorical variable is to implement categorical based splitting in the tree code itself, instead of blowing up your feature set. A primary reason is because if you are learning a RF over this feature set, you are almost certainly going to miss some categories when you subset the columns, misrepresenting the power of the feature. That being said, our categorical split for trees is currently a WIP.

Can you describe your solution a bit more, or link to a paper/reference implementartion I could look at? My understanding is you're defining, at depth 1, features you can split on, then at depth 2 another set of features, and so forth. My confusion comes from how you would (1) actually get this domain knowledge, and (2) how you would know the depth of the tree, unless the final depth you get it can be used for all remaining depths of the tree.

events.comment: I agree with @amueller. It sounds technically possibly, but requiring far more user input than we typically would like for an estimator. If you're finding that it is taking a long time to train your model, a potential solution is to do feature selection beforehand to identify features that are irrelevant, or reduce the dimensionality using something like Gaussian random projections or PCA before fitting your model. A solution that is implemented in xgboost (but not in scikit-learn) is to do histograming on the features to do approximate splits. Alternatively you could consider a simpler model, such as logistic regression, that might be more amenable to a massive number of features.

creator: waltermblair
title: use of Parallel class by OneVsRestClassifier versus BaggingClassifier
text:
#### Description
I'm just getting started looking at performance for SVM, and I found the following code that bags SVM to greatly improve speed. I tried adding in the n_jobs=-1 param for OneVsRestClassifier and for BaggingClassifier, but on my PC as well as a VM I'm using, multiple CPUs are only used in BaggingClassifier while OneVsRestClassifier only uses one. I have a feeling this represents my lack of understanding with the SVC algorithm, and I'd be appreciative of any help you could offer! In the mean time I'll try to get a handle on the SVC algorithm as well as the Parallel class that n_jobs uses
#### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Based on https://stackoverflow.com/questions/31681373/making-svm-run-faster-in-python
```import time
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn import datasets
from sklearn.multiclass import OneVsRestClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC

iris = datasets.load_iris()
X, y = iris.data, iris.target

# Single SVC
X = np.repeat(X, 100, axis=0)
y = np.repeat(y, 100, axis=0)
start = time.time()
clf = OneVsRestClassifier(SVC(kernel='linear', probability=True, class_weight='balanced'), n_jobs=-1)
clf.fit(X, y)
end = time.time()
print "Single SVC", end - start, clf.score(X,y)

# Bagging SVC
n_estimators = 10
start = time.time()
clf = OneVsRestClassifier(BaggingClassifier(SVC(kernel='linear', probability=True, class_weight='balanced'), max_samples=1.0 / n_estimators, n_estimators=n_estimators, n_jobs=-1))
clf.fit(X, y)
end = time.time()
print "Bagging SVC", end - start, clf.score(X,y)
```

#### Expected Results
I expect "Single SVC" and "Bagging  SVC" both to use all my CPUs. 

#### Actual Results
The "Single SVC" code runs on one CPU, and the "Bagging SVC" code runs on all my CPUs. Relatedly, when I try to add n_jobs=-1 to the OneVsRestClassifier of Bagging SVC, I get the warning:

sklearn/ensemble/bagging.py:337:
Multiprocessing-backed parallel loops cannot be nested, setting n_jobs=1

title: KBinsDiscretizer: allow nans
text:
Missing values, represented as NaN, could be treated as a separate category in discretization. This seems much more sensible to me than imputing the missing data then discretizing.

In accordance with recent changes to other preprocessing, NaNs would simply be ignored in calculating `fit` statistics, and would be passed on to the encoder in `transform`. I can't recall if we're handling this sensibly in OneHotEncoder yet...

creator: jnothman
title: KBinsDiscretizer: Automatic determination of number of bins
text:
One small extension to KBinsDiscretizer is to allow the number of bins to be guessed by the estimator, using one of the strategies supported by [`np.histogram`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.histogram.html). We very possibly don't want to implement all of the options, but `fd`, `sturges` and `auto` might be appropriate.

However, I'm not actually sure how useful these estimates are in discretization, when they have been designed for visualisation. So a contribution would be best accompanied by an example that showed that this automatic determination was better for machine learning than a fixed number of bins across all features.

events.author: glevv
events.comment: There is a bunch of methods for calculating number of bins for histogram ([look here](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histogram#Number_of_bins_and_width)). It's easy to implement, but I am not sure about usecases.

events.author: glevv
events.comment:
I tried and don't think it's going to work good. 

Simple example: feature ~ N(0,1) with 10_000 samples. By Scott rule we will have: n_bins = ceil(3.49*1/cbrt(10_000)) = 1. The minimum number of bins is 2. Same thing with Freedman-Diaconis rule. To summarize the problem: it's too sensitive to feature scaling.
Rules that rely only on number of samples like Sturges, Rice, Sqrt are more stable. The difference between Rice and Sqrt is tiny, Sturges rule is the most promising and works somewhat better than previous two, but I am not sure it's enough to add it to KBD.

events.author: jnothman
events.comment:
I think basing it on the number of samples might be better than the current
heuristic of "always use 5 unless the user says otherwise".

events.author: glevv
events.comment:
Agreed.

I can make the changes, it's actually a very small fix.
