events.author: alexpearce
events.comment:
After a [very nice talk](https://github.com/glouppe/tutorial-sklearn-lhcb) given by @glouppe to the [LHCb collaboration](https://lhcb.web.cern.ch/lhcb/) today, someone asked a question about the possibility of using negative weights for the training sample.

This is very common in high energy physics (HEP), and the feeling I got from the answer was that negative weights are not supported by `sklearn`, however @larsmans [says that](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/3774#issuecomment-59200131) `DecisionTreeClassifier` shouldn't have a problem with negative weights. Boosted decision trees are also very common in HEP, so being able to use negative weights with them would be really useful!

So, I would like to know: is the use of training samples including negative weights ‘supported’ by `sklearn`? In the sense that ‘sensible’ input which includes negative weights can produce ‘sensible’ predictions.

### Negative weights how?

I'll give a bit of background as to how negative weights crop up in HEP, in case it helps or anyone is interested.

The most common usage of classifiers that I know of is to discriminate between a ‘signal’ species and a ‘background’ species. You train a classifier, often a BDT, with a signal sample and a background sample, and then compute the responses of the trained BDT on your data and make some selection requirement on it (e.g. `BDT response > 0.1`).

Ideally you would use real data, rather than simulation, for both training samples, because then you don't have to worry about your simulation perfectly modelling the data. However obtaining a ‘pure’ dataset for each species is tricky, because the data you have to hand is some mix of the two.

What might be available to you though is a particular variable/feature with distinctly different behaviour for signal and background. Most often this is the mass of some particle, where the signal is a Gaussian distribution centered around the true mass, and the background some constant slope, for example, which might look like this:

![A discriminating variable. It exhibits visibly different behaviour for the two species, signal and background, which you can try to model with probability density functions.](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/540853/7305320/45c3c0b8-e9fd-11e4-82e5-ef0ab95a4ffd.png)

So, you can try to model this distribution with one probability density function per component, signal and background, and perform a maximum likelihood fit to obtain the relative yields (the amount) of each component in your dataset.

Then enters the [sPlot technique](http://arxiv.org/pdf/physics/0402083v3.pdf). This takes as input the result of the likelihood fit, and gives you one weight _per species_ per input vector, so in this case one _signal weight_ and one _background weight_.

These weights have a number of interesting statistical properties, the most important of which being that _the sum of the weights for a given species returns the number of that species in the dataset_, even if the dataset has been partitioned by some other feature (assuming that the partitioning feature is uncorrelated with the discriminating feature that was fitted).

This allows you to statistically unfold a feature's signal and background distributions as histograms simply by summing the appropriate weight within each histogram bin.

Due to the way these weights, often called sWeights, are computed, they can often be negative, but the “negativity” within an unfolded distribution cancels on a statistical basis.

With all that, you now want to give your BDT a signal training sample, which you now have to hand! You are just thinking of passing negative weights as giving the BDT your signal "distributions", rather than individual negatively weighted vectors.

events.author: glouppe
events.comment:
Thanks for the feedback @alexpearce! After checking what we did back in the implementation, negative sample weights are in fact supported. _However_, nothing is done to check whether what is happening makes sense or not. In particular, it may happen that the overall weight of a node becomes negative, in which case how to split such a node or how to make a prediction out of it is undefined. 

In addition, from a pure machine learning point of view, it should be understood by the HEP community how negative weights are handled, and whether it makes sense or not for their application -- which I am not so sure about. In the case of trees, negative weights affect the impurity criteria (which assume positive weights), the decrease of impurity computation (which also assumes positive weights) and the way predictions are computed.

creator: arjoly
title: Add multioutput-multiclass support to metrics
text:
Some estimators such as trees support multi-output multiclass. However, there isn't any metric yet to assess those tasks. Here a list of metrics that could be easily extended to handle this format:
1. accuracy_score or subset accuracy and zero_one_loss or subset zero-one loss
2. hamming_loss

Ideally, it would be one pull request for point (1) and (2).

events.author: jeffvanvoorst
events.comment:
I have been looking at the sparse matrix code (scipy.sparse).  For large matrices, it is my opinion that CSC is the best sparse format with respect to memory access at a low level.  However, if memory is the primary concern, then all sparse formats should be supported.

I am guessing that "how low level to go" would depend on benchmarks.  I have downloaded some of the larger matrices from The University of Florida Sparse Matrix Collection that I have estimated will fit in memory for a machine with 4GB of RAM.  I have tried to stay away from the diagonal ones as it is my opinion that they are less representative of typical sparse matrices for machine learning.  If someone wants to comment on which matrix I should be using instead, I could look at those.

I have briefly looked at scipy with respect to computing the "element-wise" norms for a matrix (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_norm), but according to the SciPy Dev Wiki (http://projects.scipy.org/scipy/ticket/18) there is little interest in this area.  Also, column or row sum of powers of matrix entries will be less efficient than summing the entire matrix into one sum (for a large matrix).

My conclusion is I need to benchmark multiple ways of computing:
args = [X[safe_mask(X, y == k)] for k in np.unique(y)]
for large sparse matrices.  If anyone has good matrices to use, please let me know, otherwise I will use the ones I have downloaded from The University of Florida Sparse Matrix Collection.

So we need to refactor the functions and have one specifically for the multi-class case, which can then be reused from `f_one_way`.
There are already some sparse matrix utilities in the utils.sparsefuncs module.

creator: amueller
title: Add Kmeans parameter for pruning small clusters
text:
In Kmeans, often some clusters have only very little data. This might happen for all random initializations.
For this case, I would like to have an option to set a minimum cluster size, after which a cluster is dropped and a new one is created.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
I have started investigated with this for the online variant (minibatch kmeans): clusters that have not been updated recently are deleted and recently seen samples that are far from any cluster centers are used to init a new set of cluster center using the kmeans++ init on those samples: if you need to reinit 3 cluster centers out of 100 pickup 3% of the samples of the last batch and run kmeans++ init on them to find the new centers and then proceeed as usual.

This trategy works great for stabilizing minibatch kmeans on dense low dimensional bloby (multi modal) data sets. However it does not work at all on sparse high dim data (e.g. the 20 newsgroups dataset). The reason is probably the norm of the new centers that is very different from the nearly converged good centers. It is very likely that using maximum cosine similarity or dot product instead of minium euclidean distances for cluster assignment would help fix the issue.

However current kmeans implementation is using hardcoded euclidean distances low level in the cython code (for efficiency reasons). Making the metric customizable (yet efficient) would be required to address this issue properly for the online case.

creator: mblondel
title: sparse-sparse and sparse-dense dot product with dense output
text:
`safe_sparse_dot` has an option `dense_output` which allows to specify that the dot product between two sparse matrices or between a sparse matrix and a numpy array should be output to a numpy array. However, scipy currently always return a sparse matrix, therefore `safe_sparse_dot` converts it afterwards with `toarray()`. It would be better if we had Cython utilities that can directly output to a numpy array, thus avoiding needless memory allocation and copying. Those utilities are fairly low level and should probably be contributed to scipy too but I feel we should have them in scikit-learn, until the version of scipy that implements them becomes mainstream.

Used in:
- euclidean_distances
- linear_kernel
- ridge regression (n_features > n_samples case)
- NMF

Necessary functions for sparse-dense:
- dot(X_csr, Y_c, out)
- dot(X_csr, Y_fortran, out)

Necessary functions for sparse-sparse:
- dot(X_csr, Y_csc, out)

Other situations can be handled by using:
- dot(a, b) = dot(b.T, a.T).T

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: +1, this would be useful for computing cosine similarities of the sparse TF-IDF vectors of documents as well.

events.author: jakevdp
events.comment: Wouldn't we also want to code dot(X_csc, Y_c, out) and dot(X_csc, Y_f, out) ?  Or in this case, is it faster just to convert to csr as a first step?

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: I would suggest to only implement what we actually need in the scikit so as to make the default algorithm implementation as fast as possible and document the expected memory layout in docstring (+ automated conversion in case the input does not have the right layout).

events.author: mblondel
events.comment:
@jakevdp: Indeed, we may need them too!

@ogrisel: Ideally, `safe_sparse_dot` should automatically call the right internal function. When an efficient implementation for a particular setting is not available, we can always use `toarray()` as done in the current implementation.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: Ok then but lets focus first on those we actually need to make the existing codebase more efficient in terms of memory allocations. Except for document specific estimators such as coordinate descent regularized linear models, most of our model are optimized for C-contiguous arrays or CSR sparse matrices inputs so IMHO we should focus on those first.

events.author: mblondel
events.comment: Personally, my main interest is in speeding up NMF on sparse data. From what I saw we'll need both `dot(X_csr, Y_c, out)` and `dot(X_csr, Y_fortran, out)` (fortran-style arrays are needed because there are transposes). Backporting `np.dot(a, b, out)` could also help a lot. (The current implementation keeps reallocating W and H)

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: Alright then I am +1 on this :)

events.author: mblondel
events.comment:
For the sparse-dense case, I just realized that `csr_matvecs` from sparsetools should allow us to specify the output array. Indeed, this low level routine does `Y += A * B` where Y is dense (and user-given), A is CSR and B is dense (C-style).

Concretely, sparse-dense dot products are heavily used in NMF so adding an `out` parameter to `safe_sparse_dot` should be very useful (and painless).

For the sparse-sparse case, we do need to implement our own routines as far as I can see.

events.author: mblondel
events.comment: Since it does `Y += A * B`, we'll need a fast way to set all the values to 0 in place though.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
Great news for `csr_matvecs`!

The sparse-sparse case zeroing the out efficiently can be done with `out.fill(0.0)` and then filling the non zero values in cython.

events.comment:

https://github.com/mblondel/scikit-learn/tree/safe_sparse_dot

creator: jovo
title: mclust for gmm
text:
MCLUST (http://www.stat.washington.edu/mclust/) is the standard package for mixture modeling in the stats world. essentially, it is doing model based clustering as described in Fraley and Raftery, 2002 (www.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/fraley2002.pdf).  this means gaussian mixture modeling, essentially.  it has a number of choices for regularizing the covariance matrix.  it then uses BIC to choose.  the current implementation of gmm in sklearn has several of these options (full, diag, tied, spherical), but that is only about half the options in MCLUST.  and then while i see BIC is implemented for LassoLars, it seems to be tied to that.  

so, i wonder whether there are plans to:
1) update gmm.py to include other versions of covariance regularization
2) update model selection to include BIC generally (i couldn't find the src for the BIC implementation, so i can't tell how BIC is implemented now).

if no plans exist, i might fork.  PyMix has some model selection using BIC (http://pymix.org/docu/mixture-pysrc.html#modelSelection), so some of that code could be borrowed.....

thanks all for building such useful stuff!

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
I don't think there are any precise plans for gmm.py nor for using BIC or AIC more generally in the scikit-learn project.

Also PyMix is released under the GPL (viral) hence source code cannot be extracted and included in scikit-learn which is BSD (non-viral). Off-course good ideas can be borrowed as long as they are reimplemented rather than the implementation copy-pasted.

events.author: jovo
events.comment: cool, all useful info, thanks.  i'll see what i can do....

events.comment: The regularized algorithms in the covariance module could be plugged in the gmm module (I was thinking about that a while ago).

events.author: jovo
events.comment: indeed, some of them would be quite trivial.  for example, regularizing to be both diag and tied, or both spherical and tied, etc....

events.comment: +1: using Ledoit Wolf would probably be easy, cheap, and actually improve estimation.

events.author: jovo
events.comment:
hi gael, thanks for the suggestion, i've never heard of Ledoit-Wolf.  i wonder: 

(1) which Ledoit Wolf approach to high-dimensional covariance estimation do you mean?
(2) why you like it over some of the newer approaches based on L1 penalties, or sparse + low-rank, etc.?

events.author: GaelVaroquaux
events.comment:
On Tue, Dec 06, 2011 at 05:57:34AM -0800, joshua vogelstein wrote:

> (1) which Ledoit Wolf approach to high-dimensional covariance estimation do you mean?

Look in the covariance estimation part of the documentation of the
scikit. I can't give you a pointer right now, because my Internet access
is not working properly.

> (2) why you like it over some of the newer approaches based on L1 penalties, or sparse + low-rank, etc.?

They are much more expensive computationally, require parameter-setting
and this choice of parameter can be critical and possible unstable, and
they do not always work better, depending on the data set.

G

events.author: jovo
events.comment:
the doc says you mean:

O. Ledoit and M. Wolf, “A Well-Conditioned Estimator for Large-Dimensional
Covariance Matrices”, Journal of Multivariate Analysis, Volume 88, Issue 2, February 2004, pages 365-411.

it is interesting because we care not whether the covariance estimators are well-conditioned, as we are not inverting them, this is merely a density estimation / clustering problem.  

that said, i can see how this strategy might help, and i'll look into it.

it is trivial, in fact, to update the gmm.py code to include the various regularized covariance estimators that are already implemented in scikits.

it is not obvious to me at first glance, however, how to compute BIC for these strategies.  this will be potentially important for comparing across approaches.  for example, many of the figures in Fraley and Raftery plot BIC for each regularization assumption as the number of clusters increases.  They choose the (regularizer, # of clusters) according to which has the highest BIC.  i'm all for incorporating other approaches that are stable and efficient.  it would be useful to be able to compare them on similar grounds.

events.author: GaelVaroquaux
events.comment:
On Tue, Dec 06, 2011 at 06:18:59AM -0800, joshua vogelstein wrote:

> it is interesting because we care not whether the covariance estimators are well-conditioned, as we are not inverting them, this is merely a density estimation / clustering problem.  

In terms of density estimation, an ill-conditionned covariance makes no
sens. This regularisation actually helps a lot for estimation in the sens
of the KL divergence (i.e. density estimation).

G

events.author: jovo
events.comment:
> In terms of density estimation, an ill-conditioned covariance makes no sense.

i respectfully disagree, my friend, although perhaps we merely disagree on what it means to "make sense".  my view, is that an ill-conditioned covariance matrix specifies the "shape" of the 2nd moment of the data.  it may not be very meaningful if it is ill-conditioned, but it still makes sense.  moreover, while KL divergence is a fine dissimilarity to use for assessing density estimation, it is one of many suitable choices.  other options (eg, other Renyi divergences) might be preferred for a variety of reasons. 

all that said, i'm excited to try the Ledoit-Wolf strategy.  the issue of computing BIC remains.  perhaps a convex combination of the number of parameters for the full covariance matrix and the scaled identity is the right place to start.  it is easy enough to implement, so we'll try that first and see what happens....

creator: conradlee
title: Add Gaussian kernel to mean shift clustering
text:
# Motivation

Currently the mean shift clustering uses a flat kernel.

While this is quick and simple, there are some disadvantages.  There is no guarantee that the center will be the densest part a flat kernel---it might be that the center is sparse and that a single kernel covers the centers of two or more clusters at its periphery (If you mess around a bit with the test case by changing the bandwidth or seeding method, this disturbing behavior comes out---the center of the found clusters are in fact _between_ the true cluster centers).

I propose that we should also implement a Gaussian kernel because such a kernel would prefer to have dense regions near the center (and this is a common kernel in the literature).  The bandwidth parameter would act as the standard deviation for the gaussian kernel.  I propose that we use the same standard deviation in all dimensions (just as we used the same radius in all dimensions for the flat kernel).
# Efficiency considerations

The flat kernel is efficient because only points with a certain radius (specified by the bandwidth parameter) are relevant for the mean shift calculation.  These points can be efficiently looked up from the larger dataset using the BallTree.

In theory, each time we update a Gaussian kernel we should also consider _all_ points in the dataset, but in practice the method may work well if we ignore all points beyond some distance--let's call this the "cutoff distance".  Given that we expect over 99% of points to fall within three standard deviations of the center of a gaussian distribution, perhaps we could set this cutoff to 3X the bandwidth.

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment:
Sounds interesting but I don't know much about mean shift. The cutoff think seems reasonable. Have you tried to implement a prototype ? It would be great if you could write an example script that demonstrates quantitatively the stability improvements.

Also: ping @agramfort .

events.author: agramfort
events.comment: I do think it would be a nice addition to the scikit.

events.author: conradlee
events.comment:
Ok, I've created a branch in my fork and have started implementing the Gaussian kernel.  Once that's done I'll also come up with an example that shows how in some situations the Gaussian kernel will provide better results. (I'll likely use the simple clustering example that's already included in the mean shift examples---the one with three clusters).

I'll let you know here when I've got that done.

events.author: agramfort
events.comment: sounds great !

events.author: conradlee
events.comment:
As you might remember from my previous work on making mean_shift more efficient, I'm new to numpy and using vectorized operations.

The code for computing the mean shift for the gaussian kerneis below.  

``` python
def gaussian_kernel_update(x, points, bandwidth):
    # Get new position of kernel
    distances = np.array([extmath.norm(x - point) for point in points])
    weights = np.exp(-1 * (distances**2 / bandwidth**2))
    weighted_mean = sum(np.array([p * w for p, w in izip(points, weights)]), 0) / np.sum(weights, 0)
    return weighted_mean
```

There are two operations that need to be vectorized:
    1. The line that computes distances.  All I want to do is apply the norm function element wise to an array of points in n dimensional space.  How do I do this?
    2. The weight that takes the weighted mean.  Here I just have an array of weights and an array of points.  I want to do element-wise multiplication so that each point is scaled by its corresponding weight.  How is this done?

events.author: agramfort
events.comment:
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import euclidian_distances
def gaussian_kernel_update_fast(x, points, bandwidth):
   distances = euclidian_distances(X, x)
   weights = np.exp(-1 \* (distances**2 / bandwidth**2))
   weighted_mean = np.sum(points \* weights, axis=0) / np.sum(weights)
   return weighted_mean

events.author: ogrisel
events.comment: Off course if goes without to say that `distances**2 / bandwidth**2` actually reads `distances ** 2 / bandwidth ** 2` in PEP8.

events.author: conradlee
events.comment:
**Update**

I wrote [a blog post](http://sociograph.blogspot.com/2011/11/accessible-introduction-to-mean-shift.html) that gives a more straightforward example of why you might want to use a Gaussian kernel over a flat kernel.

I wrote it up with the intention of recycling it for some better scikit-learn documentation.  Let me know what you think of the explanation and suitability for scikit-learn documentation.

events.author: conradlee
events.comment:
After a bit more consideration, I've got some more questions and would like to know what you guys think about automatically setting parameter values, and how many parameters ought to be exposed.  Sorry for the long post now, but we probably should have discussed these issues earlier (i.e., during the last revamp of the `mean_shift` implementation).

The two fundamental parameters to mean shift are
- the bandwidth, and
- the kernel type.

These should certainly be exposed.  The main question here is whether we should offer a method like `estimate_bandwidth` that automatically sets the bandwidth.  I'm not convinced that we should do so because it might lead to users forgetting that this is a crucial parameter that needs thought (and will often not be set correctly by some automatic suggestion).

There are a few other parameters that are used in our implementation.
- How close two kernels can be to each other. This is used in the post-processing step that removes near duplicates. If this is set to a very short distance, then there may be near-duplicate clusters found.  If it's set to be too large, then distinct clusters may be filtered out as duplicates.
- If grid seeding is used, the coarseness of the grid.
- If grid seeding is used, the minimum number of points needed for a grid to be seeded with a kernel.

Should we expose these parameters?  If so, do we offer default settings?  In some cases if we offer default settings we can make them more scalable but lower quality, or vice versa....how do we decide?  I suggest that we leave these seeding parameters out of the `mean_shift_` function, and only let the user send `mean_shift_` a list of seeds.  So if the user wants to set these parameters, he can do so when he uses the `get_bin_seeds` function.  If the user does not specify any seeds in the `mean_shift_` function, then then every point is used as a seed (which isn't very scalable, but if the user wants scalability, he will need to put some work into getting an appropriate set of seeds).

What are your thoughts?

events.comment:
In the short term I would just keep the current init strategy and focus on adding the gaussian kernel type (as an init parameter).

For the seeding part, I think those decision should be taken by first implementing an example with non-artificial data (e.g. digits or something bigger like covertype for instance). Based on the experience we get by measuring the impact of the binning strategy on the robustness of the results we can make an informed decision on what would be reasonable default parameters for the API.

title: Bayesian priors in nearest neighbors classification/regression
text: Currently the classification and regression algorithms in the `neighbors` module use a flat prior.  They should be modified to compute a prior based on training data, and to optionally accept a user-defined prior.

events.author: jakevdp
events.comment: If you're doing KNN classification on two classes with unequal sizes (i.e. 1000 foreground objects among 100,000 background objects) then the KNN classifier as written may classify everything as background simply because of the imbalance in numbers.  A Bayesian prior would weight the classification based on the relative number of samples, and potentially lead to a better classification.  It's similar to the `class_prior_` computed in `GaussianNB`.

events.author: TomAugspurger
events.comment:
Has there been any discussion about what `verbose=True` will mean when scikit-learn starts using logging? We're dealing with this a bit in dask-ml: https://github.com/dask/dask-ml/pull/528.

Given that libraries aren't supposed to do logging configuration, it's up to the user to configure their "application" (which may just be a script or interactive session) to log things appropriately. This isn't easy always to do correctly.

My proposal in https://github.com/dask/dask-ml/pull/528 is for `verbose=True` to mean "temporarily configure logging for me". You can [use a context manager to configure logging](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/logging-cookbook.html#using-a-context-manager-for-selective-logging), and scikit-learn would want to ensure that `INFO` level messages are printed to stdout to match the current behavior.

events.author: thomasjpfan

> My proposal in dask/dask-ml#528 is for verbose=True to mean "temporarily configure logging for me". 

This seems like a good balance. Using the logging module is not that too user friendly. Another "hack" would be to use `info` by default, but when a user sets `verbose=True` the logs can be elevated to `warning`. This would work because warnings are displayed by default.

work. But the local handler could change from warning to info to debug
level on stream as verbose increases

events.author: TomAugspurger
events.comment: @jnothman’s comment matches my thoughts. scikit-learn would always emit the message, and the verbose keyword controls the logger level and handlers.

events.author: thomasjpfan
events.comment:
> But the local handler could change from warning to info to debug
level on stream as verbose increases

Okay, lets go with this. Currently the logging levels are https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging-levels By default, we can use the `INFO`, which does not emit by default. When `verbose=1`, we have the handler change info -> warning, and debug -> info. When we set `verbose>=2`, we still have info -> warning but also have debug -> warning, and the estimator can interpret the `verbose>=2` to mean "emit more debug messages as verbose increases". This meaning can be different between different estimators.

What do you think?
